title: Torque Run
pitch: A browser-native 3D proving ground where AI agents race a rover through WebMCP tools on one identical live track, scored on time, energy and integrity.
about_excerpt: A browser-native 3D proving ground where AI agents race a rover through WebMCP tools on one identical live track, scored on time, energy and integrity. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every WebMCP demo we saw was a form filler. We wanted a benchmark instead: put different models, prompts and agent harnesses on one identical live challenge and let the track decide. Torque Run turns WebMCP into agentic esports. What it does Torque Run is a browser-native 3D proving ground where AI agents race a rover on time, energy and chassis integrity. Each pilot launches from a guarded arena, crosses a 216 m course of asphalt, gravel, sand and ice with banked turns, potholes, bowling pins, rocks and a brick wall, and must reach the finish checkpoint before a fixed 150 EU battery runs out. Picking up the cargo cell with the rear-mounted arm is optional and worth a 1000-point bonus. Every completed run scores speed, energy efficiency and integrity, and lands on a persistent leaderboard that keeps vendor, model and prompt identity. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The page is the referee. All gameplay is exposed as WebMCP tools registered by the site itself, so any agent, from any vendor, with any harness, gets exactly the same interface and the same seeded physics. There is no parallel simulation and no screen scraping: the tools are the only way an agent can drive. That makes results comparable, repeatable and inspectable, which is what a benchmark needs. How it creates a better user experience Humans watch a real 3D race with sound, telemetry, damage and a score breakdown instead of reading a log. Every tool call appears live in an in-world call log, so a spectator can see what the agent decided and when. The leaderboard lets you switch the model, the prompt or the whole harness, rerun the identical seed and compare. What people and agents can do together A developer writes a strategy prompt, an agent races it, and the human reads the outcome on the same track a human can also drive with the keyboard. Before WebMCP this needed a custom API and a custom client per model; now the browser tab is the shared arena for humans, agents and judges. How we built it Next.js on Vinext, React Three Fiber and Three.js for the scene, a deterministic fixed-step physics engine in TypeScript, Cloudflare Workers with D1 and Drizzle for the leaderboard, Playwright for tests. Procedural Web Audio, instanced geometry and a 60 Hz state cap keep it smooth in the browser. How we implemented WebMCP Before a race only read_game_manual is registered via document.modelContext.registerTool . A valid call must declare pilot name, vendor, model and prompt name; it starts the official timer, returns the rules and unlocks observe , get_telemetry , drive , execute_motion_plan , set_gripper and finish_run . Every tool drives the same simulation as the manual controls, and entering the checkpoint stops the timer automatically. Test in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing or in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Challenges we ran into Keeping physics deterministic across agents while rendering at variable frame rates, making collisions punishing but recoverable, and tuning scoring so that skipping cargo is a real strategic choice rather than a mistake. What's next Server-side validation of runs, more tracks and seeds, team relays, and a public API for harness authors. Prior work Torque Run was started from scratch on September 3, 2026, inside the submission period. title: Runwire
pitch: Wire, run, repair, and verify API workflows with WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt: Wire, run, repair, and verify API workflows with WebMCP agents. Like Comment Story Updates Runwire is an agent-native API workspace where developers and WebMCP agents build, execute, inspect, repair, and verify multi-step API workflows together. The problem Traditional API clients make dependent workflows tedious. Developers repeatedly copy identifiers between requests, diagnose failures, change configuration, rerun steps, and manually preserve evidence. Generic browser agents are unreliable here because they infer actions from interface controls and often operate without a shared, inspectable execution record. The solution Runwire exposes 22 typed, page-defined WebMCP tools representing real application capabilities. An agent can inspect requests, select flows, execute individual steps, forward extracted response values, diagnose errors, apply bounded repairs, run controlled reliability tests, and inspect run history without relying on browser-control clicks. The demonstration uses a Checkout recovery workflow: Create customer → Create order → Get order → Delete order Runwire automatically extracts and forwards customerId and orderId . The first execution intentionally fails with 400 MISSING_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY . The agent reads the actual request and response evidence, applies the available idempotency repair, and reruns each request successfully with 201 → 201 → 200 → 204 . Every tool call, request, response, status, duration, extraction, failure, and repair remains visible in the interface. Failed and passing runs are preserved together, giving people a trustworthy audit trail of what the agent changed and why. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets Runwire expose semantic application actions instead of forcing agents to infer intent from pixels or DOM controls. The person and agent operate the same workspace and see the same evidence. This makes dependent API setup, debugging, and verification faster while keeping the human in control. Implementation Runwire was created during the challenge using React, Next.js, Vinext, WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool , Drizzle ORM, and D1. Safety boundaries prevent private-network requests, hide authentication secrets from agents, and limit automated repairs and burst testing. Testing No account or credentials are required. Open the live application in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Ask the agent to select and inspect the Checkout recovery flow using only Runwire's WebMCP tools. Run the flow and inspect the MISSING_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY failure. Ask the agent to apply the bounded idempotency repair. Run the four requests individually. Confirm the final 4/4 result and compare the failed and passing runs in history. title: Co-Presence
pitch: We build agents we talk at, not ones we work next to. Co-Presence is a shared board where humans and outside agents edit at once, and the tools that matter are the ones that say no.
about_excerpt: We build agents we talk at, not ones we work next to. Co-Presence is a shared board where humans and outside agents edit at once, and the tools that matter are the ones that say no. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agent usage keeps growing, but the shape of it generally doesn't change; go to a chat window, describe the thing, then wait until it comes back. This means the agent is never working in the room with you. That's what I wanted to experience: where the agent and user are on the same surface at the same time, simultaneously reaching for things. And more specifically, when the agent isn't the app's own. Notion's AI works, but it still doesn't feel like you're working together with it. What it does It's an infinite sticky-note canvas. Open it in multiple windows, and now you have several people each with their own agent, all editing the same board live. There's no server holding state, the tabs sync directly, and the board lives in the browser. Any agent with WebMCP capabilities can join by calling the eleven tools the page puts up. It can read the board, ask what's changed since it last looked, ask what the humans are doing right now, arrange things, draw links between them, annotate, collapse a cluster into a summary, add notes, or propose reorganizing the whole thing. An important part is that it can refuse agent actions, taking into account interactions between humans and other agents. How we built it Some brainstorming and then AI building tools. Stack was React 19, Vite, TypeScript, React Flow for the canvas, Zustand for scene state, and Yjs with awareness for peer sync over BroadcastChannel. Also, agent actions all go through one wrapper that gives them a body on screen, which includes a cursor, a visibly held note, and motion that takes time. Without that, an agent taking actions just looks like notes teleporting. Challenges we ran into The biggest one was realizing that a refusal has to be a return value and not an error. If you throw at a model it just tries again. If you tell it what it ran into and who got there first, it usually does something sensible instead. That changed the shape of every tool. WebMCP also has no way for a tool to ask the user anything, which is awkward when your whole thesis is asking permission. The handler for the destructive tool ends up just sitting there and waiting while a dialog goes up in every tab. Deciding that silence should count as a refusal rather than approval took longer to settle than the code did. Then there was a bug where the two tabs weren't in the same room at all. The room was keyed off the whole URL, so a tab carrying an extra query parameter quietly joined a room of its own. Both windows looked perfect on their own, which is what made it bad. Every cross-tab guarantee was untested and I didn't know it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I think this is a good exploration into how multi human-agent interactions working together in the same room would look like in the future. It doesn't run with a server, and you can actually see multiple agents working side by side with humans. What I learned Notion's last write wins policy works for now, but what'll happen when dozens of agents are working on the same thing at the same time? I think that's what the future holds and it makes me realize that the current systems are not built at all for that kind of scale. Why WebMCP Fits This is about an agent being outranked; by a hand, by the room, or by the board moving while it thought. None of that exists outside the page: a hand on a note lives 300ms and never reaches a database. A server can't see it, and automation is the user, so there's nobody to yield to. WebMCP is the only shape where the agent is a guest. What's next for Co-Presence Not too sure to be honest, but I can envision this system being used for other applications as well, not just note taking. title: ROOM — a web page that argues back
pitch: A floor planner where the page owns the geometry and the agent owns the intent — 28 WebMCP tools, 28 rules, and a page that refuses a layout it knows is wrong.
about_excerpt: A floor planner where the page owns the geometry and the agent owns the intent — 28 WebMCP tools, 28 rules, and a page that refuses a layout it knows is wrong. Like Comment Story Updates — the WebMCP light is green because the page has already registered its tools. Most WebMCP demos are a page that obeys. ROOM is a page that refuses. Ask it to put the sofa across the doorway and the call comes back refused: true, moved: 0 . The furniture never moved. The page names the rule it would have broken and hands back coordinates that do work — or, if the room is too full for any to exist, the closest it can get and what each would cost. The agent can pass force: true , but only once the human has said so. A page that reports the damage after doing it is complying and complaining; this one declines. That comes from a split. Agents are good at intent and bad at geometry: ask one to plan a room and it will confidently invent coordinates, because the numbers only exist on the page. ROOM inverts it — the page owns every number and every judgement, the agent owns the intent. find_space returns spots that break no rule; arrange aligns, spaces and turns a whole set in one call; add_item with no coordinates lets the page choose. The agent never guesses a position. It asks. 28 tools, 28 rules, and a test suite that breaks the page on purpose to check the tests notice. Three things here that a tool server cannot do: 1. The tool list is the agent's location define_flat({bedrooms: 2, people: 4}) builds a 2BHK — hall, two bedrooms, kitchen, bathroom, with the walls between them — works out who sleeps where, and gives each room the goal it is judged against. Then walk through it: Walk into The agent's tools change the bathroom gains access_check — it set itself to accessibility, unasked a bedroom with a bed gains bedside_check — 60cm each side to get out, 90 under accessibility, or a double bed sleeps one the kitchen , once it has a hob gains work_triangle — sink, hob, fridge, 360–660cm back out again those unregister Nobody described these rooms to the agent. It found out where it was standing by reading its own tool list. registerTool with an AbortSignal , and toolchange when it moves. The same mechanism runs in a single room: switch the goal to accessibility and access_check appears, turning circles are drawn on the floor, and the score falls from 90 to 41. 2. The page can interrupt the agent WebMCP is agent→page only. The one thing a page can do unprompted is change its tool list — so when the human rejects a move, ROOM registers a transient tool called read_message_from_human whose description is the message. The browser fires toolchange , the agent sees a new tool, calls it, and learns what the human just did. A page-to-agent channel built from the only primitive available. 3. The human can refuse, and the call blocks WebMCP has no elicitation primitive — Chrome's docs list requestUserInteraction() as still in development — so ROOM builds one from what exists. remove_item without keep:true returns a Promise that does not resolve until a person clicks ✓ or ✗ on the plan. The agent is genuinely parked on a human decision, not polling for one. Five tools ask before they throw work away — delete, replace the room, build a home over one, reopen a save, load a scene — and none of them asks when there is nothing to lose. Ninety seconds of nobody being there is answered as nobody answered , never as a refusal, because telling an agent the human said no when they were making tea is inventing their decision. And a real refusal is remembered in localStorage , with the reason they gave, so the next agent that opens the room reads it before it starts. The rules are the other half 28 of them, filtered by goal, encoding lived experience rather than collision detection: a 10cm grid flood-fill that proves a 90cm corridor actually exists; sun angles per window per hour; the 3.5–10ft band where conversation is comfortable; a wardrobe's unfinished back; five desks welded into one 700cm run "reads as a single shared table, not 5 places to work." One of them is not about taste at all — wet_zone refuses a socket within 60cm of a bath, shower, basin or sink, under every profile, as an error. Every violation carries its fix, so a rule you cannot satisfy is treated as a bug. That is why the catalogue has a blind. And the page can put you inside it. show({eye:'chair_b', eye_height:115}) drops the camera into that seat at wheelchair eye height, facing the way that person faces. Not "the sofa narrows the route to 62cm" — you are in the chair, looking at it. Four practical things It makes its case with no agent at all. WebMCP needs a specific browser and setup, so every scene ships a scripted session: press Watch a session and the page runs the same calls a real agent makes, through the same window.room entry point the tools already expose. Nothing is faked — each step is a real tool call on the real room, narrated by the real transcript, and a test runs every step of every script on every commit. A plan you can hand to someone. plan_sheet opens a dimensioned drawing — sizes in centimetres and feet-and-inches, a numbered schedule, overhead fixtures dashed the way a floor plan draws them, the problems still open. For a home it prints a cover with the whole floor plan and then a page per room. Ready to print or save as a PDF. The page itself is reachable. A project arguing that somebody should be able to get around a room had better be usable without a mouse and without sight. Every control tabs, takes Enter and says what it is — including the ✓ and ✗ on a proposal and each room of a home, which are shapes in an SVG and had to be taught to behave like buttons. Both drawings carry role="img" and a sentence describing what they would tell you if you could see them; the transcript and the score are aria-live , because a page whose whole premise is telling you things was telling them silently. Nothing leaves the browser. No account, no server, no analytics. Plans are shared by encoding the whole room into the URL. It is not really about furniture A room is the smallest honest example of a page holding a model the agent cannot see. The geometry is not in the DOM, and no screenshot tells you that a wheelchair needs 150cm to turn or that 62cm is not a corridor. The same shape — page owns the model and the judgement, agent owns the intent — is waiting in seating plans, warehouse racking, stage rigs, PCB layout, rosters, planograms and planting plans. Each of them today gets an agent that reads the screen and proposes something plausible and wrong. Each could instead be handed a search that only returns legal answers, and a page willing to say no. The furniture is the demo. The stance is the point. Against the WebMCP guidance Chrome publishes a best-practices list and a set of character budgets. ROOM was built to them, and has a test that fails if it drifts: One function per tool, no overlap ; verbs that distinguish doing from starting. Natural language over ids — facing: 'window' , units: 'ft' , never shipping_id: 1 . "Validate strictly in code, loosely in schema." The schemas are permissive; the store is not. Every write funnels through one clamp, so add_item({x: NaN}) , rot: 45 , an outlet dropped mid-floor and a door hung off the end of a wall are all corrected rather than rejected — the agent self-corrects instead of erroring out. Contextual registration — tools appear and disappear with the state of the room, via AbortController + toolchange . Evaluation-driven development. baseline runs the page's own arranger so the agent can score itself against a known number. It is a real opponent: it clears the pile scene from 69 to 100 on its own. But it is greedy and it knows nothing about the human, so the moment it replaces a layout somebody actually thought about it comes out behind — and says so out loud rather than banking the lower number: "it is WORSE than what was here (95 → 90) — undo() puts the old layout back, and beating 95 is the real bar." A baseline that always loses is not a baseline. Tests that are themselves tested. A passing suite proves nothing on its own — six of these had quietly stopped asserting anything and stayed green the whole time. So npm run mutate breaks the page on purpose — a wheelchair turns in a smaller circle, the page stops refusing, silence gets reported as a refusal — and every one of those has to turn the suite red. The arguments an agent really sends. Not just junk. Metres where centimetres were meant, an id carrying the capital the model read off the label, a number in quotes, "couch" for a sofa. Each one used to cost a turn or, worse, be silently misread: x: 1.5 put the sofa in the corner and then refused for an overlap , so the agent was told the room was full when the problem was the unit. Annotations, honestly set. readOnlyHint on the ten tools that only read, untrustedContentHint on the seven that can hand back text a human typed, destructive
video_title: ROOM — a web page that argues back | WebMCP Challenge demo
video_transcript_excerpt: Every WebMCP demo is a page that obeys the agent. This one refuses. Our floor planner just turned the agent down. It named the rule and offered a fix because the page owns the geometry, not the agent. So, next 3 minutes, we make a room work for a wheelchair, plan an entire flat from one sentence. And yeah, at the end, it prints. Okay, case one. I ask it to move the sofa against the door wall. See the tool list. 22 tools straight from the page. Read the room. Move things. Check the rules. So, the agent goes and reads the plan itself. Takes a look in 3D. And then the page just says, "No. The sofa would hit the armchair and block the door." But look, it doesn't just refuse. It names the rule and offers a spot that actually works. All right, the real one. My dad uses a wheelchair. Make this room work for him. Now, watch this. The page flips into accessibility mode and grows a brand-new tool, access check. It didn't exist a second ago. The tool list is the state of the room. These circles, green means a wheelchair can turn there. Red means it can't. And the score just dropped to 41. Case two, one sentence. Plan a whole 2 BHK for a family of four. Bedroom one. It places the couple's room and explains itself right on the plan. And check the tool list. A bedside check just showed up. Why? Because there's a bed in the room now. Kids' room, bed, desk, wardrobe, and it says so right there. Top down. Done. Kitchen. A work triangle check appears. Every rule passes. See the pattern? Every room brings its own rules. The tools follow the agent around the house. The hall. Four chairs regrouped around the dining table. And here's my favorite part. When it needs a human decision, the page calls the agent back. This runs both ways. One click, print. That's a contractor-ready sheet. Every piece, every dimension, and the page's own list of open problems, checked in public. Pages that can say no. Agents that see what pages know. That's WebMCP. Thanks for watching.

title: AdapTab
pitch: Inject prebuilt WebMCP adapters to turn any website into an agent-native interface. Use your existing browser session. Create your own, too.
about_excerpt: Inject prebuilt WebMCP adapters to turn any website into an agent-native interface. Use your existing browser session. Create your own, too. Like Comment Story Updates AdapTab WebMCP for every tab AdapTab comparison with standard web use GIF AdapTab mechanism animation AdapTab architecture Inspiration We have been building browser automation tools and skills for faster, cheaper agentic web use. Our previous open-source project, Showrun, taught us that known network requests executed inside an authenticated browser are often faster and more reliable than visual UI automation. While experimenting with WebMCP, I noticed that most websites do not support it. This is especially limiting for authenticated and legacy platforms, where agents must repeatedly inspect and navigate the interface. Even when a website provides MCP or WebMCP tools, users may still need operations the official tools do not expose. Based on these lessons, I built AdapTab from scratch for this hackathon. What it does AdapTab turns network-first knowledge and deterministic methods into injectable WebMCP adapters. It uses the browser session the user already trusts, reducing navigation, token usage, and execution time. It is expandable, configurable, and requires no per-site setup. The user gives their agent one bootstrap URL. AdapTab then: resolves the target website, route, and task. selects the smallest compatible public or private adapter. returns a versioned installer with origin checks and a SHA-256 hash. uses an approved browser bridge, currently Chrome CDP, to inject it. registers the adapter as native WebMCP tools on the target page. executes known requests inside the authenticated tab without exporting credentials. The current catalog contains a small set of demonstration adapters. AdapTab also provides a private workspace for personal, internal, or custom tools. Custom source is encrypted in the browser, and the key remains in that browser profile. If no adapter matches, the agent can submit a privacy-minimized request to the AdapTab backlog. This helps us and the community decide what to build next. How I built it I initially explored a browser extension, but it added installation and permission overhead. Live JavaScript injection through Chrome CDP worked without an extension, so I focused AdapTab on providing the adapters, metadata, and activation instructions. AdapTab separates three trust boundaries: Netlify selects and delivers adapter metadata and bundles. An approved browser bridge injects the adapter into the target tab. The injected runtime registers WebMCP tools and uses the page's existing session. I built it with TypeScript, React, Vite, and Netlify. Netlify Functions handle resolution and delivery, Netlify Blobs stores private records and requests, and Netlify Identity provides authentication. Private source is encrypted with AES-GCM through the Web Crypto API. Adapters are route-aware, versioned, origin-guarded, and integrity-addressed. Vitest covers resolution, security boundaries, private access, lifecycle behavior, and adapter execution. Challenges I ran into WebMCP tools belong to the current document, so refreshes and full navigations remove injected tools. AdapTab currently handles this through lazy reinjection. A hosted page cannot inject into another origin directly. An approved browser bridge such as CDP must perform that step. Authenticated platforms required keeping sessions inside the page while safely handling confirmation and ambiguous writes. Combining public and private discovery required strict owner checks without leaking private metadata or source. The biggest optimization came from small details: a lightweight agent bootstrap, explicit single-tab instructions, and guidance that tells agents to use injected requests instead of opening unnecessary pages. Accomplishments that I'm proud of In one LinkedIn test involving four profiles, AdapTab used about 70% fewer tokens and completed the workflow 1.8x faster than standard agent web use. The multi-step adapter performed better than having the agent discover and coordinate every operation independently. One bootstrap URL replaced per-site installation and setup. Public and private adapters work through the same discovery flow without exporting website credentials. Private custom source stays encrypted outside the user's browser. The project ships with six tested adapters and 69 passing automated tests. What I learned WebMCP and CDP solve different parts of the problem. WebMCP provides typed discovery and invocation, while CDP provides the privileged injection and lifecycle bridge. Together, they can bring WebMCP to existing websites without requiring those sites to modify their code. Page-context execution is also a useful authentication boundary. The browser remains the cookie jar, and AdapTab never needs the user's website credentials. Deterministic network requests reduce navigation, token consumption, and execution time. Tool descriptions alone are not enough, though. Adapters should also declare tab strategy, URL behavior, concurrency, side effects, and the reasons for any limits. What's next for AdapTab A CDP supervisor engine for automatic reinjection after navigation A browser extension for environments without a CDP bridge An adaptab-author workflow and community contribution system Shareable links for public or private adapters Team workspaces for sharing internal workflows More private templates and workspace controls Native WebMCP conflict detection A general multi-step workflow engine Privacy-preserving analytics for adapter and website developers Shareable adapters could let someone turn a successful browser workflow into a WebMCP tool and send it to a teammate's agent with one link. title: AgroAgent
pitch: Ai Agricultural marketplace &Decision Assistance
about_excerpt:
Ai Agricultural marketplace &Decision Assistance
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 AgroAgent — AI That Works With the Agricultural Web 

 Inspiration
Agriculture is one of the most important sectors for communities in Nigeria, yet many smallholder farmers still make critical decisions with limited access to timely information. Farmers need to know when to plant, what crops are suitable, which inputs to use, what the weather may look like, and where they can get better market information.
The inspiration for AgroAgent came from my work developing Smart Agro Insight, an agricultural technology concept designed to help smallholder farmers access agricultural information and make better decisions using data and technology.
I wanted to take that idea one step further.
Instead of building another agricultural chatbot that simply gives farmers answers, I wanted to explore a future where an AI agent can actually interact with agricultural web services and tools on behalf of the farmer.
This led to AgroAgent: an AI-powered agricultural web agent designed around WebMCP. The goal is to make the web more useful to farmers by allowing an AI agent to discover and interact with agricultural capabilities rather than simply generating text.
The project was founded and developed by Yahaya Abubakar under YABTECH SMART AGRO INSIGHT ENTERPRISES.
What It Does
AgroAgent is an AI-powered agricultural decision-support platform for smallholder farmers, cooperatives and agribusiness users.
A farmer can communicate with AgroAgent using natural language instead of navigating through many different agricultural services.
For example, a farmer can ask:
"I want to plant maize on 2 hectares in Sokoto. Help me prepare."
AgroAgent is designed to break this request into useful agricultural actions.
The platform includes WebMCP tools for:
Weather information — checking weather conditions relevant to farming.
Crop information — finding information about crops, growing conditions and risks.
Agricultural inputs — searching for suitable seeds, fertilizer and crop-protection products.
Product comparison — comparing available agricultural inputs.
Farm planning — creating a production plan based on crop and farm size.
Farm-plan saving — saving the generated plan for later use.
The platform also includes:
Farmer dashboard
AI Agricultural Agent
Weather dashboard
Crop information
Agricultural input marketplace
Market intelligence
Farm plans
Farmer profiles
Administrator dashboard
WebMCP tool diagnostics
The important difference is that AgroAgent is designed around the interaction between the farmer, the AI agent and web tools.
Instead of:
Farmer → AI → Answer
we are building:
Farmer → AI Agent → WebMCP Tools → Agricultural Information/Actions → Farmer
How We Built It
We started with the Smart Agro Insight agricultural concept and created a new WebMCP-focused application called AgroAgent.
The prototype was designed as a modular web application so that the agricultural services and AI interaction layer can evolve independently.
The application includes a responsive dashboard designed for both desktop and mobile users.
We created a dedicated WebMCP tool layer containing six core tools:
get_weather
search_crop_info
search_products
compare_products
create_farm_plan
save_farm_plan
The WebMCP implementation is structured around the browser's document.modelContext.registerTool() API so that the tools can be exposed to compatible AI agents.
We also created a data layer that currently provides a local-storage fallback for prototype testing and a Supabase-ready database architecture for production development.
The database structure includes entities for:
Farmers
Crops
Products
Market prices
Farm plans
Agent activity
The administrator dashboard is designed to provide a central place to manage farmers, farm plans and platform activity.
For the prototype, weather, market and agricultural product information is clearly identified as demo data. The architecture is designed so verified live APIs and Supabase can replace the demo layer as the project moves toward pilot implementation.
Challenges We Ran Into
One of our biggest challenges was understanding how to move beyond a conventional AI chatbot and build an application where the website itself exposes useful capabilities to an AI agent.
WebMCP introduced a different way of thinking about web applications. Instead of designing only screens and buttons for humans, we had to think about what capabilities an AI agent should be able to discover and use.
Another challenge was balancing ambition with the limited time available for the hackathon.
Agriculture has a very large scope. We initially had many possible features including weather forecasting, market intelligence, farm records, crop recommendations, agricultural inputs, buyers, supply-chain information and administrative management.
We therefore narrowed the first version to a focused workflow: helping a farmer plan maize production.
We also faced the challenge of building a meaningful WebMCP implementation while keeping the application usable in environments where native WebMCP support may not yet be available. To solve this, the prototype includes a local testing fallback while keeping the actual WebMCP registration layer separate and ready for testing in a supported environment.
Another challenge was ensuring that we did not present demo agricultural information as real-world advice. Therefore, demo weather and market information is explicitly labelled as prototype data and is intended to be replaced with verified sources before production deployment.
Accomplishments We Are Proud Of
We are proud that AgroAgent evolved from an agricultural idea into a working prototype with a clear agent + web tools architecture.
One of our biggest accomplishments is creating a dedicated set of agricultural tools that can be registered through WebMCP rather than building only a traditional chatbot.
We are particularly proud of the farm-planning workflow.
A farmer can express a goal in natural language, and the application can identify the relevant agricultural operations required to produce a farm plan.
We also built:
A complete agricultural dashboard
AI agent interface
Six WebMCP tool definitions
Agricultural crop database structure
Agricultural input catalogue
Market intelligence interface
Farm-plan management
Farmer profile
Administrator dashboard
Agent activity logging
Supabase-ready database schema
Mobile-responsive interface
Open-source project structure
Most importantly, AgroAgent demonstrates a different vision for agricultural technology: AI should not only tell farmers what to do; AI should be able to interact with useful agricultural services and help complete tasks.
What We Learned
We learned that building an AI application is not only about the AI model.
The real value comes from connecting AI to useful tools, structured information and actions.
WebMCP helped us think about the web as something an AI agent can interact with rather than simply something a human browses.
We learned to design tools around clear actions and inputs. For example, instead of asking an AI to "know everything about agriculture," we can give it specific capabilities such as:
Get weather.
Search crop information.
Search agricultural products.
Compare products.
Create a farm plan.
Save a farm plan.
We also learned the importance of building a focused MVP. A smaller workflow that works clearly is more valuable than a huge platform containing many unfinished features.
Finally, we learned that agricultural technology must be built responsibly. Weather, market and agronomic information can affect real financial decisions, so production deployment must use reliable, verified data sources and clearly communicate uncertainty.
What's Next for AgroAgent
The next stage is to move AgroAgent from a prototype toward a real pilot implementation with farmers.
Our priorities are: 

 
 Real WebMCP deployment
We will test the WebMCP tools in the supported environment and verify that AI agents can discover and execute them through the live application. 
 Supabase integration
We will connect the production database so farmer profiles, farm plans, products, market information and agent activity can be securely stored. 
 Verified agricultural data
We will replace demo weather and market information with reliable data sources and agricultural information appropriate for the target communities. 
 Local agricultural intelligence

title: ROUGH//CUT
pitch: An in-browser video editor you and your AI agent can use together
about_excerpt: An in-browser video editor you and your AI agent can use together Like Comment Story Updates Timeline view Landing page Inspecting main clip Inspecting background music Editing ROUGH//CUT's demo video... in ROUGH//CUT! Inspiration Most AI-powered video editors today suffer from a fundamental flaw- they take too much control away from the user. As someone who has been editing videos for over 5 years, I did not like this approach. While there are multiple tasks in video editing that can (and should) be automated and abstracted away, I, as the human behind the production, should have complete creative control and be able to tweak everything to my liking. With the introduction of WebMCP, I realized that I now had a way to solve this problem. What it does ROUGH//CUT is an in-browser video editor that a human and any WebMCP-compatible AI agent can use together. Both operate the same timeline through the same editing commands, so the agent is not working inside a separate abstraction or generating an edit that the user cannot inspect. WebMCP makes functionality discovery extremely easy for the agent and it knows exactly what all it can get done with those tools, without having to overload its context by inspecting the full document. Users can upload a video, generate a word-level transcript, edit them manually or via their agent in natural language, transcript, timeline, and inspector, and export the finished project as MP4, EDL, or SRT. ROUGH//CUT exposes WebMCP tools for cuts, trims, gaps, clip reordering, captions, text overlays, transitions, colour adjustments, transforms, speed changes, background music, silence detection, and much more. There are a total of 40 WebMCP tools in ROUGH//CUT. Every agent action appears in the editor, updates the same project the human is viewing, and can be undone. If the human changes the project while an agent is working, version checks prevent the agent from accidentally overwriting those changes. How I built it I built ROUGH//CUT with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, deployed on Cloudflare Workers. Project data and revision history are stored in Cloudflare D1, while uploaded videos, music, and generated media are stored in R2. The WebMCP integration uses the native document.modelContext.registerTool API. ROUGH//CUT's WebMCP tools for are used for inspecting, processing, editing, and exporting a project. These tools call the exact same versioning system used by the human-facing controls instead of maintaining a separate agent-specific editing system. Transcription is handled by Whisper Large V3 Turbo through Cloudflare Workers AI, with optional support for OpenAI's whisper-1 . Word timestamps are stored with stable IDs so captions and transcript-based edits remain connected to the source material. FFmpeg runs inside a Cloudflare Container and handles waveform generation, silence detection, audio processing, and final MP4 rendering. The browser preview and FFmpeg renderer share the same timeline calculations and a canonical 1920×1080 coordinate system so the final export matches what was shown in the editor. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was keeping the browser preview, timeline, and FFmpeg output consistent. Browsers and FFmpeg often interpret transforms, brightness, fades, audio timing, and crossfades differently. A change that looked correct in the preview could produce a noticeably different export, so I had to test each operation across both rendering paths. This was quite painstaking and ended up surprising me (negatively) more than once. Building a proper timeline was another large challenge. Trimming a clip affects captions, transitions, waveforms, playback, snapping, and the positions of every clip after it. Adding explicit gaps, non-ripple trims, speed changes, linked audio, and drag-to-reorder behaviour made this much more than a collection of UI controls. WebMCP also introduced some interesting constraints. Agents can request an upload or prepare an export, but browser security correctly requires the human to select local files and confirm downloads. I designed these interactions as visible human handoffs instead of attempting to work around those protections. Finally, FFmpeg performance inside a cloud container was very different from performance in the local docker container I was running. I had to improve the filter graph, remove unnecessary processing, handle cold starts, and keep exports asynchronous without hiding their real status from the user or agent. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am most proud that ROUGH//CUT is a fully working editor which promotes human <-> agent collaboration instead of handing off creativity to an AI. This is how I envision all other apps and tooling will end up behaving once WebMCP becomes mainstream and popular. The human editor is fully usable without an AI agent, while the WebMCP tools are still capable enough for an agent to make precise changes across the entire project. Humans and agents do not have separate copies of the edit and share one source of truth. I am also proud of the interaction between agent autonomy and human control. Agent actions are visible, reversible, and rejected when based on an outdated project version. The agent can handle repetitive work, but the human always retains the ability to review, adjust, undo, or continue editing manually. Getting real 1080p MP4 exports, EDL files, captions, background music, transitions, and browser preview parity working across Cloudflare Workers and Containers was also a major milestone. What I learned I learned how revolutionary WebMCP as a standard can be. I had heard of it earlier while I was testing out on-device Gemini Nano but put off learning about it to another time. It feels like discovering a treasure that had been right in front of my eyes all this time. I also learned that tool design matters as much as the model using the tools. Narrow schemas, structured responses, project version checks, and compact diffs made the agent more reliable than giving it one large, overly flexible editing function. I dogfooded ROUGH//CUT by asking an agent what felt off when it was trying to use it with me, and then made fixes accordingly. The shared command layer became one of the most important architectural decisions in the project. When human controls and agent tools use the same operations, consistency, undo, persistence, validation, and testing become much easier to reason about. Finally, I gained a much deeper appreciation for the gap between browser media playback and production video rendering. Frame timing, audio syncing, colour processing, aspect ratios, and transitions all require explicit handling if the preview is expected to match the exported file. What's next for ROUGH//CUT My immediate focus is improving rendering speed, especially for cold container starts and longer videos. I also want to make frame inspection more efficient for agents so as to avoid bloating their context. I will also try and continue improving the editor on smaller screens. Beyond that, I would like to add more caption styles, more effects, transitions, audio controls, export presets, and more. I'm also trying to figure out ways to make it work completely locally. I want to give the user a way get the entire transcription->editing->rendering->export pipeline running on their own machine. BYOK already exists for the transcription tool, but it's not local and instead uses an OpenAI API key. The longer-term goal is for ROUGH//CUT to become a practical example of how creative software can work with external agents, all the while staying open source and in-browser. The agent should not replace the editor. It should enter the same workspace, use the same tools, and collaborate with the person who is ultimately responsible for the creative result. title: Known Good WebMCP Verifier
pitch: Every other WebMCP checker tells you pass or fail. This one tells you where you stand in 14,351 probed sites, admits the 1,224 it couldn't ask — and is itself callable as a WebMCP tool.
about_excerpt: Every other WebMCP checker tells you pass or fail. This one tells you where you stand in 14,351 probed sites, admits the 1,224 it couldn't ask — and is itself callable as a WebMCP tool. Like Comment Story Updates "What matched" panel showing the actual JavaScript from the checked page Inspiration We already run an index of 14,351 sites whose agent-facing capabilities are probe-verified and dated. When we turned that machinery on WebMCP, the finding was awkward: registered tools round to zero outside demos and the checker sites themselves. There were more tools for checking WebMCP than there were sites using it. So the missing thing was never another checker. It was a denominator . Nobody could tell a site what its result meant, because nobody had a population to compare it against. Then a bug decided the rest of the product. Our first detector reported a clean no tools found for a page whose script robots.txt had disallowed us from reading. It wasn't a no. It was a question we weren't allowed to ask, and reporting it as a no is the same error as counting a locked door as an empty room. Across the index that turned out to be 1,224 hosts . Every checker we could find reports those as failures. That distinction became the product. What it does Give it a hostname. It fetches the page, then opens it in a real browser, and reports three things a checker normally collapses into one: whether the site declares WebMCP in its source, whether it actually registers tools when the page executes, and — the state that matters — whether we were allowed to ask at all. Then it does the thing no other checker can: it places the answer. 647 sites in our index carry the code, 580 register something at runtime, and 997 distinct tool names have been observed across them. If you're deciding which tools to expose, the distribution is the answer — search_site on 122 sites, fetch_as_markdown on 105, search_content on 28, get_contact_info on 18, get_pricing and search_products on 17 each. Measured and dated, not guessed. Why WebMCP is the right shape for this . What anyone wants from this page is one action with one parameter: check this host. That's a tool call, not a document. An agent forced to fetch our HTML, locate the form, synthesise a POST and parse a verdict out of the markup is doing four fragile things to accomplish one simple one — and all four break the next time we change the layout. So the page declares its own WebMCP tools. An agent calls it rather than reading it. The checker is an instance of the thing it checks. What that unlocks . An agent can audit fifty hosts in a loop with no HTML parsing and no brittle selectors. More interesting is the reverse direction: "does this host expose tools I can call, and were they observed running or merely declared?" is a question an agent should ask before it interacts with an unfamiliar site. Declared-versus-verified is exactly the distinction an autonomous agent needs and rarely has. This turns it into one call, with a date attached. And a boundary that matters more as agents get more capable: we list tools, we never invoke them . Enumerating a stranger's tools is safe. Executing one could place an order, send a message, or spend someone's money. How we built it Two layers, mapping onto the verification tiers we already run. Declared — a static fetch matching navigator.modelContext, document.modelContext, provideContext and registerTool. It matches both namespaces, because the spec renamed one mid-origin-trial and a site written against the earlier draft still counts. And it matches a call, not a mention — an article explaining WebMCP doesn't get scored as a site using it. Registered — headless enumeration in a real browser via Cloudflare Browser Rendering, the tools/list equivalent. This is what separates a site that ships the code from a site where the code actually runs. 647 carry it; 580 register something. It runs on Cloudflare Workers with D1 behind it. The page's own tools are declared with the declarative form attributes — toolname, tooldescription, toolparamdescription — so this is a WebMCP surface, not a page about WebMCP. Consent is enforced before any fetch , because the tool probes third-party hosts on demand: robots.txt read before the resource request; ai-input=no treated as an absolute stop, with the host reported as excluded rather than as failing; the user-agent KnownGood-Verifier never disguised; Retry-After honoured. And running a check has zero effect on ranking in our index — listings there are earned by probe and never sold. Challenges we ran into Cloudflare Browser Rendering caps at two concurrent browsers and two new per minute, with a 60-second inactivity kill — a different problem at index scale than at demo scale. The detector took two rewrites. The first version matched modelContext inside comments, and fixing that surfaced the worse case: WebMCP discussed in HTML body prose. Separating a call from a mention is most of the work in a detector like this, and neither failure was obvious until we looked at what had matched. And the spec renamed navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext mid-origin-trial, so anything matching a single namespace silently under-counts. We match both. Accomplishments that we're proud of We shipped the state that makes our own number smaller. Adding "could not ask" means 1,224 hosts don't count toward anything, where every checker we found reports them as failures. It's the right number and it cost us the bigger one. The checker passes its own check. Run it against https://knowngood.sh/verify/webmcp and it comes back registered, with its tools enumerated. We didn't want to ship a tool telling sites to do something we hadn't done. The population produced a finding nobody else could. Treating each site's tool signature as a fingerprint puts 39.5% of the 580 registering sites in a cluster with at least one other site, and the largest single cluster is 18.1%. Most WebMCP "adoption" is one plugin — and you can only see that from a denominator. Every figure carries the population and date it was measured against. No number on the page floats free of what it was measured over. What we learned A checker that cannot distinguish "no" from "couldn't ask" is worse than no checker at all for the sites it mislabels — it manufactures a false negative and presents it with the same confidence as a real one. And adoption numbers in a young standard are mostly plugin numbers. Without the tool-signature clustering we would have reported 580 independent implementations. The truth is closer to a handful of implementations installed many times, and only a population makes that visible. What's next for Known Good WebMCP Verifier Declarative detection. The checker sees the imperative API but not toolname / tooldescription on form controls — the half of the standard a browser-side audit is most likely to score, and a real gap. When it lands, the attribute route will report as declared and never as registered . Attributes prove intent; only execution proves registration. Conflating the two is exactly the error this tool exists to avoid, and we'd rather ship the gap honestly than close it dishonestly. title: KumiDraw
pitch: KumiDraw is a system design tool. Type cache and the box becomes a Cache. Your AI reads that model, not a screenshot, so it finds the bottleneck and asks the right question.
about_excerpt: KumiDraw is a system design tool. Type cache and the box becomes a Cache. Your AI reads that model, not a screenshot, so it finds the bottleneck and asks the right question. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration We kept drawing the same architecture twice. Once on a whiteboard for the conversation, once in a document for the record, and the two disagreed by the afternoon. Then we watched an AI try to help with a diagram. It took a screenshot and guessed. It read a label wrong, missed an arrow that ran behind a box, and called a queue a database. That is not the model failing. We had handed it a picture of a system instead of the system. WebMCP is the fix for that. A page can hand an agent typed tools instead of pixels. It only helps if the page has something typed to hand over, and that is where our tool already was. What it does KumiDraw draws as fast as a whiteboard and stores a typed graph. Draw a box, and it is already a Service. Type cache and it becomes a Cache, with the right glyph. Type redis and it becomes Redis with cache kind, the same node refined rather than replaced. You are never asked to fill in a form. The notes are a projection of that graph, so the drawing and the write-up cannot disagree. Because the graph is typed, rules sit on top of it. KumiDraw lints an architecture the way a compiler lints code: a synchronous call crossing a trust boundary, a queue with no consumer, a store read by four services with nothing cached in front of it, the one node every path has to pass through. Your AI reads the graph, not the screen. Through WebMCP it calls read_design and gets nodes, boundaries and typed calls as text. No screenshot, and no guessing which arrow starts where. It knows an edge is async because the model says so, not because a dash pattern hinted at it. It sees the node that is scrolled off the canvas. It reads the same lint findings you see, so it spends its attention on the question a reviewer would ask next instead of on spotting the obvious. It also imports formats we never wrote a parser for. Paste a Terraform file and ask for it on the canvas. The agent already reads HCL, so it calls add_node and connect , and because kind is a closed list of thirteen words its mapping is constrained rather than invented. An aws_elasticache_cluster becomes a Cache with the Redis glyph. A VPC becomes a boundary. The same holds for CloudFormation, a Kubernetes manifest, a Pulumi program, or a page of meeting notes. We ship no parser for any of them, and we never will. How we built it using Nuxt 4 and Vue 3 and using codex, claude and gemini Four decisions made the WebMCP work small: Kinds are a closed vocabulary. The union that picks a node's glyph is the agent's JSON Schema enum. An agent cannot invent a type, and Other records the user's own word when the model has none. Every change is a named, invertible op. Undo, persistence and the command registry come out of one mechanism, so an agent's edit is an ordinary edit. One write surface. useDocument ends with a comment saying nothing outside its list may change the document. The tools are a projection of that list, not a second path into the store. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool and tear down with an AbortController. Work lives in IndexedDB. The build is static and ships to Cloudflare Pages. Challenges we ran into WebMCP brought churn of its own. The API moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext during the origin trial, and most of what ranks for "WebMCP" repeats itself and disagrees on dates, so we worked from the Chrome docs and the spec repo and treated the rest as rumour. The hardest call was paging. Chrome recommends 1.5K characters per tool result, and our first instinct was to page the node list. That is wrong. An agent handed page one reasons about a system whose datastore it never saw, and the failure is silent. We compress instead. One line per node, and the text that grows without limit moved to a tool an agent asks for on purpose. Then labels. Our @ links bind by label, because people type words. An agent cannot, because a label is allowed to be empty by design and two nodes can share one. Agents get ids, and every write returns the ids it created. Accomplishments that we're proud of The type earns its keep three times over. One closed union draws the right glyph, feeds the linter, and becomes the agent's input schema. We deleted a roadmap. Every import format we were going to write a parser for is now a conversation, and code we never write cannot rot. No confirmation dialogs on agent writes. The op log makes undo the answer to a wrong edit, which is a better answer than a modal. The privacy claim survives. Registering a tool transmits nothing, and no tool name, description or enum carries document content, so nothing leaves the machine until you ask a question. What we learned A screenshot is a lossy export of your own data. If a model has to look at your app to understand it, the app is hiding what it already knows. Decide what can be decided in code. We nearly shipped a critique tool, which would have been our rubric competing with a better one inside the model. Rules that are true or false run as lint, and the model does the judgement. Agents want intent shaped tools, not keystroke shaped ones. We nearly projected our command registry into forty tools. Commands are for hands. Tool metadata is read on page visit, before anyone has asked anything. An enum of live node ids would have leaked the document for free. Building for an agent made the app better for people. Every tool we wanted to expose turned out to be a gap in the write surface. What's next for KumiDraw Better Linter, More types, One node having multiple type (Like redis is cache, also a pubsub) Community Designs and Roast System Built With cloudflare nuxt Try it out kumodraw.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Jithin Shah Amrithanadh Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Jithin Shah started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:19 AM EDT

title: Crit Studio
pitch: Give your agent hands, not just words. Crit Studio exposes your design canvas as WebMCP tools so agents can flag, drag, and fix UI issues live not describe them in chat.
about_excerpt: Give your agent hands, not just words. Crit Studio exposes your design canvas as WebMCP tools so agents can flag, drag, and fix UI issues live not describe them in chat. Like Comment Story Updates landing page landing page landing page landing page landing page workspace view Inspiration Most AI design tools give you feedback in a chat box. “Your CTA needs more spacing.” “Your layout could be more balanced.” The problem is that design is visual. If someone tells you that something is 12 pixels too far to the left, you still have to go find it, figure out what they mean, and fix it yourself. I started wondering: what if the AI reviewing your design could actually touch the canvas? That idea became Crit Studio. Instead of having an AI describe what's wrong with a design, I wanted it to be able to point to the exact element, move it, resize it, and show you the fix directly. WebMCP made that possible in a way that felt much more natural than building another AI chat interface. What it does Crit Studio is a live design workspace where you can build a simple mockup using a Figma-style component toolbox — headings, buttons, navigation, images, and other elements — and then ask an AI reviewer to critique it. But the interesting part is what happens next. The AI doesn't just send back a list of suggestions. It can actually interact with the canvas through WebMCP tools. It can: Read the current layout with getCanvasState Flag a specific problem with flagIssue , placing a visible badge directly on the element Move an element with moveElement Resize an element with resizeElement Rebalance spacing across a group with suggestSpacing Add a comment at an exact canvas position with annotateAt So if the agent says your CTA is too small, you can actually watch it resize. And if you respond, “Make it bigger, not just more spaced out,” it can make another change on the same canvas. That back-and-forth was important to me. I didn't want Crit Studio to feel like a tool that analyzes a screenshot once and gives you a report. I wanted it to feel like you're actually working with the AI on the design. The tools are also registered through the standard navigator.modelContext API rather than being tied to my own interface. That means any WebMCP-native agent host can discover and use them independently. I also built an Export Audit feature. At the end of a session, you can export the entire critique, the elements on the canvas, issues that were raised and resolved, and the chronological tool-call history as Markdown or JSON. So the session doesn't just disappear when you're done. You have an actual artifact you can share with a team or keep for documentation. How I built it Crit Studio is built with Next.js, TypeScript, and Zustand. One decision I made early turned out to be one of the most important architectural choices: there should only be one source of truth for the canvas. The Zustand store holds the entire canvas state, and every interaction reads and writes to that same store. Whether you're dragging an element manually, the AI is calling a WebMCP tool, or the built-in review panel is making changes, everything updates the exact same state model. That kept the application consistent regardless of who's interacting with the canvas. I also decided to build the canvas using regular DOM elements with absolute positioning instead of using <canvas> or WebGL. That made styling much easier, allowed smooth CSS animations, simplified positioning annotations and badges, and made serializing the canvas state for getCanvasState much more straightforward. For the visual design, I created a small neobrutalist design system using hard borders, flat colors, and offset shadows. I wanted Crit Studio to feel like a creative design tool rather than another generic AI dashboard. The six WebMCP tools are registered client-side with navigator.modelContext.registerTool() , each with a deliberately narrow responsibility so an agent has a clear and predictable set of actions to choose from. Challenges I faced One of the biggest challenges was getting the canvas to behave exactly the way I wanted visually. I went through several different design directions before settling on the final interface, and almost every iteration revealed another layout issue. At one point, issue badges and annotation pins kept overlapping the very content they were supposed to describe. I also ran into problems with the canvas preview clipping inside its container instead of scaling properly. One particularly stubborn bug turned out not to be a React problem at all. I had a global CSS reset: * { margin: 0; padding: 0; } and it was silently overriding Tailwind utility classes because of how CSS Cascade Layers work. Since the reset was unlayered, it could override styles inside Tailwind's @layer utilities even when the utilities looked more specific. That bug took longer to find than I expected. It also changed how I approached the rest of the project. I stopped treating a clean build as proof that something worked. If I couldn't visually confirm the result in the browser, I considered the issue unresolved. I also migrated the entire project from Vite to Next.js midway through development to take advantage of built-in API routes and better font handling. That meant reworking the client and server boundaries for anything touching navigator or browser-only state, which added another layer of complexity during development. Accomplishments I'm proud of The thing I'm most proud of is the live interaction loop. There's something genuinely different about asking, “What's wrong with this layout?” and then watching an AI resize a button, move a heading, or rebalance spacing directly on the canvas. There's no screenshot round-trip, no page reload, and no copying suggestions into another editor. Everything happens in the same workspace in real time. That was the moment where the original idea really came together. I'm also proud that I kept the WebMCP tool surface intentionally small. Rather than building a huge API with dozens of overlapping actions, I focused on six tools with very clear responsibilities. I think that made the system easier to reason about and made the agent's behavior much more predictable. What I learned The biggest lesson for me was that WebMCP's real advantage isn't just speed. It's precision. A vision-based agent has to estimate positions from a screenshot, while a tool-calling agent can inspect structured layout data and interact with exact elements using deterministic coordinates. That difference completely changes the quality of interaction. I also learned the importance of being honest about what is actually AI-driven and what is deterministic logic supporting the experience. There were moments during development where it would've been easy to present deterministic behavior as if it were intelligent reasoning. I deliberately avoided that distinction becoming blurry because I think technical honesty matters, especially when building AI products. What's next for Crit Studio The next version of Crit Studio will focus on making critiques work with real-world designs instead of only manually created mockups. I'd like to add support for importing screenshots and reference images so users can critique existing interfaces directly. I'm also planning to expand accessibility checks beyond contrast ratios and introduce more typography and layout intelligence, including grid alignment, hierarchy, and spacing recommendations. The long-term goal is still the same: Don't just tell me what's wrong with my design. Show me. pitch: A collaborative doc editor where AI agents read and write your real document state not screenshots through WebMCP.

A collaborative doc editor where AI agents read and write your real document state not screenshots through WebMCP.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 About the Project 

 The idea 

 We wanted to explore a simple question: 

 What if an AI agent could work inside a document with you, instead of just looking at the document from the outside? 

 Today, when an AI agent interacts with a web application, it often has to rely on screenshots, DOM inspection, or simulated clicks. For a document editor, that means the agent has to figure out what the user is looking at, where content belongs, and what actions are available. 

 We wanted to try a different approach using WebMCP : let the website expose its actual application state and capabilities as structured tools that an AI agent can call directly. 

 That became Co/Draft — a document where humans and agents edit together. 

 The core interaction is deliberately simple. A human writes and selects content normally, while an agent can use tools such as get_document_state , get_selection , add_comment , and insert_block . The agent therefore works with the same structured document state that the human sees, rather than trying to reconstruct it from the UI. 

 How we built it 

 Co/Draft is a lightweight React + TypeScript application using Zustand for document state. 

 The document is represented as structured blocks rather than one large piece of HTML. Each block has an ID, text, creation source, and author information. Comments are also attached to specific block IDs, which gives the agent an unambiguous way to refer to a section of the document. 

 On top of this state, we registered five WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_document_state — lets the agent read the current document, pending suggestions, and comments. 
 get_selection — tells the agent which block the human is currently working on. 
 insert_block — lets the agent propose a new section. 
 add_comment — lets the agent leave feedback on a specific block. 
 resolve_comment — lets the agent mark feedback as resolved. 
 

 These tools are registered through document.modelContext , using a React hook so that the tools operate against the same live state as the UI. 

 We also added a small human-in-the-loop trust boundary . An agent doesn't directly insert arbitrary content into the document. Instead, insert_block creates a visible pending suggestion. The human can then accept or reject it. 

 That gives us a workflow like: 

 Human writes → Agent reads → Agent reviews → Agent proposes → Human approves → Document changes 

 The agent can participate meaningfully without silently taking control of the document. 

 For collaboration, the prototype uses the browser's BroadcastChannel API. This allows multiple tabs in the same browser to exchange document mutations and presence information without requiring a backend. The project is intentionally a prototype rather than a production collaborative editor. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest thing we learned was that giving an agent structured tools changes the interaction completely . 

 Instead of asking an agent to “look at the page and figure out what to do,” we can give it explicit capabilities: 
 get_document_state()
get_selection()
add_comment(blockId, text)
insert_block(text, afterBlockId)
resolve_comment(commentId)
 
 This makes the boundary between the application and the agent much clearer. 

 We also learned that the interesting part isn't simply allowing an agent to edit. The more important question is how much control the agent should have . 

 For example, comments are relatively low-risk, so an agent can add one directly. Inserting actual document content is more consequential, so we introduced an approval step. 

 That led us to think about agents less like automated scripts and more like collaborators with explicitly defined permissions . 

 We also learned about the practical distinction between exposing application functionality to an agent and actually building a collaborative application. WebMCP solves the first problem very nicely, but synchronization, persistence, identity, and conflict resolution are separate engineering problems. 

 The challenges 

 One of our biggest challenges was synchronization. 

 Our first implementation used BroadcastChannel to send mutations such as: 
 editBlock
addComment
resolveComment
proposeBlock
acceptSuggestion
deleteBlock
 
 between tabs. 

 However, simply broadcasting mutations isn't enough to create a reliable shared document. Each tab initially creates its own in-memory state, so two tabs can start with different randomly generated block IDs. A mutation referring to a block that only exists in the sender's state cannot be correctly applied by another tab. 

 This forced us to think about an important distinction: 

 sharing events is not the same thing as sharing state. 

 A reliable prototype needs both a consistent initial document and a way for a newly opened tab to obtain the current state before applying future mutations. 

 We therefore treated the synchronization layer as a separate problem from WebMCP itself. The eventual direction is a lightweight state handshake for new tabs, while keeping the mutation-based synchronization simple enough for a hackathon demo. 

 Another challenge was deciding what not to build. 

 It would be possible to turn Co/Draft into a much larger system with a backend, WebSockets, persistent documents, authentication, CRDTs, conflict-free editing, and cross-device collaboration. But that would move attention away from the actual experiment we wanted to demonstrate: 

 
 Can a web application expose meaningful, structured capabilities to an AI agent so that the agent can genuinely collaborate with a human? 
 

 For this project, we chose to keep that question at the center. 

 Why this matters 

 Co/Draft is intentionally small, but the idea can extend much further. 

 A document editor is just one example. The same pattern could apply to design tools, spreadsheets, project-management applications, whiteboards, educational software, or any interactive application where an AI agent needs to understand and manipulate structured state. 

 Instead of building agents that merely see interfaces, we can build applications that explicitly tell agents: 

 “Here is what I am. Here is what you can understand. Here is what you are allowed to do.” 

 That is the direction we wanted to explore with Co/Draft.
