title: TubeSaku WebMCP
pitch: TubeSaku turns Japanese YouTube data into WebMCP tools: agents discover live streams or cover-song opportunities, then render their personalized picks back into the site.
about_excerpt: TubeSaku turns Japanese YouTube data into WebMCP tools: agents discover live streams or cover-song opportunities, then render their personalized picks back into the site. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector ChatGPT - Codex Inspiration YouTube’s recommendation algorithms are highly sophisticated, yet there are still situations where users struggle to find exactly what they want—for example, finding the right upcoming live stream at a specific time, or identifying a song that is popular but not already overcrowded with cover videos. We operate TubeSaku , a website that collects and organizes Japanese YouTube data for creators and viewers. As the amount of data grew, however, we encountered a new problem: more data did not always make decisions easier. Users could see rankings, schedules, demand signals, and historical observations, but still had to decide where to start. That led to the first idea behind TubeSaku WebMCP: Let the website remain the expert on its domain data, while an external AI agent becomes the expert on the individual user. The agent can understand what the user actually wants, query TubeSaku's structured evidence, compare the candidates, and then return its selections—and the reasons for those selections—back into the TubeSaku interface. There was also a broader motivation. AI is changing how people discover information on the web. Independent research from Pew Research Center found that users who encountered an AI-generated search summary clicked traditional search results less often than users who did not, while Google has reported that overall organic click volume remains relatively stable and that the clicks it sends are increasingly high-quality. The exact aggregate impact is still debated, but the underlying incentive question is important for the open web: What happens if websites continue producing useful information, but users increasingly consume the answer somewhere else without visiting the source? For many websites, a visit is not only a click. It is how users discover a new service, understand who created the information, build trust, see related features, subscribe, purchase, or take another action. TubeSaku WebMCP explores a different relationship between websites and AI agents: instead of treating the website only as raw material for an answer generated elsewhere, the agent can enter the first-party experience, use capabilities explicitly provided by the site, and make that site more useful for the user. What it does TubeSaku currently offers two WebMCP workflows. Live Schedule The first is designed for viewers. Agents can search TubeSaku's Japanese YouTube live-stream data using criteria such as: date time keyword category debut status For example, a user can ask: “Find three gaming live streams tomorrow evening that look interesting.” The agent searches TubeSaku, compares the returned candidates against the user's request, and then calls a second WebMCP tool to display its choices directly on the TubeSaku page as AI Picks . The agent can also provide a short explanation for each selection. Those reasons are rendered inside TubeSaku alongside the underlying stream information. So the result is not only: agent → answer in chat but: agent → decision → explanation → personalized first-party page Cover-song Planner The second workflow is designed for VTubers, YouTubers, vsingers, and singers deciding what song to cover next. TubeSaku combines several kinds of evidence, including: Japanese YouTube Charts recent cover-song upload activity historical cover availability where observed existing cover performance early-stage spread signals such as Shorts growth The agent can answer questions such as: “Find popular Japanese songs that are not currently overcrowded with new covers.” TubeSaku does not hard-code one universal recommendation. Instead, it exposes the evidence. The agent decides how those signals should be weighted for this particular user. A creator seeking maximum demand might choose differently from a small VTuber looking for a less competitive opportunity. At the time of submission, the live Cover Planner dataset compared 154 tracked songs against 4,891 recent cover observations from 3,439 YouTube channels. After making its decision, the agent can create AI Cover Picks directly inside TubeSaku, explain why each song was selected, and build an in-page listening playlist from validated existing YouTube cover videos. This also enables cross-lingual use. An English-speaking user can ask a question in English, the agent can reason over TubeSaku's Japanese data, explain its recommendation in English, and still preserve the original Japanese song and video titles. How we built it Hackathon scope TubeSaku.com and its YouTube data pipeline existed before this challenge. During the WebMCP Challenge submission period, we added the WebMCP layer shown in this submission: search_live_streams show_live_streams search_cover_songs show_cover_playlist first-party AI Picks interfaces agent-generated selection explanations an in-page cover-song listening playlist a standalone runnable demo using sample data The public repository and dated commit history document the work completed during the challenge period. A production data pipeline was already in place for TubeSaku. Local collectors and GCP-based jobs gather and clean observational data about YouTube in Japan, including live-stream schedules, YouTube Charts, recently uploaded cover videos, and observations of existing cover-song supply. The WebMCP Challenge WebMCP gave us a lightweight way to expose selected capabilities from that system directly to browser agents. Both workflows use the same pattern: TubeSaku first-party data ↓ WebMCP search tool ↓ Agent combines evidence with user context ↓ WebMCP show tool ↓ TubeSaku first-party UI Live Schedule Live demo search_live_streams → agent compares candidates → show_live_streams → AI Picks + selection reasons Cover-song Planner Live demo search_cover_songs → agent compares demand and supply evidence → show_cover_playlist → AI Cover Picks + reasons + Listening Playlist We deliberately separate the search and display tools. The display tools only accept IDs that appeared in the most recent search result. An agent therefore cannot arbitrarily inject unrelated streams or songs into the page. Selection explanations are also associated with those validated IDs and rendered as text rather than trusted HTML. For the Cover Planner, URLs exposed to the UI are validated, and listening examples are filtered before being exposed to the agent/player using checks including duration, obvious dance/clip false positives, public availability, and embeddability. We also made the tool execution wrappers tolerant of browser implementations that invoke a WebMCP tool without an optional execution-context argument, which improved interoperability during testing across agent browsers. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was data quality. Searching YouTube for Japanese cover-song terminology can also return: dance Shorts clips tutorials instrumental videos commentary unrelated songs with similar titles videos that technically match the query but are useless as listening examples We therefore added multiple validation layers instead of trusting YouTube search results directly. We also learned that browser lifecycle and first-party page architecture matter. TubeSaku serves some pages as generated static HTML, so modifying a template did not necessarily update the deployed page immediately. Playlist development exposed another set of subtle issues. YouTube's embed playlist behavior did not match our initial assumptions, and dynamically initializing the IFrame Player API behaved differently inside an agent browser than in our minimal local environment. We eventually simplified the implementation. TubeSaku keeps the validated selected video IDs itself and changes a standard YouTube iframe when the user presses Previous or Next. That solution was both simpler and more reliable. Browser interoperability also produced a useful lesson: different WebMCP-capable environments do not necessarily supply every optional execution argument in exactly the same way. We adjusted our tools defensively and added regression tests for this case. Accomplishments that we're proud of We achieved a complete end-to-end WebMCP interaction on the live TubeSaku website: natural-language request → WebMCP search → agent reasoning → validated selection → WebMCP UI action → first-party TubeSaku update The latest version goes one step further. The agent does not only return its selections—it can return the reason for each selection , and those explanations become part of the TubeSaku page. The Cover Planner is especially exciting because the user can immediately inspect and listen to the evidence behind a recommendation while continuing the conversation with the agent. title: WebMCP Doctor
pitch: Audit any live WebMCP website, trace agent failures, repair unsafe tool contracts, and expose human–agent capability gaps in one read-only report.
about_excerpt: Audit any live WebMCP website, trace agent failures, repair unsafe tool contracts, and expose human–agent capability gaps in one read-only report. Like Comment Story Updates Live AX Health Score from a real self-scan: seven WebMCP tools discovered and audited across 42 checks. AX Health breakdown across discoverability, clarity, reliability and recovery, and safety. Human × Agent Digital Twin showing 100% capability parity for the scanned WebMCP interface. Failure X-Ray leading into Tool Surgeon, with the primary contract risk and repair workflow. Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a native way to expose tools to AI agents, but a valid tool contract is not automatically a usable one. A tool can be hidden, ambiguously named, underspecified, unsafe, or impossible to recover from when it fails. Developers need the agent equivalent of accessibility and reliability testing. WebMCP Doctor is a read-only diagnostic workbench for that missing layer: Agent Experience (AX) . What it does Enter any public website URL and WebMCP Doctor loads the real page in an isolated Cloudflare browser session. It discovers the site's WebMCP surface, audits it, and turns the result into one focused report. AX Health Score runs 42 deterministic checks across discoverability, tool clarity, reliability and recovery, and safety. Agent Failure X-Ray visualizes the path from a goal through discovery, selection, input, execution, and root cause. Tool Surgeon diagnoses weak or unsafe contracts, proposes a repaired definition, and compares the same rubric before and after. Human × Agent Digital Twin compares actions available in the rendered human interface with actions exposed through WebMCP, highlighting capability gaps. The scanner never invokes a target site's tools. It inspects definitions and visible controls only. How we built it The interface is built with Next.js 16, TypeScript, React, Tailwind CSS, React Flow, Motion, and Lucide. It is deployed as a Cloudflare Worker. For real-site inspection, the Worker uses Cloudflare Browser Rendering / Browser Run to load the submitted URL and capture multiple WebMCP registration paths: imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) calls; native document.modelContext.getTools() results when available; declarative tool forms and their input metadata. The browser session also extracts visible human capabilities from buttons, links, forms, and controls. A deterministic audit engine then evaluates the collected tool metadata. Score weights are 25% discoverability, 30% clarity, 25% reliability/recovery, and 20% safety. The Failure X-Ray and parity views are derived from observed metadata; they do not pretend to execute autonomous agents. Tool Surgeon applies explicit repair heuristics, reruns the same checks, and shows the resulting score delta. The production scanner blocks private and local network targets, blocks unnecessary subresources, and caches results for five minutes. No paid model API, database, login, or analytics service is required. WebMCP Doctor also exposes its own native WebMCP tools so an agent can operate the diagnostic workflow: scan_agent_experience inspect_tool trace_agent_failure compare_human_agent_paths simulate_tool_change run_ax_test explain_ax_score These calls visibly update the same interface a human uses. Challenges we ran into The largest challenge was that WebMCP implementations are not uniform. Some sites register tools imperatively during page startup, some expose native inspection, and others use declarative forms. We built a layered collector so the audit remains useful across these patterns without invoking real actions. Another challenge was keeping the score explainable. Rather than hiding judgment inside an LLM prompt, each finding maps to a deterministic rule with severity, evidence, and a concrete recommendation. Finally, comparing human and agent capability required careful normalization. Human labels and tool names often describe the same action differently, so the parity engine combines normalized tokens, descriptions, and control context while keeping every match inspectable. Accomplishments that we're proud of It audits real public websites instead of relying on prefilled demo fixtures. It makes agent failures visual and traceable instead of returning a generic pass/fail result. It can show whether a proposed tool repair actually improves the same test suite. The public repository includes 13 unit/security tests, 3 browser tests, and a passing CI quality gate. The complete app runs on a free, minimal Cloudflare architecture. What we learned Agent-facing interfaces need the same discipline as human-facing interfaces: clear affordances, safe defaults, actionable errors, and recovery paths. WebMCP makes tools discoverable; AX engineering makes them dependable. We also learned that static analysis becomes much more useful when it is tied to a visual causal model. A developer can understand a red node in the Failure X-Ray faster than a long list of disconnected lint messages. What's next for WebMCP Doctor Next steps include reusable CI policies, historical score comparisons, exportable audit reports, deeper declarative-form coverage, and opt-in authenticated scanning for staging environments. The core will remain deterministic, explainable, and safe by default. A WebMCP-powered campus agent that lets students and AI agents discover spaces, check availability, plan tasks, and execute campus actions together—with humans always in control.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Campus life involves many small tasks that become surprisingly difficult when information is scattered across different systems. Students may need to find a quiet study space, check availability, plan their day, or perform campus-related actions, but they often have to manually search through multiple pages and interfaces. 

 We wanted to explore a different approach: what if a campus website could be used directly by an AI agent as a set of structured tools, while still keeping the student in control? 

 That idea led to CampusPilot — Agentic Campus OS , a WebMCP-powered campus assistant designed to connect students and AI agents with useful campus actions. 

 What it does 

 CampusPilot provides an agent-friendly interface for common campus workflows such as: 

 
 🔎 Discovering available campus spaces 
 📚 Finding suitable study locations 
 🗓️ Planning campus-related tasks 
 ⚡ Executing actions through structured WebMCP tools 
 🤖 Showing an agent's reasoning and planned actions 
 👤 Keeping the human involved through approval before important actions 
 

 Instead of treating the website as something an agent can only read, CampusPilot exposes functionality through WebMCP tools that an AI agent can understand and invoke. 

 How we built it 

 CampusPilot was built as a modern React web application with a premium, responsive interface. 

 The core architecture is organized around a WebMCP tool layer. We created structured tools with defined schemas and handlers so that an agent can interact with campus functionality in a predictable way. 

 The application includes: 

 
 React + TypeScript for the application 
 Tailwind CSS for the interface 
 Lucide icons for UI elements 
 WebMCP imperative APIs for agent-tool interaction 
 A deterministic demo agent for demonstrating the complete workflow 
 An Agent Reasoning timeline to make agent actions understandable 
 A Plan Card that allows the human to review and approve planned actions 
 

 The most important part of the implementation is that the demo agent and the WebMCP interface use the same underlying tool logic. This helped us demonstrate how an AI agent could move from understanding a user's request to selecting tools and executing a campus workflow. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that building an agentic application is not only about adding an AI model. 

 The interface between the agent and the application matters just as much . 

 WebMCP provides a structured way to expose website capabilities to agents. Designing clear tool names, schemas, inputs, outputs, and handlers made us think about the application from an agent's perspective rather than only from a human user's perspective. 

 We also learned that human-in-the-loop interaction is important . An agent should be able to plan and recommend actions quickly, while the user should still understand what is going to happen before approving important operations. 

 Challenges we faced 

 One of the main challenges was designing WebMCP tools that were both useful for humans and understandable to an AI agent. 

 We had to carefully structure tool inputs and outputs so that each action had a clear purpose and predictable behavior. 

 Another challenge was creating a convincing agent experience without hiding what the agent was doing. Instead of simply showing a final result, CampusPilot exposes an Agent Reasoning timeline and planned actions so users can follow the workflow. 

 We also had to ensure that the application remained reliable during the demo. We tested the application build and the complete tool interaction flow to make sure the WebMCP functionality worked consistently. 

 Why CampusPilot? 

 CampusPilot is a small step toward a future where websites are not just pages that humans navigate, but interactive environments that AI agents can safely operate through structured capabilities . 

 Our goal is to extend this concept beyond a demo into a real campus operating layer where students can ask an agent to accomplish tasks across campus systems while remaining in control of the final decisions. 

 
 CampusPilot turns a campus website into an agent-ready environment — connecting human intent, WebMCP tools, and AI agents in one workflow.

title: BridgeAble - Bridging The Gap
pitch: BridgeAble turns any confusing website into an accessible one — an AI agent fills forms and navigates for people with disabilities, while they see and approve every step.
about_excerpt:
BridgeAble turns any confusing website into an accessible one — an AI agent fills forms and navigates for people with disabilities, while they see and approve every step. 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Why This Use Case Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP 

 Assistive form-filling is one of the few agentic use cases where "just scrape the DOM and click around" is actively dangerous: 

 
 The cost of a wrong guess is serious. A shopping-assistant agent that misclicks can be retried. An agent that misreads an unlabeled housing-benefits field and submits a wrong income figure or the wrong document can cost someone real benefits, or force them to redo a multi-step application alone. WebMCP's structured, explicit tool schemas ( fill_field(field_id, value) , not "click the third gray box") remove the guessing entirely — the page tells the agent exactly what's fillable, what it's called, and what values are valid (e.g. the housing_status enum), instead of the agent inferring it from pixels and placeholder text. 
 Screen scraping and vision models are exactly what disabled users can't rely on. A blind user's agent can't "look" at a tiny unlabeled button any better than a screen reader can — both need the page to declare its own semantics. WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool is that declaration, machine-readable and unambiguous, which is precisely the gap screen readers have never been able to close on their own. 
 Retrofit, not redesign, is the only realistic path for legacy government/benefits sites. These are exactly the sites least likely to ever get an accessibility redesign. WebMCP lets a site owner bolt on a config object and one <script> tag and get agent-legible tools immediately — no rebuild, no waiting on a procurement cycle. 
 The same tool surface serves both a real browser-native agent and our own bundled LLM loop , so the use case naturally showcases WebMCP as a genuine web platform primitive (via document.modelContext ) rather than something that only works inside one vendor's chat widget. 
 

 

 How It Creates a Better User Experience 

 
 From "hand over your laptop" to "stay in control." Before WebMCP-style structured tools, the only real options for someone who can't operate a confusing form were to struggle through it alone or hand full control to a caregiver/bot. BridgeAble's tool-gated actions mean the person can direct an agent conversationally while remaining the one who approves every change — no full hand-off of control required. 
 Every action is visible, not a black box. Because each tool call acts on the real DOM element (via the BridgeableConfig selector), the actual page visibly highlights and updates as the agent works — the person watching (whether low-vision, using a screen reader, or a family member helping) sees the same ground truth the agent is acting on, in real time. 
 Plain language replaces jargon. explain_field and read_field_aloud turn a confusing government-form label into a spoken, plain-language explanation on demand — something a static form or a generic screen reader narration cannot do, because the form itself doesn't know what its own fields mean. 
 Mistakes are cheap to fix. undo_last_change and simply re-calling fill_field mean a correction is a single spoken sentence ("actually my income is $2,600"), not a re-navigation of a multi-step wizard with tiny, hard-to-hit controls. 
 Consent is structural, not just polite. request_submit can only ever open a large-text, high-contrast confirmation card — it can never submit. The person (or their caregiver) always makes the final, deliberate tap. That single design choice is what turns "an agent that could act for me" into "an agent I can actually trust to act for me." 
 

 

 What People and Agents Can Now Do Together That Was Difficult or Impossible Before 

 
 Reliable multi-step form completion by voice or plain chat, with zero blind trust. Before, a person with a motor or visual disability could either painstakingly tab/zoom/scroll through a 4-step, unlabeled form themselves, or dictate instructions to a human/bot that had no structured way to confirm it acted correctly. With WebMCP tools exposed, a person can say one natural sentence and watch, in real time, exactly which fields were set to what — then correct or undo any single one without redoing the rest. 
 Mid-conversation correction without losing progress. Because each field is an addressable tool call (not a scripted macro), a person can course-correct ("actually, two dependents, not one") at any point, and the agent calls fill_field again on just that field — something a recorded macro, a scripted RPA bot, or a caregiver relaying instructions secondhand can't do cleanly. 
 A meaningful, plain-language "explain this to me" conversation embedded in the task itself. explain_field lets someone ask "what does housing status mean?" in the middle of filling out the form and get an answer that maps to that exact field, then keep going in the same flow — rather than leaving the page to search a FAQ or call a helpline. 
 Human-gated agentic submission that's provably safe, not just prompted to be careful. Previously, "the agent will ask for confirmation" was a matter of trusting a prompt. Here, the agent literally has no callable tool that finalizes anything — request_submit only opens a UI, and the real submit path is wired exclusively to a human click handler. That means a person can delegate the tedious, error-prone filling work to an agent while keeping the consequential, irreversible submitting action entirely their own — a split of labor between human and agent that wasn't safely possible when agents only had "click here" style access to a page. 
 The exact same tool surface working for a real WebMCP-aware browser/extension and our own accessible chat panel. A person isn't locked into one vendor's assistant; any WebMCP-compliant agent (verified here with the Model Context Tool Inspector extension) can discover and drive the same accessible form-filling flow. 
 

 

 How We Implemented WebMCP (Briefly) 

 
 Each host page (e.g. portal.php ) declares a small window.BridgeableConfig object mapping semantic field/document/step keys to real CSS selectors, human-readable labels, and types — the only integration work a site owner does. 
 assets/bridgeable-widget.js defines one canonical TOOLS array (name, description, JSON Schema, handler) for get_application_state , fill_field , go_to_step , upload_document , explain_field , read_field_aloud , review_summary , request_submit , and undo_last_change . 
 Every tool in that array is registered with the browser via document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) , per the WebMCP Imperative API , so any WebMCP-aware agent or extension can discover and call it directly against the live page. 
 The same TOOLS array is mirrored into a local registry that powers BridgeAble's own bundled chat/voice panel and agent loop ( agent_api.php / llm.php ), so the identical tool implementations run whether they're invoked by a real WebMCP client or by our fallback LLM loop — no duplicated logic, and the demo works even where document.modelContext isn't available yet. 
 The one deliberately un -registered function, finalizeSubmission() , is wired only to a human click event on the confirmation card — enforcing human-in-the-loop consent at the architecture level rather than via a system prompt. 
 

 See How We Built It below for the full architecture breakdown. 

 

 Inspiration 

 Every day, millions of people with disabilities hit a wall online — not because they can't use a computer, but because the web was never built for them. A 12-step government benefits form with no screen-reader labels. A healthcare portal with tiny, unlabeled buttons scattered across five tabs. A visually impaired parent trying to book a school appointment through a form that assumes perfect vision and fine motor control. 

 Existing "solutions" force a bad trade-off: either the person struggles through alone, or they hand over their laptop entirely to a caregiver or an autonomous bot that clicks blindly and makes mistakes on their behalf — with zero visibility or consent along the way. 

 We kept coming back to one moment in the WebMCP spec: the idea that a website can expose structured, trustworthy tools that an agent calls directly — no guessing, no fragile scraping, no misclicks. That's not just a technical convenience. For someone with a disability, it's the difference between an agent that might get it

title: MintPaw
pitch: Alibaba-sourced pet tech, sold across a border. Its WebMCP tools check your mains voltage, your LTE bands and your router — and refuse to cart what will not work when it arrives.
about_excerpt: Alibaba-sourced pet tech, sold across a border. Its WebMCP tools check your mains voltage, your LTE bands and your router — and refuse to cart what will not work when it arrives. Like Comment Story Updates Dog owner, 5GHz-only router. The agent fills in the store's own compatibility panel: Add to cart goes dead and express checkout disappears. Two cats with 2.4GHz available. Caveats instead of a block, and the buy buttons return - the gate is not a blanket no. Product copy rendered from the same record the agent reads, including a plain list of what MintPaw has not checked itself. The cross-border trap: plug variants for eight countries, and an input voltage the supplier never stated. The open questions put to the supplier, published on the product page instead of hidden. Inspiration Smart pet devices are returned at a punishing rate, and mostly not because they are broken. They come back because of a mismatch that was knowable before checkout and invisible while scrolling: a 2.4GHz-only device meeting a 5GHz-only mesh router — it will never finish setup a 4G tracker on LTE bands that do not exist in the buyer's country a companion app not published in the buyer's region a single-cat litter box arriving in a two-cat home Every one of those sits somewhere on the product page. Nobody reads it. So we built the store that reads it for you and then says no. What it does MintPaw is a live Shopify storefront selling five smart pet devices. Its WebMCP layer is not a faster way to buy — it is a gate. An agent records the shopper's household: species, weight, how many animals share the device, which Wi-Fi bands the router actually broadcasts , country, and willingness to add a cellular plan. It then returns, per product, a verdict of ok / caution / unknown / blocked with the specific reason in plain language. A blocked product cannot be added to the cart. The tool refuses, the Add to cart button goes dead and relabels itself "Not compatible with your home", and Shopify's express checkout button is removed from the page. A caution product is also held back until the agent has actually told the shopper the caveat and passed acknowledged_caveats: true . Informed consent, enforced in code rather than requested in a prompt. And the store says what it does not know. Our product data comes from Alibaba sourcing documents full of unconfirmed manufacturer claims. Instead of laundering those into spec, every tool returns them separately as notYetVerifiedByMintPaw — "the listing says 10000mAh, MintPaw has not measured it." unknown and ok are deliberately different verdicts. How we built it — and the discovery that shaped the whole project Partway in we found that Shopify's storefront now injects its own WebMCP adapter automatically ( cdn.shopify.com/storefront/webmcp/webmcp-0.1.1.js ). Out of the box our store already exposed ten generic commerce tools: search_catalog , get_product , get_cart , update_cart , cancel_cart , proceed_to_checkout , browse_store , show_variant , manage_orders and search_shop_policies_and_faqs . Our first draft had re-implemented five of those and collided with get_product outright — two tools with one name and an agent picking between them at random. We deleted it. That reframed the project: The interesting question WebMCP raises for a merchant is not "how do I expose my storefront?" — the platform now does that. It is "what do I know that the platform cannot?" For MintPaw that is compatibility: which device works in this home for this animal, and which claims we have not verified. That knowledge exists nowhere in Shopify's data model. So our seven tools are the layer above the platform, with zero name overlap: Tool set_household_profile always on pet, weight, count, Wi-Fi bands, country, SIM willingness get_household_profile always on read it back — the shopper may have edited it by hand clear_household_profile always on erase it, and withdraw the gated tools check_compatibility always on the core: per-product verdict and reason explain_product_fit always on one product in depth + every unverified claim find_compatible_alternative gated what works instead; "nothing does" is a valid answer add_compatible_to_cart gated refuses blocked items; holds caveats until acknowledged The two gated tools do not exist until a household profile does — without one they cannot answer honestly, so they are withdrawn rather than left to guess. On the live page the tool count goes 15 → 17 the moment a profile is set, and back to 15 when it is cleared. Registration uses AbortController , per the spec. Why cross-border sourcing makes this necessary Every product here is sourced on Alibaba.com and shipped to a buyer in another country. That is not incidental — it is the reason the gate has to exist. Cross-border sourcing produces a class of failure a domestic store never sees, and our own sourcing research (done with Alibaba Accio Work ) turned up exactly these: Sourced fact What it means for the buyer The feeder lists plug variants for 8 countries , input voltage not stated A plug adapter changes the pins, not the voltage. A 220–240V unit on 120V US mains is destroyed on first use. The tracker lists LTE 850/900/1800/1900 MHz — frequencies, no band numbers, no 700MHz US carriers lean on 700MHz for rural and in-building coverage. Bars on the street, nothing in the basement. Tuya companion app, regions not stated The app is published per app-store region. No app, no setup. "Waterproof" with no IP rating A word, not a specification. Both of the first two are live checks in check_compatibility , driven by the shopper's country. Provenance, not just "unverified" Every field carries where its value came from, and the verdict engine reads it: confirmed (supplier's written spec), platform_listed (on the Alibaba detail page), inferred_tbc (a conservative inference — a hint, not a fact), pending (no source; the supplier must be asked). Not one field in this catalogue is confirmed . No supplier has returned written specifications, and the store says so on the page, next to the price. The open questions we have put to each supplier and not had answered are published there too. An earlier version of this data asserted four products were 2.4GHz-only and that the litter box had a multi-cat limit. Re-checking the listings showed both were our guesses . We deleted them. That made the demo less dramatic and the store more honest — and we rewrote the tests to assert the honest behaviour instead. People and agents on the same object The product template already shipped an "AI Compatibility Check" block with five rows, rendered as static placeholders. Rather than bolt on a competing widget, we restructured the verdict engine around exactly those five axes — Network compatibility, Region lock, Power requirement, Pet profile match, Essential extras — so the agent fills in the storefront's own block. The shopper is not reading a chat transcript about the product. They are watching the product page itself change, row by row, with a panel in the corner logging every tool call and letting them clear the profile by hand. WebMCP's trust model assumes a human is watching; this is the watching part. One source of truth for the shopper and the agent Every product arrived with no description at all . The supplier gave us specification fragments, not marketing copy — and writing confident prose around numbers we have not verified is the exact thing this store exists to avoid. So the product copy is rendered from MINTPAW_COMPAT — the same record, the same fields, in the same order that check_compatibility reads. A shopper and an agent cannot be told different things about a product, because there is only one source for both. It also means the unverified claims appear on the page , under a heading that reads "What we haven't checked ourselves", rather than only inside a tool response the shopper will never see. The honesty is not a property of the agent. It is a property of the store. Challenges we ran into Not duplicating the platform. Described above. It cost a rewrite, and it was the best thing that happened to the project. A stale-verdict bug. Changing the household left the previous run's verdicts painted on the page. Our own test suite caught it, not a person. Dawn renders two forms pointing at /cart/add , and only one holds the submit button; the obvious selector picks the wrong one. The refusal was cosmetic at first. We disabled Add to cart, but Shopify's express checkout button sat right underneath, still live, one tap from payment. A gate with a hole in it is not a gate. Accomplishments we're proud of It is a real store, live, with a refusal you can trigger yourself in about thirty seconds. And it ships 29 headless tests that run the real theme asset against the real catalogue and assert the things that would make the store a lie if they broke — chiefly that a 2.4GHz device is never ok in a 5GHz-only home, and that a hard block cannot be acknowledged away. What we lear

title: WardRound
pitch: Wardround is a WebMCP ICU shift co-pilot where agents read live risk, propose actions with visible provenance, and nurses approve every clinical workflow change.
about_excerpt: Wardround is a WebMCP ICU shift co-pilot where agents read live risk, propose actions with visible provenance, and nurses approve every clinical workflow change. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration ICU handover is a high-stakes coordination problem: vital signs change, teams need a shared view of risk, and every action needs a clear owner. We wanted to explore a more trustworthy role for an AI agent in that workflow. Wardround is built around one principle: the agent can prepare the next action, but a nurse remains the person who commits it. Instead of treating AI as an autonomous decision-maker, we designed it as a visible, accountable co-pilot. Wardround uses synthetic demo data only. It is not medical software and must not be used for clinical care. What it does Wardround is a simulated ICU shift-handoff and triage co-pilot built with React and WebMCP. The live ward board updates simulated patient vitals every four seconds, calculates risk from configurable thresholds, and ranks patients by urgency. An agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser can use scoped WebMCP tools to: identify patients by clinical risk; explain the top concern and recent trend; propose a patient flag, note, alert acknowledgement, or manual triage order; draft a shared, risk-sorted handoff summary. Clinical workflow changes are never applied by the agent directly. Write tools create a pending proposal with visible clinical provenance. A nurse can then approve or reject it in Wardround, and every proposal and decision is recorded in the audit trail. The shared handoff is the one deliberately narrow exception: an agent can draft it, while the nurse can edit and explicitly save it, turning it into a co-authored shift artifact. How we built it Wardround is a client-side React application built with Vite, JavaScript, CSS, and Zustand. A synthetic vital-sign feed updates the ward state every four seconds. A threshold-driven risk engine scores heart rate, SpO2, respiratory rate, temperature, and blood pressure, then produces a severity level and a visible top concern. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext and read live Zustand state only when invoked. Two read tools return tightly scoped patient-risk information. Four proposal tools can request clinical workflow changes, but can only add to the approval queue. A separate handoff tool updates only the shared handoff draft and cannot alter patient, triage, or approval state. The interface includes live risk cards, approval controls, provenance, a persistent audit log, a shared handoff surface, and keyboard-accessible dashboard views. Wardround is deployed on Cloudflare Pages and can be opened inside ChatGPT's in-app browser, where the agent discovers and calls the WebMCP tool surface. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was not making an agent call tools. It was making the safety model structural. We had to ensure that a write-capable tool could never bypass human review. The solution was to make every clinical write tool a thin translator from agent intent into a proposal object. Only the nurse approval path can apply a proposal to patient workflow state. Other challenges included: keeping tool results scoped and schema-tight; ensuring tools always read the current live ward state rather than stale data; preserving a nurse-approved manual triage order while the live feed continues to recalculate risk; making alert acknowledgements specific to the active concern so an old acknowledgement does not hide a new alert; creating a responsive dashboard that remains usable in desktop, split-pane, tablet, and mobile contexts; designing deterministic demo mode so the core workflow is reliable to show in a short presentation. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Wardround is more than a dashboard with AI language around it. The agent, interface, and audit model are connected through a real WebMCP tool surface. In particular, we are proud of: seven intentional WebMCP tools with clear boundaries; human-gated clinical proposals rather than autonomous workflow changes; visible provenance that explains why the agent made a suggestion; a real approval and rejection loop with patient-state changes only after approval; a shared handoff that preserves agent authorship, nurse edits, and audit history; a risk board that stays live while the human decision process remains explicit; a polished, responsive command-center interface designed for fast clinical scanning. What we learned We learned that trustworthy agent design is as much about product architecture as it is about prompting. A good tool description is not enough. The strongest safeguard is designing the system so that the tool cannot take an unsafe shortcut in the first place. Separating “propose” from “apply” made the safety story easy to demonstrate, easier to audit, and easier for a user to understand. We also learned that responsive UX matters for agentic products. A judge might experience Wardround in a full browser, a narrow split pane beside ChatGPT, or a mobile-sized viewport. The product has to preserve clarity and control in all three. What's next for Wardround Next, we would add authenticated roles, real clinical-system integrations, persistent audit storage, role-based escalation policies, and clinician-configurable thresholds. Before any real-world use, Wardround would require clinical governance, privacy and security review, validation against real workflows, and extensive safety testing. The current project is intentionally a synthetic prototype that demonstrates the interaction model: AI can help teams see and prepare; humans remain accountable for action. title: Muster — The Agentic Fire Drill
pitch: A shared command room where fire-safety teams and an agent rehearse changing conditions, trace every action, and keep final approval human.
about_excerpt: A shared command room where fire-safety teams and an agent rehearse changing conditions, trace every action, and keep final approval human. Like Comment Story Updates Muster command room: the human facilitator and agent work from the same live floor plan. Human-gated review: actions, missing responsibility, and the after-action report remain visible. Rehearse the decision before conditions change A stair becomes unavailable. Two people need assistance. Who owns the next action, and is everyone looking at the same plan? Muster is a shared tabletop fire-drill workspace for a building Fire Safety Manager and their exercise team. The facilitator and an agent work on one visible plan, instead of passing screenshots, checklists and chat summaries between disconnected tools. This is fictional training software, not a system for a live emergency. Try the working loop Open https://muster-fire-drill.vercel.app/ — no login is needed. Click Start scenario . Muster opens the Floor 07 rehearsal. The same button becomes Resume scenario , so exploring the building does not lose progress. Open 3D rooms · F07 . Orbit the cutaway, select a room, inspect its dimensions, and locate the planned equipment. The 2D drawing, 3D view and tool results share the same authored coordinates. Ask “Where is the extinguisher?” in Full chat . The answer names the item and its location. Expand the actual read_equipment call to inspect its input and output. Ask “Prepare S Tan for an assistance handoff to the Studio.” A cyan room-to-room path and four explicit checks appear. The assignment has not happened yet. Use the separate Confirm assignment control; the 3D figure, 2D marker, profile, roster and tool readback then show the same assignment. Continue the orange Next action controls. Introduce the unavailable stair, compare the authored alternatives, record the team's decisions, check responsibility gaps and prepare the after-action draft. Final report approval remains a separate human control. An assignment is not arrival, a cleared room or completed assistance. These states are deliberately not inferred from the animation. Why this is a WebMCP use case The important part is not another chatbot explaining fire safety. It is an agent operating the same inspectable work surface as the person. Muster registers 20 page-tool contracts through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each has a name, description, input schema and execution handler. The tools read or change the browser's deterministic exercise state; the interface and the trace show the consequence. Examples: read_room_profile can focus a 3D room and return its dimensions and fictional use. read_equipment can locate a planned item without activating it or certifying it. compare_routes returns both authored alternatives and can open a five-checkpoint 3D preview. The scripted blocked Stair B stops the preview before the landing. analyze_route_sketch measures a facilitator-drawn path and checks its endpoint against the exercise state. It does not approve a real escape route. prepare_team_handoff proposes a named responder, destination and task. There is no agent confirmation tool for this assignment. A changed exercise invalidates an older preview. read_status_board returns recorded responsibilities and confirmed assignments. stage_report prepares the after-action draft. It cannot approve it. The run_drill_manager tool routes a high-level intent through named plan, people, equipment and review functions. These are bounded software functions, not a claim that four autonomous AI agents are running. The built-in conversation is explicitly a local deterministic tool router, not a hosted LLM . It handles supported questions, shows its recognized purpose and actual calls, and asks for clarification when it cannot interpret a request. An external WebMCP-capable agent can discover and use the same page tools. Ordinary browsers retain the manual controls. What makes the interaction better The building has 18 selectable floors, but only three loaded schematic fixtures. Floor 07 is the executable office rehearsal; the retail and care-suite files are reference views. Unloaded floors say so instead of borrowing Floor 07 data. Inside Floor 07, the cutaway has six inspectable zones, original procedural furniture, equipment markers, responder figures, orbit controls, a true orthographic top view and a marker-follow route preview. People, places and tasks are connected through a reviewable assignment record. The complete chat session can be expanded. Each call exposes its purpose, input, output, duration and visible effect. Unsupported questions do not receive a recycled occupancy answer. A drill staged by an external agent goes to human review even if that agent skipped optional tutorial inspections. The Print pack captures the current training state in two A3 pages, a resolution-independent SVG and a 5500 × 4250 PNG. The numbered plan, equipment locations, responsibilities and facilitator checks travel together. Observed-at-assembly counts remain blank until a person verifies them. The preview fits the screen; printing retains full-size geometry. Implementation and proof Muster uses static HTML, CSS and JavaScript, a vendored Three.js runtime, a deterministic state machine and browser-local persistence. There is no building-system backend. The source and license are public: https://github.com/Arnie016/muster-webmcp The latest verification includes: 20 unit cases and 500 shuffled core-state workflows covering transitions, repeat-safe actions, path boundaries and human approval. Desktop and 390-pixel mobile interaction tests for chat history, distinct answers, next actions, room inspection, assignment confirmation, stale previews and reload. No-WebGL checks showing that the data, assignment and print workflows remain usable. Wall-intersection tests for all ten authored room-to-exit paths and the room-to-room handoff connections. Native Chrome WebMCP discovery of all 20 tools and execution against the deployed page, not just a mock API. Native agent preparation of an assignment, a separate human UI confirmation, and native tool readback of the shared result. A scripted native rehearsal reaching a review draft without approving it, including an alternate path that skips optional guide inspections. These tests establish compatible-browser execution, not autonomous planning, universal browser support, real emergency effectiveness or adoption by fire-safety teams. What existed before, and what was added Earlier projects explored ocean education and filmmaking review. They did not contain this fire-drill product, floor model or tool contracts. Muster's source, fictional training data and WebMCP interaction were built for this challenge. The first version exposed many controls but made it hard to know where to start. This iteration adds a clear Start/Resume action, a decision-by-decision guide, inspectable 3D rooms, meaningful question routing, real in-session tool receipts, human-confirmed team handoffs and printable training records. Codex assisted with implementation, test generation, debugging and visual iteration. The media package combines an AI-generated planning-room illustration and AI narration with real browser captures and an explanatory architecture diagram. Watch the latest 2:05 working-product demonstration : 3D room inspection, a human-confirmed responder assignment, a typed question with real tool results, and the printable review. The public YouTube demo shows this updated working build, with audio, English captions, actual page interactions and the tool architecture: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nY-HxnzdF2s Boundaries and next steps All people, counts, locations, dimensions, equipment records and incidents in the demo are fictional. The model does not establish equipment serviceability, accessible egress, fire spread, real occupancy or floor clearance. It cannot place calls, raise alarms, control doors or dispatch responders. The next meaningful validation is a facilitated usability session with Fire Safety Managers: can they find the next action, explain an unresolved owner, and distinguish a proposed assignment from a confirmed one? Real operational use would require approved plan imports, access controls, professional review and separate evidence. We have not demonstrated it. title: GenScape WebMCP
pitch: A persistent creative run that people and browser agents can inspect, pause, resume, and move into Canvas together.
about_excerpt: A persistent creative run that people and browser agents can inspect, pause, resume, and move into Canvas together. Like Comment Story Updates Creative work is not a single prompt. It moves through intent clarification, skill selection, model routing, asynchronous generation, review, and revision. Screen-driven agents are brittle in this environment: they can click the wrong model, lose a long-running job, repeat a paid request, or expose internal execution prompts. We wanted people and browser agents to share the same visible, recoverable workflow while the human keeps control of consequential creative choices. What it does The page registers six WebMCP tools for the current authenticated user: discover professional skills by workspace; start one real Agent, image, video, or audio run; read bounded public run status and result asset IDs; answer a pending Human-in-the-Loop question and resume the same run; list recent Canvas projects; create a visible Canvas project and return its stable URL. Mutating calls appear in the normal GenScape interface. Status recovery reuses the original run identity instead of silently creating another paid request. Tool results exclude system prompts, planning prompts, optimized execution prompts, provider channel IDs, credentials, routing diagnostics, and hidden model reasoning. How we built it We added a dependency-injected WebMCP layer on top of GenScape's existing authenticated client APIs. The imperative tools use document.modelContext.registerTool() , JSON Schema inputs, WebMCP annotations, one registration AbortSignal , and per-invocation cancellation signals. A React bridge owns registration for the signed-in page identity. Persistent Agent Run IDs connect start, status, Human-in-the-Loop answer, and resumed status. The Apache-2.0 public repository contains the competition adapter, clean standalone reference runtime, tests, and documentation. The existing VOZEB-PRO-derived GenScape host predates the challenge and remains under its existing BUSL/proprietary boundary; it is not copied or relicensed in the competition repository. The hosted demonstration integrates the new adapter with that existing host. The standalone runtime is explicitly a schema and lifecycle fixture and does not claim to generate paid AI media. Challenges The hardest boundary was returning enough state for an agent to make progress without leaking internal planning content. Long-running creation also required stable run identities, idempotent request identities, explicit Human-in-the-Loop state, and cancellation that stops pending browser requests without pretending an already accepted upstream task never happened. Accomplishments Six discoverable tools backed by the same visible workflows as the human UI. A complete start -> status -> answer -> status loop on one persistent run. Canvas creation with a stable URL. Registration removal on logout or page-owner change. Invocation cancellation forwarded through AbortSignal . Public result shaping with tests proving internal fields stay isolated. What we learned WebMCP works best when tools map to durable domain actions rather than UI controls. A reliable creative tool returns stable identities and visible state transitions, while the page remains the review and control surface. Browser-native tools are also a useful privacy boundary: the agent receives the public workflow state it needs, not the host's internal execution context. What's next Add tools scoped to the active Canvas selection, browser-mediated confirmation before high-cost generations, standardized output schemas when the proposal stabilizes, and progress notifications for long-running media work. title: OJS-WebMCP: Agent-Native Scholarly Publishing
pitch: An agent-native editorial control room for 58,000+ academic journals - AI triages submissions and synthesizes peer reviews while human editors retain final authority.
about_excerpt: An agent-native editorial control room for 58,000+ academic journals - AI triages submissions and synthesizes peer reviews while human editors retain final authority. Like Comment Story Updates Published OJS article demonstrating an agent-native scholarly workflow with seven native WebMCP tools available to in-browser AI agents. List all submissions example MCP Get full abstract details MCP 💡 Inspiration: The Plight of a Two-Person Editorial Team Years ago, I served as a journal editor for an academic journal ( cogito.unklab.ac.id ). Our editorial team consisted of just two people . Every week, a flood of new submissions arrived in our Open Journal Systems (OJS) queue. The administrative burden was suffocating: We spent hours manually reading through abstracts just to verify if papers met our scope. Finding and assigning reviewers with relevant domain expertise took days of cross-referencing past archives. Reviewers routinely missed deadlines, forcing us to constantly track due dates and send manual reminders. Reading divergent reviewer reports and drafting customized, polite, constructive decision letters drained our remaining mental energy. Academic peer review is the bedrock of human knowledge, yet over 56,000 journals worldwide are managed by small, overworked academic teams suffering from click fatigue and administrative burnout. When the WebMCP standard emerged from W3C, Chrome, and OpenAI, a lightbulb went off: Why should academic editors spend hours navigating dozens of nested tabs when an in-browser AI agent can co-pilot the editorial desk using the editor's live session? ⚡ What It Does OJS-WebMCP turns standard Open Journal Systems installations into an Agent-Native Editorial Control Room . Instead of relying on fragile scrapers or complex command-line MCP servers, our plugin directly registers 7 native WebMCP tools into the editor's browser session via document.modelContext.registerTool : Intelligent Desk Screening : The agent queries active queues across all 4 workflow stages ( ojs_list_submissions ) and retrieves full abstracts and verified author affiliations ( ojs_get_submission_details ) to evaluate scope compliance. Automated Peer-Review Tracking : Inspects reviewer assignments, identifies overdue reviews, and monitors reviewer recommendations ( ojs_get_review_rounds ). Live Review Synthesis : Connects directly to real reviewer feedback to synthesize a formal decision letter ( ojs_draft_editorial_decision ), accurately distinguishing between Minor Revisions , Major Revisions (Resubmit for Review) , Acceptance , and Decline . Approval-Gated Reviewer Reminder : Prepares and dispatches polite reminder notifications to overdue reviewers ( ojs_send_reviewer_reminder ). It enforces strict Human-in-the-Loop safety: the agent can only preview the reminder until the human editor explicitly approves it ( confirmSend: true ). Issue & Volume Planning : Discovers upcoming unpublished future issues ( ojs_list_issues ) to help editors schedule accepted papers for publication. 🛠️ How We Built It Universal OJS Generic Plugin : Packaged as a clean, modular plugin ( plugins/generic/webmcp ) compatible with modern OJS 3.4+ and 3.5+. Zero API Key Friction : Academic editors are researchers, not DevOps engineers. Our plugin leverages the editor's active browser session cookie and CSRF token. When ChatGPT or Chrome Agent opens the tab, it inherits authoritative editorial permissions immediately-no API keys or environment variables required. Granular REST Integration : Extended OJS's core routing architecture with custom, authenticated REST endpoints ( /submissions/{id}/reviewAssignments ) to expose granular review progress without leaking unnecessary personal identifiers. W3C WebMCP Standard : All tools implement structured JSON Schemas and async execution handlers conforming strictly to the official WebMCP spec. 🧗 Challenges We Faced Navigating OJS's Deep RBAC & Security Policies : OJS has a strict multi-layer authorization system ( SubmissionAccessPolicy , PolicyAuthorizer ). Ensuring that our WebMCP tools respected editorial permissions without bypassing journal security required deep reverse-engineering of OJS's internal routing stack. Ensuring Human Authority Over AI Actions : We did not want an agent going rogue and emailing professors unsolicited rejection letters. Designing the Approval-Gated Action pattern ( confirmSend gate) ensured that the AI serves as an indispensable assistant while the human editor always retains final academic authority. Data Sanitization & Metadata Quality : Normalizing OJS 3.5's multi-table author affiliation schemas ( author_affiliations and author_affiliation_settings ) and stripping raw HTML tags from abstracts so that LLMs receive clean, token-efficient context. 📚 What We Learned In-Browser MCP is the Future : Traditional MCP requires running local processes, configuring port forwarding, or sharing sensitive API tokens. WebMCP completely democratizes agentic AI for web-first workflows: you log into your web app, and your agent is immediately ready to help. The "Control Room" Dynamic : The winning paradigm for AI in knowledge work is not total automation, but co-browsing : the human provides the high-level strategy and moral judgment, while the agent handles workload tracking, data retrieval, and first-pass drafting. 🚀 What's Next Automated Reviewer Matching : Using paper embeddings and CrossRef/OpenAlex APIs to suggest the top 3 best-matching reviewers based on published citation history. Submission to PKP Plugin Gallery : Submitting this plugin to the official Public Knowledge Project (PKP) Plugin Gallery so that all 58,000+ academic journals worldwide can install OJS-WebMCP in a single click. An agent-native command center for freelancers and

 1 2 



 
 About the Project 

 ClientOps was inspired by a common problem for freelancers
 and small agencies: client work is scattered across task
 lists, email, spreadsheets, invoices, and notes. This
 makes it easy to miss follow-ups, lose track of delivery
 work, or delay billing. 

 I built ClientOps as an agent-native client-work command
 center. It brings projects, tasks, invoice drafts, and
 follow-ups into one workspace that both humans and AI
 agents can use. Through WebMCP, an agent can retrieve a
 workspace briefing, create work items, update task status,
 and prepare invoice or follow-up drafts. 

 The app was built with a lightweight HTML, CSS, and
 JavaScript frontend, Supabase REST persistence, and Vercel
 deployment. WebMCP tools are registered with
 document.modelContext.registerTool() and include
 structured JSON schemas so agents can interact with the
 app reliably. 

 A core design principle is human approval. Agents can
 prepare an invoice or message, but they cannot send it or
 charge a client automatically. This keeps automation
 useful without giving it unsafe control over financial or
 external actions. 

 While building the project, I learned how to design AI-
 facing tool schemas, expose browser actions through
 WebMCP, persist frontend state to a hosted database, and
 create safe human-in-the-loop workflows. 

 The main challenges were working with an evolving WebMCP
 API, supporting browsers where WebMCP is unavailable, and
 deciding which actions should be automated versus approved
 by a person. I addressed these with feature detection,
 fallback behavior, explicit read-only annotations,
 structured outputs, and draft-only financial workflows. 

 ClientOps demonstrates how websites can become reliable
 working environments for both people and agents—not just
 interfaces that an AI has to interpret visually.

title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: HomeOps
pitch: Your home remembers. Your agent can act.
about_excerpt:
Your home remembers. Your agent can act.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent reviews household data and proposes a safe, prioritized 30-day maintenance plan for human approval. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 HomeOps gives homeowners and AI agents one shared view of upcoming, overdue, and safety-critical maintenance. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent reviews household data and proposes a safe, prioritized 30-day maintenance plan for human approval. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 HomeOps gives homeowners and AI agents one shared view of upcoming, overdue, and safety-critical maintenance. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent reviews household data and proposes a safe, prioritized 30-day maintenance plan for human approval. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Home maintenance often breaks down for a simple reason: people lose track of what was done, when it was done, and what needs attention next. 

 That information is often scattered across reminders, receipts, manuals, notes, and memory. Traditional maintenance apps also create another system the homeowner must constantly update. 

 HomeOps creates one shared household-maintenance workspace that both a person and an AI agent can understand. 

 HomeOps tracks recurring household responsibilities such as HVAC filter replacement, smoke-detector testing, dryer-vent cleaning, and water-heater flushing. 

 For each item, it stores: 

 
 The last service date 
 The recurring maintenance interval 
 The calculated next due date 
 Overdue status 
 Estimated completion time 
 Useful notes, such as filter sizes or service instructions 
 

 Through WebMCP, an agent can: 

 
 Read the current household-maintenance record 
 Find overdue and upcoming work 
 Look up the history of a specific item 
 Create a prioritized maintenance-session proposal 
 Wait for the homeowner to approve it or request a revision 
 Read the homeowner’s decision 
 Record completed maintenance after explicit human confirmation 
 Add a new recurring responsibility after explicit human confirmation 
 

 The homeowner sees the same shared information in the visual interface. Agent actions and human decisions are also displayed in an activity history. 

 The central HomeOps workflow is collaboration rather than uncontrolled automation. 

 A homeowner can ask: 

 
 Audit my home for the next 30 days and propose the best three-task work session. 
 

 The agent reads the maintenance record, identifies urgent work, and creates a visible proposal. 

 It then stops. 

 The homeowner can approve the proposal or request a revision, such as asking for only the two shortest tasks. The agent can read that decision through a separate WebMCP tool before continuing. 

 HomeOps also prevents an agent from recording completed service or adding a recurring maintenance item unless explicit human confirmation is included in the tool call. 

 This allows the agent to take useful initiative while keeping meaningful decisions under human control. 

 HomeOps registers seven structured tools: 

 
 homeops_get_state 
 homeops_list_due 
 homeops_lookup_item 
 homeops_propose_session 
 homeops_get_plan_status 
 homeops_log_service 
 homeops_add_item 
 

 Each tool includes: 

 
 A focused natural-language description 
 A narrow JSON input schema 
 Required fields and validation limits 
 Read-only or state-changing annotations 
 A dedicated execution handler 
 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would need to inspect page text, locate interface elements, and guess which sequence of clicks changes the correct record. 

 With WebMCP, the website explicitly tells the agent what capabilities are available, which inputs are valid, and which operations modify state. 

 The visual interface and the WebMCP tools operate on the same household data. 

 HomeOps is a lightweight browser application built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. 

 The application: 

 
 Registers WebMCP tools directly in the browser 
 Stores household records in browser local storage 
 Calculates overdue and upcoming maintenance dynamically 
 Displays agent proposals and human decisions in one interface 
 Uses constrained schemas for safer tool calls 
 Requires no account, external database, paid API, or API key 
 Includes a fallback demonstration using the same tool handlers when experimental WebMCP browser support is unavailable 
 

 The working application is deployed publicly, and its complete source code is available in a public MIT-licensed GitHub repository. 

 The main challenge was designing a useful human-agent workflow rather than simply exposing buttons to an agent. 

 We wanted the agent to make meaningful progress while preserving clear human control. That led to the proposal-and-approval workflow: the agent may analyze the household record and recommend a plan, but the homeowner makes the final decision. 

 Another challenge was defining tools narrowly enough for an agent to choose the correct action reliably. We used descriptive names, limited responsibilities, strict schemas, bounded values, and explicit human-confirmation requirements for durable changes. 

 Because WebMCP is experimental, we also made the core application functional in ordinary browsers while exposing its full structured tool layer in supported environments. 

 
 Seven functional WebMCP tools 
 A working public application 
 Shared state between the interface and agent tools 
 A visible human approval and revision loop 
 Explicit confirmation requirements for important changes 
 Auditable human-agent activity 
 Persistent browser-based household memory 
 Responsive desktop and mobile design 
 No paid API or account requirement 
 Public MIT-licensed source code 
 

 WebMCP is most valuable when it does more than make an existing button easier for an agent to press. 

 It allows a website to become a shared workspace where a person understands the context visually while an agent receives precise and structured capabilities. 

 We also learned that good human-agent collaboration needs explicit intermediate states. “Proposed,” “approved,” and “revision requested” give both sides a reliable understanding of what should happen next. 

 The best agent experience is not necessarily the one with the most autonomy. It is the one with useful capabilities, reliable, shared context, clear boundaries, and understandable stopping points. 

 Future versions could add: 

 
 Optional calendar and reminder handoffs 
 Shared household-member roles 
 Appliance manuals and model information 
 Maintenance receipts and service records 
 Seasonal maintenance templates 
 Parts and supply lists 
 Contractor coordination 
 Proactive maintenance briefings 
 Optional encrypted cloud synchronization 
 

 The broader vision is a household operations layer where people remain in control while agents help organize, remember, and coordinate the work required to maintain a home.
