title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Tradeoff Cafe Simulator
pitch: Build a better café through simulation: set the goals, let WebMCP agents test operating choices, then decide which trade-offs are worth making.
about_excerpt: Build a better café through simulation: set the goals, let WebMCP agents test operating choices, then decide which trade-offs are worth making. Like Comment Story Updates Tradeoff Cafe Simulator Inspiration Small business owners make difficult decisions all the time, usually without the data, tools or spare time that larger businesses have. A café owner might notice long queues on a Saturday and think about adding another barista. But that simple change affects wages, customer numbers, service speed and weekly profit. These decisions are often made through experience or instinct. Experience is valuable, but it can be difficult to compare several options or understand every trade-off before making a change. I built Tradeoff Café to explore what this could look like with an agent involved. The owner still decides what matters and sets the boundaries. The agent does the repetitive testing, while the simulator handles the actual calculations. What it does Tradeoff Café is a browser-based decision simulator for a fictional café called Wicks Lane Coffee in Marrickville, Sydney. Owners can adjust: Staff numbers across different days and shifts Menu prices Opening hours Food and drink preparation levels The application simulates the café minute by minute and shows how those choices affect profit, revenue, queues, customers served, customers lost and waste. Users can save different scenarios, compare them side by side and inspect the calculations behind each result. The project is not described as AI-powered because the agent does not calculate the answers. The simulation engine owns the numbers. WebMCP simply gives an agent a safe and structured way to operate the same controls available to the user. Human and agent collaboration The most important part of the project is the relationship between the café owner, the agent and the application. The owner provides the real-world judgement. They decide what matters, set non-negotiable limits and lock any settings that should not be changed. For example, the owner might ask to reduce Saturday lunch waits without lowering weekly profit or changing Saturday's opening hours. The agent handles the repetitive work. It can read the current café setup, test staffing and pricing changes, run simulations, compare the results and save the strongest option. The application remains the source of truth. It performs every calculation, checks every constraint and records every action. The agent cannot silently replace the café's baseline plan. It can only suggest the change, and the owner must approve it. This creates a practical form of collaboration: the human provides context and makes the decision, while the agent explores the options and explains the trade-offs. How I built it I built Tradeoff Café with Next.js, React, TypeScript and Zustand. The simulation engine models a representative trading week using seeded, minute-by-minute calculations. It includes customer demand, queue behaviour, staffing capacity, preparation levels, waste, Australian wage assumptions, operating costs and GST. Seeded simulation means the same inputs and seed produce the same results, making comparisons repeatable and easier to trust. The interface includes editable controls, a visual week board, headline results, comparison charts, a scenario library, an activity log and a Show the working ledger. The ledger explains how revenue, labour, cost of sales, overheads and profit were calculated. I implemented WebMCP by exposing six tools directly from the webpage: get_cafe_context set_parameters run_simulation read_metrics save_scenario compare_scenarios These tools use the same store actions as the visible buttons. When an agent changes the roster, the controls, simulation results, charts and activity log all update on the page. There is no separate agent-only calculation or hidden copy of the application state. Challenges One challenge was making the café model realistic enough to create meaningful trade-offs. If staffing had no clear cost, the best answer would always be to add more people. If higher prices did not affect demand, the best answer would always be to charge more. I had to balance these relationships so that each decision had both benefits and consequences. Another challenge was keeping the agent and the user completely synchronized. I solved this by routing both tool calls and interface actions through the same state operations. This means the owner can always see what the agent changed. Safety and control were also important. The agent must respect locked settings and owner-defined limits. Invalid actions return clear explanations, and changing the baseline requires explicit human approval. Finally, the results needed to be understandable. A number alone is not enough for a small business owner. The interface therefore shows comparisons, plain-language summaries, likely ranges and a detailed financial ledger. What I learned I learned that WebMCP is most useful when it supports human judgement rather than trying to replace it. Agents are good at testing many combinations and handling repetitive work, but the owner understands the business, its customers and its real-world constraints. I also learned that trust depends on visibility. Users should be able to see what changed, why it changed and where every result came from. Giving an agent tools is only part of the experience; the actions and outcomes must also remain clear to the person making the final decision. Tradeoff Café shows how a normal interactive website can become a shared workspace for a person and an agent. The owner makes the decisions, the agent does the legwork, and the simulator keeps them both honest. title: AgentOps Command Center
pitch: AgentOps CC turns AI agents into safe SRE teammates. Using WebMCP, agents investigate incidents, analyze logs, recommend fixes, and execute approved remediations directly through the web app.
about_excerpt: AgentOps CC turns AI agents into safe SRE teammates. Using WebMCP, agents investigate incidents, analyze logs, recommend fixes, and execute approved remediations directly through the web app. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Steady state before the incident: error rate 0.32%, p99 110ms, five services green. Root cause, traceable to data: deploy dep_0006 cut DB_POOL_MAX from 50 to 5. The console during a SEV-2: environments on the left, live evidence in the centre, the incident record and available actions on the right. The smoking gun, one tool call away: "pool exhausted: 5/5 connections in use, 250 waiters." What the agent reads rather than guesses. p99 steps from flat to 3.13s, error rate to 16%, CPU pinned at 100%. Nothing changes without a human. The agent proposes the rollback, cites its evidence, and waits for Approve or Deny. Inspiration Modern incident response is still highly human-driven. When production breaks, engineers jump between dashboards, logs, traces, deployment systems, runbooks, and incident-management tools to understand what happened and decide what to do next. We wanted to explore a different model: what if an AI agent could actually operate an observability application, while humans remain in control of high-impact decisions? AgentOps Command Center was inspired by the idea that WebMCP can turn the web from something an AI merely reads into something an AI can meaningfully operate. What it does AgentOps Command Center is an AI-native incident response and SRE platform designed for collaboration between humans and AI agents. When an incident occurs, an agent can use WebMCP tools exposed by the application to: Monitor service health and production metrics Investigate logs and traces Analyze recent deployments Identify likely root causes Retrieve relevant runbooks and service ownership information Recommend remediation actions Request human approval for high-impact operations Execute approved actions such as rolling back a deployment Update incident status and generate a postmortem Instead of forcing an agent to navigate a complex UI like a human, WebMCP gives it structured, intentional capabilities. The human remains the decision-maker while the agent handles the investigation, reasoning, and execution. How we built it We built AgentOps Command Center as a web-based simulated production environment with an observability dashboard, incident center, deployment history, logs, runbooks, and remediation workflows. The key innovation is the WebMCP tool layer . We exposed application capabilities as structured tools that an AI agent can discover and invoke directly, including tools for: Service health Metrics and logs Incident investigation Deployment analysis Runbook retrieval Deployment rollback Incident updates Postmortem generation The application maintains a realistic incident scenario so the entire investigation and remediation flow can be demonstrated deterministically. The architecture separates read-only investigation capabilities from state-changing actions , allowing us to demonstrate a human-in-the-loop safety model. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what an AI agent should be allowed to do autonomously versus what should require human approval. We designed the system around three levels of interaction: Observe → Recommend → Act The agent can freely investigate the environment, but potentially destructive actions such as deployment rollback require explicit human approval. Another challenge was designing WebMCP tools around meaningful business actions rather than simply exposing individual UI buttons. We wanted each tool to represent an intentional capability an agent could reason about. We also had to make the simulated production environment realistic enough that the agent could correlate metrics, logs, deployments, and runbooks to arrive at a defensible root-cause hypothesis. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that AgentOps Command Center demonstrates WebMCP as more than an integration layer. The agent doesn't simply retrieve information from the website. It can investigate a live operational scenario, reason across multiple sources of evidence, recommend a remediation, obtain human approval, and execute the approved action through the web application. We are particularly proud of the human-agent interaction model: Agent investigates → Agent explains → Human approves → Agent executes → System recovers This creates a practical example of how WebMCP could enable a new generation of agent-native web applications. What we learned We learned that the most powerful agent experiences aren't necessarily about giving an AI unrestricted autonomy. The real opportunity is designing clear boundaries between what an agent can observe, what it can recommend, and what it can execute. We also learned that WebMCP changes the role of the website itself. Instead of being only a visual interface for humans, the website can become a structured operational environment that both humans and AI agents can interact with. The best tools are not necessarily the ones that expose the most functionality. They are the ones that expose the right capabilities with clear intent and safe boundaries . What's next for AgentOps Command Center Our next step is to connect AgentOps Command Center to real observability and infrastructure platforms. Future versions could integrate with: Grafana and Prometheus OpenTelemetry Kubernetes Cloud monitoring platforms CI/CD systems Incident management platforms Enterprise runbooks and knowledge bases We also want to introduce multi-agent collaboration, where specialized agents handle detection, diagnosis, security validation, remediation planning, and executive communication. Ultimately, our vision is an agent-native operations control plane where humans set the intent and guardrails, while AI agents continuously investigate, coordinate, and safely operate complex production environments. SDK for managing agent traffic that uses WebMCP
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Agentronics — Project Story 

 Inspiration 

 Somewhere in the last year, the web quietly got a second audience. Every mid-market e-commerce and SaaS site is now being visited not just by people, but by AI agents — ChatGPT with browsing, Gemini, Claude, Operator-style computer-use agents, and increasingly, structured tool-callers built on protocols like WebMCP . They search, they compare, they click "Add to Cart," they check out. Sometimes on behalf of a real human sitting one layer removed; sometimes fully autonomously. 

 Nobody asked these sites whether that was okay, and almost nobody's analytics stack can tell an agent-driven session apart from a human one. Conversion funnels are quietly getting corrupted. Attribution is breaking. And there is no identity layer, no permission model, and no audit trail for any of it — the equivalent of letting an entirely new class of user into your storefront with no ID check and no receipt. 

 That gap — agents are already transacting on the web, and nobody is governing it — is what started Agentronics. WebMCP's arrival ( navigator.modelContext , a native browser API letting a page register real tools an agent can call instead of scraping the DOM) was the moment the thesis stopped being speculative. It's not "agents might browse your site someday." It's "here's a W3C draft spec letting them do it natively, today, in Chrome." Someone has to sit in the middle and measure, govern, and eventually settle that traffic — the DoubleVerify/IAS role, but for the agentic web instead of the ad-tech web. 

 What We Built 

 To make the problem tangible instead of theoretical, we built a small but complete demonstration: a 4-page Amazon-style shopping flow (Home → Search → Cart → Checkout) where every user action is also exposed as a native WebMCP tool . searchProducts , addToCart , updateCartItemQuantity , proceedToCheckout , placeOrder — a dozen tools in total, registered directly against navigator.modelContext.registerTool() , no DOM-scraping polyfills, no screenshot loops. 

 Point an agent (we tested against Gemini CLI, connected through the Model Context Tool Inspector Chrome extension) at the site and give it a single instruction — "search for headphones, add the wireless noise-cancelling ones with quantity 2, go to cart, checkout, place the order" — and it completes the entire flow through structured tool calls instead of guessing at pixel coordinates. That's the world Agentronics is built to sit inside of: a web where agents transact through declared, inspectable tools, and where every one of those calls is an event someone can measure, authorize, and eventually reconcile. 

 How We Built It 

 
 The demo storefront : React 19 + Vite, Tailwind for styling, React Router for the four-page SPA flow, Zustand for cart state shared across pages. No backend — a hardcoded 12-SKU catalog across four categories, so the whole flow runs entirely client-side. 
 The WebMCP layer : a small useWebMCPTool hook wraps navigator.modelContext.registerTool() with mandatory feature detection ( "modelContext" in navigator ) and AbortSignal -based cleanup, so tools register on mount and cleanly unregister on unmount as the SPA routes between pages. Read-only tools ( searchProducts , viewCart , getProductDetails ) are marked readOnlyHint: true so an agent can call them freely; mutating tools ( addToCart , placeOrder ) route through client.requestUserInteraction() for confirmation before anything irreversible happens. 
 A visible trust surface : a small floating badge shows "WebMCP Active — N tools registered," with every registration and execution logged to console — because a governance thesis is only credible if you can actually see what an agent is doing on your page, not just trust that it's well-behaved. 
 The platform underneath : the @agentronics/sdk (published on npm) is what would sit behind a real deployment of this — agent detection across three ingestion paths (WebMCP-native, Web Bot Auth–signed agents like Operator and AWS AgentCore, and stealth Chromium-based agents caught via behavioral fingerprinting), feeding a GCP-hosted intelligence platform (Cloud Run, a GCS Parquet lake, Neon Postgres with pgvector, Vertex AI Gemini for natural-language insight generation). 
 Design system : a small, deliberate palette — near-black, periwinkle indigo, warm amber — built as reusable CSS/Tailwind v4 tokens with a proper light/dark flip (not a simple inversion; the accent colors are re-tuned so they glow instead of vibrate on a dark canvas). 
 

 Challenges We Ran Into 

 
 WebMCP is brand new and under-documented. It's a February 2026 W3C draft with almost no production examples to learn from beyond the spec text and a handful of Google demo repos. We had to work directly from the IDL rather than from tutorials, which meant a lot of double-checking against the spec to avoid hallucinating APIs that don't exist yet ( ModelContextClient.requestUserInteraction , the exact shape of a tool's content response array, the fact that tools are scoped to page lifetime and vanish on navigation). 
 SPA navigation vs. tool lifecycle. Because this is a client-side-routed React app, "navigating" between pages never actually reloads the document — so we had to be deliberate about which tools live at the Layout level (global, persistent: getCartCount , navigateToPage ) versus which are page-scoped and need to cleanly register/unregister via AbortSignal as components mount and unmount. Getting that boundary wrong either leaks stale tools or drops live ones mid-session. 
 Confirmation without friction. Mutating actions like addToCart and placeOrder need a human-in-the-loop checkpoint, but over-gating every tool call makes the agent flow no faster than a person clicking through manually. Deciding which tools get readOnlyHint: true and which route through requestUserInteraction() was less a technical problem than a governance-design one — which is, not coincidentally, the exact judgment call Agentronics exists to help other sites make at scale. 
 Making an invisible problem visible. The hardest part wasn't the code — it was building something that makes a genuinely abstract thesis ("your analytics are already being corrupted by agent traffic you can't see") into something a judge, or a Head of Growth at a DTC brand, can watch happen in front of them in thirty seconds. 
 

 What We Learned 

 Building the demo end-to-end sharpened the thesis rather than just illustrating it. Watching an agent complete a full purchase flow through declared tools — cleanly, quickly, with zero DOM guesswork — made the underlying problem concrete: this is not a hypothetical future traffic class. It is a fast, cheap, and increasingly common way for both real customers and their agents to transact, and right now it looks identical to a human session in every standard analytics tool. The measurement gap isn't coming — it's already open. That's the wedge Agentronics leads with, and building this demo is the clearest proof of it we've been able to put in front of anyone.

A shared WebMCP decision workspace where people and agents turn a rough structure idea into a transparent, reviewable project brief.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Planning a workshop or vehicle shelter starts with ordinary language but quickly becomes structured: use case, footprint, height, roof, openings, material, anchoring, budget, and unresolved site constraints. A normal chat can suggest an answer, but the reasoning often disappears into prose and the page on screen drifts out of sync. 

 BuildBrief Studio makes WebMCP the product interface between those two modes. The visual worksheet and six imperative Website Tools share one validated configuration. An agent can discover catalog options, compare two or three candidates, apply a partial recommendation, read the result back, review constraints, and create a preliminary brief. Write tools update the visible UI before returning and leave exact field-level receipts. If the person changes a value afterward, the revision advances and the old brief is visibly marked stale. 

 The demo is deliberately safe and easy to judge: no login, no personal information, no external API, and no production system. Every dollar value comes from a bundled synthetic catalog and a deterministic formula. Strict schemas and runtime validation reject extra fields and incompatible choices. Read-only annotations match behavior. Permit, access, anchoring, snow-load, and site conditions remain explicit human work rather than being hand-waved by automation. 

 The result is a small but complete example of what WebMCP enables: not an agent operating beside a website, but a person and agent collaborating through one observable decision surface. 

 How WebMCP is used 

 
 search_catalog discovers relevant structures from natural-language needs. 
 get_build_state grounds the agent in the person’s latest visible choices. 
 compare_builds evaluates two or three validated alternatives in one call. 
 apply_build performs a partial visible update and returns exact before/after changes. 
 check_constraints separates catalog fit from human verification. 
 create_build_brief renders a deterministic handoff artifact on the page. 
 

 All tools are registered imperatively from the top-level page through document.modelContext.registerTool . They use strict JSON Schema, truthful read/write annotations, concise structured output, and an AbortSignal lifecycle. 

 Quick judge path 

 Open the live demo in ChatGPT’s in-app browser, wait for “6 Website Tools ready,” and send the demo prompt shown on the page. Verify that the agent searches, compares against the $15,000 illustrative budget, applies an enclosed 20 × 24 workshop with a roll-up door, surfaces human checks, and creates the visible project brief. No credentials are required.

 Project Story — AgriVision AI 

 Farming decisions shouldn't require farmers to become experts in complicated software. 

 A farmer sees something wrong with a crop. They take a picture, but then they have to figure out what the problem is, check the weather, research treatments, calculate costs, and decide what to do next. 

 We built AgriVision AI to bring all of those decisions together. 

 But for the WebMCP Challenge, we wanted to go one step further. 

 Instead of making the farmer learn how to navigate every feature, AgriVision can now work with an AI agent. 

 A farmer can simply say: 

 “Analyze my tomato crop and create the cheapest recovery plan under ₹500 per acre.” 

 The agent can use AgriVision's WebMCP tools to analyze the crop, check relevant weather conditions, find treatment options, calculate costs, and build a recovery plan. 

 The farmer stays in control throughout the process. They can change constraints, ask the agent to optimize the plan, review the recommendation, and approve it before it is saved. 

 For example, if the first plan costs ₹700, the farmer can simply say: 

 “I can only spend ₹300.” 

 The agent can then use AgriVision again to find a better option. 

 That's what WebMCP changes for us: AgriVision isn't just a website that a farmer operates. It's a set of useful capabilities that an AI agent can operate with the farmer. 

 We designed AgriVision around a simple principle: 

 The farmer sets the goal. The agent handles the complexity. The farmer makes the final decision. 

 Our goal is to make agricultural technology feel less like another complicated tool to learn and more like an intelligent assistant that works alongside the people who need it. 

 AgriVision AI — AI-powered agricultural intelligence, built for humans and agents.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 I moved from Tampa to Cary earlier this year, and apartment hunting turned into a browser-tab nightmare almost immediately — one listing on apartments.com, another only on Zillow, a third found through a plain Google search, none of them agreeing on how to present rent, deposit, pet fees, or what utilities were included. I found myself manually retyping every listing into a note just to compare them side by side: with $n$ apartments and $m$ fields each, that's roughly $n \times m$ copy-paste operations before you can actually decide anything. My first instinct was "this needs a recommender system," but the more I sat with it, the clearer it became that recommendation was solving a step after the one actually costing me time — comparison had to come first. 

 NestCompare is the result: a spreadsheet-style comparison sheet where each apartment is a column and each row is a field — rent, lease terms, fees, amenities, your own notes — with the best value in each row highlighted automatically. If the built-in fields miss something, you add your own row on the spot, and the whole sheet exports to CSV or PDF. It also exposes itself as WebMCP tools (add_apartment, update_apartment_field, add_row, export_csv, and more) through the draft navigator.modelContext browser API, so an agent like Claude or OpenAI Codex can fill in or export the sheet directly. 

 It's built as a deliberately boring stack — static HTML/CSS/JS, no framework, no build step, deployed as-is — with data persisted to localStorage and PDF export via jsPDF. The shape of the product changed a lot along the way: it started as two separate paths ("pre-built" vs. "create your own"), which I eventually collapsed into one button and one sheet once it was clear the real missing feature was letting people add their own comparison criteria, not choosing a starting template. I also built a folder of fictional Cary, NC listing pages so the tool can be demoed without pointing at a real property's site. 

 The hardest part was resisting the urge to over-model apartment data — real listings don't agree on what matters, so the sheet needed a stable core plus an escape hatch, without becoming a spreadsheet clone. WebMCP itself is a moving target with no shipped implementation, so I had to feature-detect it and mirror every tool on a plain window global so it stays testable regardless. Without a live browser to check work in for parts of this build, I leaned on an automated jsdom test harness — which caught a real bug mid-refactor (a new apartment's name silently resetting to blank), a good reminder that "it looks right in the code" and "it works" are different claims. 

 Next steps 

 Save the data into database and make it sharable link, so can come back to the results after filling it up and select the best nest to stay.

title: WebMCP Chess Coach
pitch: An interactive chess coach that uses WebMCP and Stockfish to understand live positions, give Elo-aware guidance, and teach visually with hints, highlights, arrows, and candidate lines.
about_excerpt: An interactive chess coach that uses WebMCP and Stockfish to understand live positions, give Elo-aware guidance, and teach visually with hints, highlights, arrows, and candidate lines. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most chess engines are very good at telling players what the best move is, but not always at helping them understand why . For beginner and intermediate players, an engine output like +3.2 or a long principal variation can be useful, but it often feels more like an answer sheet than a coach. I wanted to build something that teaches the player how to think. That led to WebMCP Chess Coach — an interactive chess-learning experience where an AI agent can inspect the live board, analyse the position with Stockfish, and then teach directly on the board using highlights, arrows, candidate lines, and short coaching guidance. The goal is simple: do not just reveal the move — help the player notice the idea. What it does The user can play or analyse a chess position and then ask natural-language questions such as: "What am I missing here?" "Give me a hint, but don't tell me the answer." "Show me the threat." "Why was my last move bad?" "Show me the candidate line." The agent can then use WebMCP tools exposed by the page to understand and interact with the chessboard. The current toolset includes: get_board_state — reads the current FEN, side to move, game state, and legal moves evaluate_position — analyses the live position using Stockfish running locally in WebAssembly get_move_history — reviews how the current position was reached highlight_squares — draws attention to important pieces or squares show_move_arrow — visually demonstrates a move or threat show_candidate_line — displays a legal continuation without changing the real game clear_annotations — removes agent-created visual annotations show_coach_message — displays coaching guidance directly inside the website This creates a loop where the agent can read, analyse, explain, and visually teach on the same interface the player is using. Why WebMCP WebMCP is a strong fit for this project because chess coaching is not just a text problem. An AI model can describe a chess position, but the experience becomes much more useful when the agent can interact with the board itself. Instead of saying: "Your queen on h5 is hanging." the agent can: inspect the current board analyse it with Stockfish highlight f6 and h5 draw the move arrow from f6 to h5 show the continuation only if the player asks for it That turns the website into an agent-native teaching surface rather than a static chessboard with a chatbot beside it. How I built it The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite . react-chessboard renders the interactive board, while chess.js acts as the authoritative game state and validates all legal moves. For engine analysis, I use Stockfish 18 compiled to WebAssembly , running entirely client-side inside a Web Worker . This keeps the UI responsive and avoids requiring a backend for chess analysis. The engine receives the current FEN through the UCI protocol and returns: evaluation search depth best move principal variation The WebMCP layer is implemented using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool connects an agent capability to either the chess state, Stockfish, or React UI state. For example: User asks a question ↓ get_board_state ↓ evaluate_position ↓ Stockfish WASM ↓ highlight_squares / show_move_arrow ↓ React chessboard updates visually The real chess position is never mutated by coaching annotations. Candidate lines are validated on a temporary chess.js instance before they are displayed. Elo-aware coaching The interface also includes a player-level selector so the experience can be adapted for different skill levels. A lower-rated player may need a guided hint such as: "Before calculating your attack, check whether any of your pieces can be captured." while a stronger player may prefer something more direct: "Your queen is loose. Nxh5 wins material." The long-term idea is for the same position to be taught differently depending on the player's level and preferred coaching style. Challenges One of the biggest challenges was connecting several independent systems cleanly: React UI state chess.js Stockfish WASM Web Workers WebMCP tool registration agent-triggered board annotations The most important architectural decision was keeping a single authoritative chess state and making all coaching visuals non-destructive. Another challenge was making WebMCP tools useful beyond simple data retrieval. The project became much more interesting once the agent could not only read the position, but also visually modify the teaching interface through highlights, arrows, and coaching messages. I also had to handle browser-specific WebMCP behaviour, tool registration lifecycles, argument serialization during testing, and Stockfish's UCI messaging. What I learned This project changed how I think about agent interfaces. The most useful agent experiences are not necessarily ones where an AI replaces the interface. In this case, the board remains important because chess is fundamentally spatial and visual. WebMCP lets the agent and the user share the same interface: the human moves pieces normally the agent understands the exact live state the engine provides reliable chess analysis the agent decides how to teach the website visualises the explanation That combination feels much closer to an actual coach than a traditional engine window. What's next The next steps would be: deeper Elo-adaptive coaching progressive hint levels automatic post-game review puzzle and training modes stronger mistake classification opening and endgame-specific coaching personalised learning based on recurring mistakes The broader goal is to make engine-strength chess analysis easier to learn from, especially for players who understand the rules but still struggle to understand what the engine is trying to teach them. title: AetherDraw
pitch: An agent-native infinite whiteboard that turns visual canvases into structured spatial playgrounds for autonomous AI agents via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An agent-native infinite whiteboard that turns visual canvases into structured spatial playgrounds for autonomous AI agents via WebMCP. Like 2 Comment Story Updates One-shot AI Inference Pipeline generated via create_diagram with automated Dagre layout, smooth cubic Bezier routing. Bi-directional co-creation: Agent detects human-drawn Auth Service and routes a smart Bezier connector from API Gateway in 1ms. WebMCP Inspector drawer displaying all 11 registered browser tools, JSON parameter schemas, and real-time execution telemetry. Console inspecting document.modelContext.getTools(), exposing typed WebMCP tool definitions directly to AI agents. Autonomous diagram synthesis running directly inside the browser runtime via native WebMCP tool invocation. Full AI inference architecture on infinite canvas with responsive camera auto-framing and zero shape collisions. Spatial introspection via get_canvas_state followed by instant atomic connector routing using connect_elements. One-click visual styling: apply_theme restyles the entire canvas into the handcrafted Nordic Frost color palette. Hierarchical Microservices Architecture template with multi-tier services and obstacle-avoiding edge routing. Public open-source repository on GitHub (ShreyashChaurasia/AetherDraw) with full source code, MIT license, and tests. In-app architecture modal detailing the 4-layer WebMCP tool suite, W3C protocol integration, and Excalidraw attribution. Project Story: AetherDraw Inspiration Visual whiteboards like Excalidraw, Miro, and FigJam are the ultimate playground for human thinking. Whenever I need to design a backend architecture, trace a data pipeline, or brainstorm an idea, I immediately open a blank canvas. Spatial thinking feels natural to humans because our brains process relationships, hierarchies, and groupings through physical distance and layout. However, for AI agents, these visual canvases have always been a complete black box. Today, if you want an AI model to interact with a spatial whiteboard, you are forced into one of two terrible compromises: The Vision Approach: Taking screenshots, feeding them into a multimodal LLM, and hoping the model can approximate pixel coordinates. This is slow (taking several seconds per step), costly, and prone to severe spatial hallucinations. The Brittle Automation Approach: Simulating fragile mouse drag-and-drop events on raw HTML5 <canvas> elements that easily break whenever the viewport pans, zooms, or resizes. When I saw the WebMCP specification, the lightbulb turned on. WebMCP provides the exact missing bridge: instead of forcing AI agents to squint at canvas pixels from the outside, the web application can expose its internal scene AST, geometric bounds, and layout engines directly to the browser runtime via document.modelContext . I wanted to build a whiteboard where AI agents and humans collaborate as equals: an agent-native infinite canvas where an AI can read, build, style, and route complex diagrams in single-digit milliseconds with deterministic precision. That is why I built AetherDraw. What It Does AetherDraw is an open-source, agent-native infinite whiteboard powered by WebMCP. It extends Excalidraw core with a suite of 11 schema-typed tools organized into four functional layers: Spatial Inspection (Layer A): get_canvas_state , get_selected_elements , and find_elements serialize the visual canvas into a structured abstract syntax tree (AST). The agent receives bounding boxes, node types, text labels, and connection graphs without needing a single pixel screenshot. Algorithmic Synthesis (Layer B): create_diagram takes high-level intent (nodes, roles, connections, title, and direction) and executes automated graph layout in a single call, dynamically framing the result to the viewport. Fine-Grained Mutation (Layer C): add_elements , update_elements , delete_elements , and connect_elements allow agents to perform atomic edits, relabel nodes, modify styles, and route smooth Bezier arrows that snap to human-drawn shapes. Layout & Styling (Layer D): apply_auto_layout reorganizes messy hand-drawn clusters into clean hierarchical structures; apply_theme transforms palettes across 7 themes (Classic, Nordic Frost, Cyberpunk Neon, Pastel Dream, Blueprint, Minimal Dark, Solarized); and export_canvas creates high-res PNG or SVG artifacts. Crucially, AetherDraw enables bi-directional co-creation . A human can sketch a couple of boxes and type "Auth Service". The agent calls get_canvas_state , detects the human's shapes, understands where they sit in space, and uses connect_elements to hook up the rest of the backend architecture seamlessly. How I Built It I built AetherDraw as a solo developer using React 19, TypeScript 5, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. 1. Canvas Engine Foundation I chose Excalidraw core ( @excalidraw/excalidraw ) because it represents the gold standard of hand-drawn collaborative canvases. However, Excalidraw was built strictly for human input. To make it agent-native, I wrapped the imperative canvas API with an adapter layer that tracks non-deleted scene elements, manages selection state, and coordinates camera zoom. 2. WebMCP Protocol Implementation I integrated @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill to register all 11 tools directly on document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool defines a strict JSON Schema for its parameters, validates inputs, and reports structured telemetry. In addition to the runtime polyfill, I published a static discovery manifest at /webmcp.json following the official WebMCP specification. 3. Automated Graph Layout Theory Rather than asking the AI model to guess coordinates, AetherDraw uses battle-tested layout algorithms: Dagre (Sugiyama Hierarchical DAG Method): Computes vertex layers, minimizes edge crossings, and assigns discrete ranks. ELK.js (Eclipse Layout Kernel): Handles orthogonal graph layouts and complex topologies. The agent simply specifies the relational graph $G = (V, E)$. The layout engine solves the layering and coordinate assignment in $O(|V| + |E|)$ time, placing each node $v_i \in V$ at an optimal coordinate $(x_i, y_i)$ with zero shape collisions. 4. Organic Cubic Bezier Arrow Routing Connecting boxes with straight lines looks messy and cuts across neighboring elements. I wrote a dedicated router that calculates smooth cubic Bezier curves: $$B(t) = (1-t)^3 P_0 + 3(1-t)^2 t P_1 + 3(1-t) t^2 P_2 + t^3 P_3, \quad t \in [0, 1]$$ Where: $P_0 = (x_{\text{start}}, y_{\text{start}})$ is the anchor point on the source shape. $P_3 = (x_{\text{end}}, y_{\text{end}})$ is the anchor point on the target shape. $P_1$ and $P_2$ are dynamically computed control points offset along the primary flow axis. The router detects intervening obstacle nodes within the direct corridor. If an obstacle exists, the route dynamically diverts through outer gutter channels to avoid line crossings. For horizontal peer nodes sitting side-by-side, it routes directly from the right border of the source to the left border of the target without piercing the shape boundary. 5. Viewport Fit-Screen Mathematics When generating large diagrams, placing shapes off-screen ruins the user experience. I implemented a dynamic framing calculation that computes the total bounding rectangle of all diagram nodes: $$x_{\min} = \min_{i} (x_i), \quad x_{\max} = \max_{i} (x_i + w_i)$$ $$y_{\min} = \min_{i} (y_i), \quad y_{\max} = \max_{i} (y_i + h_i)$$ Given available viewport dimensions $W_{\text{avail}} = W_{\text{window}} - 2 \cdot \text{pad} x$ and $H {\text{avail}} = H_{\text{window}} - 2 \cdot \text{pad}_y$, the camera zoom factor $z$ is computed as: $$z = \text{clamp}\left(\min\left(\frac{W_{\text{avail}}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}, \frac{H_{\text{avail}}}{y_{\max} - y_{\min}}\right), z_{\min}, 1.0\right)$$ The canvas camera pans directly to the center coordinates: $$(x_{\text{center}}, y_{\text{center}}) = \left(\frac{x_{\min} + x_{\max}}{2}, \frac{y_{\min} + y_{\max}}{2}\right)$$ This ensures the entire diagram immediately fills the screen at crisp resolution with proper toolbar clearance. 6. Developer Telemetry & Inspector To make WebMCP observable, I built a slide-out Inspector drawer that lists all registered tool schemas, streams live invocation events, and displays execution duration timers down to the millisecond. Challenges I Faced Imperative Canvas State vs. Asynchronous Tool Calls: Excalidraw maintains its own internal React reconciliation cycles, selection maps, and rendering loops. Bridging asynchronous WebMCP tool executions into Excalidraw's imperative API required careful synchronization so that rapid sequential tool calls wouldn't cause state tears or canvas flickering. Smart Arrow Routing without Box Penetration: Early prototypes had arrows that routed straight through boxes or connected to the far side of target nodes. Writing the horizontal peer detection logic and obstacle corridors required extensive coordinate geometry and edge-case testing, especially ensuring that arrowheads snap flush

 Inspiration 

 Theatre information is scattered across articles, PDFs, venue announcements, and historical lists. Finding a reliable answer often means opening several documents, searching manually, and checking whether every detail is supported. 

 I built Praxa to explore a better model: a shared research workspace where a person can ask naturally and a browser agent can use purpose-built tools to retrieve evidence, compare productions, and present a concise answer with page-level citations. 

 What it does 

 Praxa is a WebMCP-native research assistant focused on Broadway and West End theatre. It exposes three typed browser tools: 

 
 ask_theatre answers factual theatre questions using indexed source documents. 
 search_theatre_archive performs semantic search and returns the strongest page-level passages without requiring an LLM response. 
 compare_productions compares two productions using a user-selected focus, such as venue, opening date, or run length. 
 

 Every agent action updates the same visible workspace used by the person. This keeps the human in the loop: the user can see the request, answer, latency, sources, page numbers, and supporting excerpts. 

 Why WebMCP 

 A conventional assistant must scrape page text, infer controls, or imitate clicks. Praxa instead publishes explicit tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . 

 The tools have JSON input schemas, bounded inputs, read-only annotations, untrusted-content annotations, cancellation support, and structured results. This gives agents a reliable interface while preserving the normal human-facing website as progressive enhancement. 

 Before WebMCP, a person could ask Praxa questions manually, but an agent could not reliably discover its research capabilities or invoke them directly. Now people and agents can work in the same interface: an agent can search the archive, inspect evidence, ask a grounded question, compare productions, and leave the result visible for the person to review. 

 How I built it 

 The production application uses: 

 
 FastAPI and Uvicorn for the web service and research APIs 
 the WebMCP imperative API for browser-native tool registration 
 LangChain for retrieval-augmented generation 
 Chroma for persistent vector search 
 Hugging Face sentence-transformer embeddings 
 OpenRouter for grounded answer generation 
 Railway for containerized production hosting 
 GitHub Actions for linting, tests, coverage enforcement, and Docker builds 
 

 The retrieval system downloads theatre PDFs, divides them into overlapping chunks, embeds them, and stores the index on a persistent Railway volume. Answers are restricted to retrieved excerpts and include citation labels matching the page-level source records shown in the interface. 

 The production pipeline also rejects provider metadata and uncited generated claims, retries invalid responses once, and safely abstains if a grounded answer cannot be produced. 

 Challenges I faced 

 The first major challenge was converting a human-only Streamlit prototype into a genuine WebMCP product. I replaced the original entry point with a same-origin FastAPI application and created tool-specific APIs that both return structured results and update the visible interface. 

 Cold-start behavior was another challenge because the embedding model must be loaded before retrieval. Persistent Chroma storage prevents the source index from being rebuilt after each deployment. 

 Live testing also exposed an intermittent model-provider response that returned safety metadata instead of a theatre answer. I added a tested output-quality gate that rejects metadata and uncited claims before they can reach users. 

 Challenge-period work 

 Praxa existed before the hackathon as a theatre RAG prototype. During the submission period, I meaningfully extended it with: 

 
 three working WebMCP tools; 
 a new shared human–agent interface; 
 FastAPI research and semantic-search endpoints; 
 structured tool schemas and annotations; 
 visible agent-driven UI updates; 
 citation-alignment and output-quality safeguards; 
 Railway deployment, CI checks, and WebMCP regression tests. 
 

 The dated GitHub pull requests and commit history clearly separate this work from the earlier prototype. 

 What I learned 

 This project taught me that WebMCP is more than browser automation. It creates a stable contract between websites and agents while preserving the website as the place where people understand and supervise the work. 

 I also learned that agent-ready applications need more than tool registration. They need careful schemas, visible state, deterministic evidence retrieval, cancellation handling, security boundaries, production monitoring, and graceful failure behavior. 

 What’s next 

 Next, I would expand Praxa into a broader performing-arts research network with licensed data sources, venue and ticket integrations, saved research collections, multilingual retrieval, evaluation datasets, and tools that help audiences, journalists, students, and theatre professionals collaborate with agents.

title: Relay WebMCP
pitch: An AI stand-in that handles what you'd approve, refuses what you'd not, and hands off the rest while you're away.
about_excerpt: An AI stand-in that handles what you'd approve, refuses what you'd not, and hands off the rest while you're away. Like Comment Story Updates the tightened copy, heartbeat dot, RELAY label, one-line pitch Project Links Inspiration People who need to step away unexpectedly, a scheduled procedure, a custody handoff, a hospital stay with no warning, have always faced the same bad choice: hand someone full access and hope they use good judgment, or go dark and let everything queue up until they're back. Password managers solve access, not judgment. Auto-replies solve nothing, they just defer. What was missing was a way to hand off exactly the part of a decision someone is comfortable handing off, nothing more, with everything outside that boundary going to a person they trust instead of an inbox nobody's watching. WebMCP made a genuine version of that possible: a tool surface that changes based on who is looking and what state things are in, computed live in the browser rather than fixed on a server, is what lets the boundary actually get enforced instead of just described in a policy nobody reads. What it does Relay lets someone prepare a delegate agent before they become unreachable, one that keeps answering the people who depend on them, inside limits they set in advance, escalating anything outside those limits to a person they trust. The absence doesn't have to be the same shape twice. A contractor covering client work during a scheduled procedure. Two co-parents who need logistics handled without every message pulling one of them out of their day. Someone who ends up in the hospital with no warning and no time to write instructions for anyone. A support lead pulled into a family emergency mid-shift. Relay works the same way whether the absence was planned six weeks out or started an hour ago. A person prepares a delegate agent in advance: an interview-style briefing agent asks about their specific situation and drafts a full configuration for them to review, rather than making them author policy from scratch. When the person goes unreachable, the delegate starts answering the people and agents who depend on them, inside a boundary of autonomy the principal defined, escalating anything outside that boundary to a named human, and producing a complete accounting of what happened. How we built it Relay registers seven WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, but which tools are visible depends on who's looking and what state the relay is in: the principal sees five configuration tools while their relay is still in draft, a recipient sees nothing until the relay goes active and then sees exactly one tool (ask_delegate) scoped to their own access token, and everyone can request a record of what happened, filtered to what they're allowed to see. That conditional, per-visitor tool surface, not just per-server but per-session, is something a hosted MCP server can't express, and it's the core of why this is a WebMCP-native product rather than a chatbot with extra steps. Underneath that, the delegate's reasoning loop uses Claude to classify every incoming request into a tier (autonomous, flagged, refused) and propose a reply, then a deterministic check runs after the model and before any action is taken. Challenges we ran into The interesting part of building this turned out not to be the AI, it was the governance. Anyone can wire a chatbot to answer messages while someone's away. The harder problem is making sure it never quietly does more than it was authorized to do. If a request's dollar value exceeds an autonomous ceiling, it has to be forced to flagged regardless of what the model said. If nothing matches, it has to fall through to a configured default and never default to autonomous. The model proposes. The code disposes. Getting that rule to actually hold, every time, took more iteration than the AI side of the build did. The other hard challenge was the permission surface itself, described above, getting the tool set to genuinely change per visitor and per state rather than just claiming to. Late in the build, rehearsing the actual demo flow surfaced a genuine problem: the briefing interview was losing its own memory mid-conversation, because session state lived in server memory with no guarantee two requests land on the same instance. We caught it by testing the exact path a judge would take, not by reading the code, and moved session state into the database before it ever reached a recording. Accomplishments we're proud of The deterministic override actually holds under a live test, not just in theory: a request the model classified one way gets forced to a different tier the moment it crosses a rule the principal set, and the reply shown updates to match, so the tier badge and the words never contradict each other. The tool surface is genuinely live, not simulated, confirmed by calling document.modelContext.getTools() directly in an actual WebMCP-enabled browser and watching the exact same page return a different tool list depending on who's asking. And we found and fixed the session-memory bug above before it ever showed up in a recording, by actually rehearsing the demo end to end instead of assuming the happy path would hold. What we learned For a product where an agent has a multi-turn conversation, the failure modes that matter show up in an actual multi-turn conversation, not in a single request, and the only way to catch them is to actually run the conversation end to end rather than trust that a single successful test proves the whole path works. What's next There's no principal login yet, a relay's own URL currently acts as the access credential the way a recipient's token does, which is fine for a single-user demo but not for a multi-tenant product. Principal authentication is the next piece. Beyond that, more activation conditions (calendar-based, not just missed check-ins) and letting an approver resolve a flagged request directly through their own agent, not just by clicking Approve, are the two directions we'd take this next. title: Corre
pitch: programmable financial infrastructure that gives AI agents the ability to hold, receive, spend, save, and manage USDC autonomously.
about_excerpt: programmable financial infrastructure that gives AI agents the ability to hold, receive, spend, save, and manage USDC autonomously. Like Comment Story Updates The Architecture of Economic Sovereignty: Building Corre "Technology is at its most potent not when it dazzles with complexity, but when it dissolves the invisible borders that dictate a person's financial destiny." Inspiration: The Weight of an Invisible Boundary Growing up in an era defined by hyperconnected digital highways, I was struck by a jarring paradox: while information travels across continents in milliseconds, financial opportunity remains chained to geography. I watched friends and families in emerging markets watch their life savings erode under the quiet violence of local currency devaluation, barred from basic wealth preservation vehicles like dollar-denominated yields or fractional shares of the world’s most innovative enterprises. To open a brokerage account or access an inflation-resistant yield vault often required arbitrary minimum balances, weeks of bureaucratic verification, and exorbitant cross-border wire fees. The traditional financial apparatus had decided that billions of people were simply too expensive to serve. At the same time, we stood on the precipice of another revolution: autonomous AI agents capable of reasoning, analyzing market data, and orchestrating complex tasks. Yet, these agents were trapped in sandbox silos—intellectually capable, but economically paralyzed. Corre was born at the intersection of these two convictions: Financial self-sovereignty must be a universal human right, not a geographical privilege. The future of global wealth creation belongs to autonomous, user-aligned AI agents interacting natively with decentralized rails. What Was Already There vs. What We Built During This Period Before this project, Corre already had a working foundation: Existing Backend & Core App : A dashboard for savings vaults (~$8.5\%$ standard yield, ~$6.2\%$ shielded yield) and US stock trading via Jupiter. Remote MCP Server ( mcp.corre.bond ) : An SSE endpoint where external AI assistants like Claude Desktop or ChatGPT could read public vault rates and search stocks remotely. What We Built & Updated During This Period: Created the Client-Side WebMCP Engine ( frontend/src/webmcp ) : We built an in-browser runtime that taps into the emerging Chrome document.modelContext API, with a fallback bridge on window.__correWebMCP . Instead of relying on a backend server, the web app itself registers tools directly into the browser session. Built Client-Side WebMCP Tools : We created a dedicated suite of browser tools: get_savings_yield : Pulls live vault APYs in real time. get_savings_balance : Reads the user's active shielded and standard balances. deposit_savings_vault : Generates and signs on-chain Solana deposit transactions right inside the browser. get_stock_quote & list_available_stocks : Queries live tokenized stock prices and directs users to exact asset pages. get_naira_exchange_rate & get_supported_banks : Provides real-time fiat on/off-ramp conversion rates. Integrated Native In-Browser Wallet Signing : We connected Privy’s Solana wallet provider directly into the WebMCP context so an AI agent can prepare a transaction, and the browser wallet can sign it without ever exposing private keys. Interactive WebMCP Inspector UI & Agent Toast System : We designed an in-app inspector badge and dialog where users can see every tool registered with their browser, test tools with live JSON output, and copy JavaScript snippets. We also built an agent notification system ( WebMcpAgentToast ) that shows live toasts whenever an AI agent calls a tool. ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Autonomous AI Agents │ │ (Browser Agents, ChatGPT, Claude Desktop, Cursor) │ └────────────┬───────────────────────────────┬─────────────┘ │ │ [Browser ModelContext] [Remote MCP / SSE] │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │ Corre WebMCP │ │ mcp.corre.bond │ │ Client Runtime │ │ Remote Gateway │ └────────┬─────────┘ └────────┬─────────┘ │ │ └───────────────┬───────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Corre Core Settlement Engine │ ├─────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┤ │ Yield Engine │ Equities Engine │ Identity & Safety │ │ • Standard Vault │ • Fractional US Stocks │ • Privy Embedded Solana Wallet │ │ (~8.5% APY via Lulo) │ (AAPL, TSLA, NVDA...) │ • Gas-Sponsored Relayer │ │ • Shielded Vault │ • Jupiter Liquidity V2 │ • Session Circuit Breakers │ │ (~6.2% APY pUSD) │ • Zero-Commission Swaps │ • Local Fiat Ramp (PAJ / NGN) │ └─────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘ 4. Democratized Tokenized US Equities By routing through liquidity aggregators directly on-chain, Corre allows anyone with an internet connection to purchase fractional shares of US stocks (Tesla, Apple, Nvidia, S&P 500) starting from as little as $\$5.00$ USDC, with instant settlement and $0\%$ broker commissions. 5. The Native Browser WebMCP & Remote Agent Gateway We pioneered a dual-rail agent interface: In-Browser WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) : Direct browser-level tool registration exposing real-time portfolio telemetry, stock quotes, and savings deposits directly into browser-native AI agents without exposing private keys. Production MCP Gateway ( https://mcp.corre.bond ) : A secure Server-Sent Events (SSE) protocol endpoint allowing ChatGPT, Claude Desktop, and Cursor to analyze vault positions, project multi-year compounding scenarios, and prepare in-chat transactions. 6. Frictionless Onboarding & Key Quorum Security Web3's steepest hurdle has always been the friction of 12-word seed phrases and gas fees. We integrated: Privy Embedded Solana Wallets : Instant email/social login with cryptographic key quorums. Automated Gas Relayer : A backend fee-payer service that subsidizes Solana transaction fees, providing a pure, Web2-grade user experience with Web3 custody. Challenges We Ran Into: The Forge of Complex Engineering Building a production-ready application at the frontier of Web3 and AI forced us to confront problems that textbooks rarely cover: 1. Reconciling Asymmetric Cryptographic Signing Environments Browser AI agents require fast, deterministic execution, but signing financial transactions requires strict user consent. When integrating Privy’s Solana signers into the WebMCP runtime, EVM wallet hooks initially collided with Solana keypairs. We refactored the entire context lifecycle to decouple wallet discovery, handle partially signed serialized versioned transactions ($V0$), and implement structured error propagation so that AI agents receive actionable diagnostic feedback instead of silent failure states. 2. Defense-in-Depth Against Agentic Exploits Exposing financial actions to autonomous agents introduces novel threat vectors. We developed strict server-side validation layers: Transaction size limits ($\le \$500$ per in-chat operation). Transaction instruction inspection (stripping out malicious CloseAccount instructions or fee-payer drainage attempts). Rate-limiting circuit breakers backed by persistent PostgreSQL state. 3. The Gas Relayer Payload Mismatch Once the wallet was recognized, deposits failed with an HTTP 400 error. The frontend was posting { signedTransaction: serializedTransaction } , but our backend controller was strictly checking for req.body.transaction . We fixed the payload key to { transaction: serializedTransaction } and updated the response parsing to correctly capture sponsorData.transactionHash || sponsorData.signature . 4. Opaque Chrome Model Context Errors When a tool threw an error (like an invalid deposit amount), Chrome displayed a generic message: "Tool was executed but the invocation failed. For example, the script function threw an error" Because the engine was letting exceptions bubble up as unhandled promise rejections, Chrome hid the real cause. We wrapped tool invocations in structured try/catch blocks inside engine.ts . Now, if something goes wrong, the AI agent receives a clear, readable JSON error (e.g., {"status": "error", "error": "Minimum deposit is 1 USDC"} ) and can tell the user what to fix. What We Learned: Beyond Code and Syntax Building Corre was a masterclass in systems thinking. I learned that: Simplicity is the highest form of security : The most resilient distributed systems are those that hide mathematical complexity behind intuitive, human-centered interfaces. AI Agents need native economic primitives : The next billion on-chain transactions will not be initiated by manual human clicks, but by autonomous agents executing financial strategies programmed to maximize their owners' long-term welfare. AI Agents need clear contracts, not just text prompts : If an API returns an unhandled rejection, an AI agent gets confused. Robust err

title: GoSX 3D Studio
pitch: A 3D studio where browser agents stage exact scene edits and artists keep the only Apply.
about_excerpt: A 3D studio where browser agents stage exact scene edits and artists keep the only Apply. Like Comment Story Updates The problem 3D editors are dense and stateful. An artist can see which object matters; an agent needs stable identities, exact properties, and the current revision. Pixel automation guesses through controls, while a detached API pulls the work out of the artist's spatial context. That leaves a bad choice: manually repeat the agent's suggestions, or trust an invisible write. GoSX 3D Studio keeps person and agent aligned before anything becomes canonical. What it does The webpage itself is a shared collaboration surface. It registers exactly four focused tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...): scene_get_state reads canonical scene state and its revision. scene_find_objects searches stable IDs and names with typed filters. scene_focus_object brings the hierarchy and Inspector to the object under discussion without changing canonical state. scene_preview_actions validates and stages 1–12 reversible operations at an exact revision. A browser agent can inspect 150 entities, resolve Board to stable ID board, focus the visible Studio, and stage a rename plus material assignment. The artist sees the exact before/after diff in the live 3D viewport, can orbit the reversible result, and keeps the only Apply action. There is intentionally no WebMCP commit tool. The review retains affected IDs, actor, policy evidence, revision boundary, and result fingerprint. Apply sends only an opaque proposal ID; the server commits the exact stored transaction through the existing revision-safe engine. Stale work is rejected. Activity distinguishes agent://webmcp proposal authorship from human://webmcp-review approval. That makes WebMCP the product interaction model, not a badge or generic CRUD wrapper: the person and agent point at the same stable object, reason from the same revision, and create an auditable handoff from machine-prepared preview to human-approved canonical state. Why the experience is better Agents handle precise hierarchy search and proposal preparation without taking commit authority. Artists stay inside the spatial context of the real editor instead of translating detached advice. Focus, preview, approval, and discard reconcile in the same document without tearing down the Scene3D canvas. Every staged edit is bounded, policy-checked, attributable, and visibly reversible. A persistent viewport outcome makes the R → R+1 handoff obvious after approval. Implementation browser agent -> four WebMCP tools -> same-origin proposal service -> server checks -> Workspace.Execute(propose, revision R) -> visible non-applied review card -> human Apply UI -> exact stored transaction -> Workspace.Execute(direct, revision R) -> canonical R+1 Both human and agent paths reuse Workspace.Execute; WebMCP is an adapter over the same SceneDoc and typed SceneIR used by the Studio. Proposals are session-owned and one-use, expire, carry revision checks, and are committed through CSRF-protected UI actions. Server-side review checks fail closed and expose pass evidence for each staged operation. The demo uses GoSX server rendering, WebGPU-first Scene3D with WebGL fallback, Go, JavaScript, and Kubernetes deployment by immutable image digest. Challenge-period work GoSX 3D Studio existed before August 25, 2026. It already had its SceneDoc model, 3D workbench, stable IDs, fingerprints, undo/redo, revision conflicts, and a shared transaction path for human and agent commands. Those foundations are not claimed as Challenge work. During the submission period we added the WebMCP adapter; structured inspection, search, and focus; session-owned non-canonical proposals; server checks; the visible review and exact-commit boundary; typed-call evidence; shared-demo reset; focused tests; and deployment materials. We also added same-document Scene3D reconciliation, WebGPU-first rendering, a compact evidence dock, and a refined PBR sample scene. Final polish added the in-app native-tool disclosure, presentation-size reversible diff, sticky human-only approval, persistent revision outcome, race-safe reset, conflict-free hierarchy keyboard behavior, and a recorder that verifies the exact handoff. The pre-Challenge comparison point is commit a216194ebc0f415a011aa780386773c0750bccf9 from July 29, 2026. How we used AI A WebMCP-capable browser agent interprets the artist's goal, chooses page tools, finds relevant objects, and prepares a typed proposal with rationale. The Studio retains schema validation, revision checks, policy, fingerprints, authority, and canonical state; it does not hide a second chat backend or give the agent a privileged write path. OpenAI Codex helped trace the architecture, connect WebMCP to Workspace.Execute, implement and review boundaries, author tests, debug native-browser behavior, run checks, and prepare documentation and demo materials. Buckley generated and pushed the final structured commit, and Buckbot ran the pre-merge review. Verified public flow The current immutable deployment was built from main merge commit 1e68684cbe6d5a8a10257c1ea9b85e40c9046125 and pinned as sha256:facffa246e9377d49db38c5d0c008e4e6db1a593f10e1e5ebfaff8f2475e9b9c. On September 4, native Windows Chrome 152 completed the deployed flow at 1920×1080 using native document.modelContext and WebGPU: exactly four registered page tools and 145 rendered meshes; Inspect, Find, Focus, and Stage completed against stable ID board; the exact Board → Launch Board and Carved Wood → Brushed Steel proposal left canonical revision 3 unchanged; the visible Apply control advanced the scene exactly once to revision 4; PROPOSED and APPROVED activity shared the same plan token; Evidence remained 31/31 current; the same mounted WebGPU canvas survived with zero document reloads and three managed same-document transitions; the shared demo was then visibly reset to a clean canonical Board at revision 5 for judges. Then, it searches the structured scene data for board and resolves the stable object ID board. Notice that the coral piece is still selected. The search has not imitated a user click.
