title: Prompt Lab
pitch: Prompt Lab — an agent-ready prompt library where humans and AI can create, organize, and reuse prompts together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Prompt Lab — an agent-ready prompt library where humans and AI can create, organize, and reuse prompts together through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Create and test prompts with structured inputs, variables, and AI-assisted generation. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Create, organise, and manage reusable prompts in one workspace. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Browse a structured prompt library with categories, ratings, and reusable templates. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Build specialised AI agents and manage their prompts directly inside Prompt Lab. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Discover community prompts and reusable workflows created for different use cases. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Create and test prompts with structured inputs, variables, and AI-assisted generation. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Create, organise, and manage reusable prompts in one workspace. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Browse a structured prompt library with categories, ratings, and reusable templates. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Build specialised AI agents and manage their prompts directly inside Prompt Lab. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Discover community prompts and reusable workflows created for different use cases. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Create and test prompts with structured inputs, variables, and AI-assisted generation. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Prompt engineering is becoming an important part of how people work with AI, but good prompts are often scattered across documents, chats, notes, and different AI tools. 

 We wanted to build a place where prompts could be treated as reusable assets rather than disposable messages. 

 That led to Prompt Lab — an agent-ready prompt library where humans can create, organise, improve, and reuse prompts, while AI agents can interact with the same library through WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 Prompt Lab helps users: 

 
 Create and organise reusable prompts 
 Group prompts into categories 
 Build specialised AI agents 
 Generate prompts through agent conversations 
 Select and save useful prompts directly from the chat 
 Search, update, and manage an existing prompt library 
 

 With WebMCP, Prompt Lab also exposes structured actions to AI agents. 

 Instead of an agent visually interpreting the interface and guessing which buttons to click, it can discover supported actions such as creating, searching, retrieving, or updating prompts and execute them directly through the website. 

 This creates a shared workspace where both humans and agents can work with the same underlying prompt library. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Prompt Lab is a strong fit for WebMCP because the product contains many structured actions that are useful to both people and AI agents. 

 Traditionally, an AI interacting with a website may need to rely on screenshots, DOM interpretation, or browser automation. 

 WebMCP allows us to expose the capabilities of Prompt Lab explicitly. 

 For example, an agent can understand that the application supports actions such as: 

 
 search_prompts 
 get_prompt 
 create_prompt 
 update_prompt 
 delete_prompt 
 create_agent 
 get_agent_prompts 
 

 This makes agent interactions more reliable, understandable, and efficient. 

 It also creates a better user experience because a user can describe what they want naturally while the agent performs structured operations within Prompt Lab. 

 How we built it 

 Prompt Lab was built as a modern web application using React, TypeScript, Vite, and supporting backend/data services. 

 We designed the product around two main experiences: 

 
 A human-facing prompt management interface 
 An agent-facing capability layer powered by WebMCP 
 

 For the WebMCP implementation, we registered application capabilities using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . 

 Each tool includes a clear description, input schema, validation, execution logic, and structured output. 

 Where possible, the WebMCP tools reuse the same underlying application logic as the normal user interface rather than creating a completely separate system. 

 This means both humans and agents operate on the same prompt data and workflows. 

 We also designed the agent chat so generated prompts can become interactive content directly inside the AI response. Users can select the prompts they want and save them into their library without switching to a separate workflow. 

 Challenges we faced 

 One of the biggest challenges was understanding how WebMCP should fit into an existing product architecture. 

 It was tempting to treat WebMCP as a separate integration layer with duplicated application logic, but we learned that a better approach is to expose existing product capabilities through shared services. 

 We also faced challenges around: 

 
 Detecting whether WebMCP was available in the current browser environment 
 Preventing duplicate tool registration during development 
 Keeping the application functional in browsers without WebMCP support 
 Designing tool schemas that were simple for agents to understand 
 Making agent-generated prompts interactive without duplicating the same content elsewhere in the UI 
 Maintaining a consistent experience between human-driven and agent-driven actions 
 

 Another challenge was designing the demo itself. We wanted to demonstrate WebMCP as more than browser automation, so we focused on showing an agent interacting with Prompt Lab through clearly defined application capabilities. 

 What we learned 

 The project changed how we think about websites designed for AI agents. 

 A website no longer has to expose functionality only through buttons, forms, and visual interfaces. 

 With WebMCP, applications can expose their capabilities directly to agents while still maintaining a normal interface for humans. 

 We learned that the strongest implementation is not about adding as many tools as possible. It is about exposing a small set of useful, well-defined actions that map directly to real product capabilities. 

 We also learned that designing for humans and agents together creates new product possibilities. Instead of replacing the human interface, the agent becomes another way of interacting with the same application. 

 What's next 

 We would like to continue developing Prompt Lab into a broader collaborative prompt workspace. 

 Future improvements could include: 

 
 Prompt version history 
 Shared team libraries 
 Agent-created prompt collections 
 Prompt performance and evaluation data 
 More advanced search and filtering 
 Additional WebMCP capabilities 
 Cross-agent prompt sharing 
 Collaborative workflows where humans review and approve agent-generated changes 
 

 Our broader goal is to explore what software looks like when websites are designed from the beginning for both humans and AI agents .

 I also performed a design audit to ensure the UX is understood and the UI to be appealing.

title: Flock docs
pitch: Agent-native spreadsheet and document writing
about_excerpt: Agent-native spreadsheet and document writing Like 1 Comment Story Updates One workspace for people and agents. Organize Papers and Spreadsheets in the same live, browser-based workspace Flockdoc exposes workbook structure, ranges, formulas, formatting, and sheet operations through WebMCP. Document roles and sharing remain part of the product experience while agents receive context-appropriate tools. Inspiration Flockdoc began with a frustration I repeatedly encountered while using ChatGPT to create schedules for my family I liked creating a visual calendar with ChatGPT, but iteration happened at the wrong level of abstraction. When using ChatGPT with images, it would generate a file that I could not edit. Alternatively, if it used Google Sheets, the agent was limited with a set of point and click tools. Even a small request (change a cell value, restyle a header, add one column, or update a single section) could turn into another complete file-generation cycle with images. If I used Sheets, it would be painful watching ChatGPT stumbling to make the most simple edits on the page. The model did not have a structured way of reading or editing the spreadsheet, so it usually meant it was easier for me to just make the edits myself. Ultimately, I want my agent to be able to collaborate with me on the same document at the speed and accuracy I expect from coworkers. That idea became Flockdoc , a collaborative workspace for Documents and Spreadsheets where people use a familiar visual editor while agents interact with the same live application through WebMCP. What it does Flockdoc lets people create, organize, share, and edit documents in a browser-based workspace. Its spreadsheet editor exposes structured WebMCP tools that allow an agent to understand and modify the workbook currently open on the page. An agent can: inspect the workbook and discover its worksheets; read a targeted range, including values, formulas, styles, merges, and dimensions; write values and formulas into a precise A1 range; format cells without rewriting their contents; merge cells and adjust rows or columns; create, rename, reorder, or remove worksheets; and read the edited range again to verify the result. Flockdoc also exposes workspace-level tools for listing, creating, renaming, moving, and safely trashing documents. The important difference is that the agent is not manufacturing a replacement workbook somewhere else. It is operating on the same spreadsheet the person can see and edit. A person can define the goal and apply judgment where it matters. The agent can handle repetitive structure, formulas, formatting, and bulk changes. The person can then refine the result manually and ask for another targeted change without starting over. Why WebMCP Spreadsheets are especially difficult for agents to operate through ordinary visual automation. A grid may contain hundreds of similar-looking cells, hidden formulas, merged regions, formatting, and multiple worksheets. Clicking based on coordinates is slow and fragile, while passing entire files back and forth discards the live context of the application. WebMCP gives Flockdoc a typed, page-defined interface to the editor’s real capabilities. Instead of guessing which visible cell corresponds to a request, an agent can call read_range for Budget!A1:F20 . Instead of regenerating a workbook, it can call write_range to update only the required cells, format_range to apply presentation changes, and then read the range again to confirm the outcome. This makes the interaction more accurate, auditable, and efficient. It also lets Flockdoc expose only the tools appropriate to the current context. For example, users with view-only access receive inspection tools but not mutation tools. WebMCP turns the application itself into the source of truth. How I built it I built Flockdoc as a React and TypeScript application using Vite. The spreadsheet and rich-text editing surfaces are powered by Univer. When the browser provides document.modelContext , Flockdoc registers two contextual groups of tools: Workspace tools for document lifecycle operations such as listing, creating, renaming, moving, and trashing flockdocs. Spreadsheet tools that are registered while a workbook editor is mounted and operate directly through Univer’s workbook and range APIs. Each tool has a JSON schema, a focused description, input validation, and structured results. Spreadsheet writes use explicit A1 ranges and rectangular JSON matrices. Inputs are bounded, worksheet names are validated, range dimensions must agree with the supplied data, and tool failures are returned as useful errors rather than silently corrupting the workbook. Tool registration follows the page lifecycle. Spreadsheet tools appear when the editor is mounted and are removed with an AbortController when the user leaves it. Read-only users receive only read_me , inspect_workbook , and read_range . Flockdoc also includes real-time collaboration infrastructure, operation-based spreadsheet synchronization, Yjs CRDT updates for Papers, durable revision recovery, checkpoints, sharing roles, and recoverable deletion. The frontend is deployed through AWS CloudFront and integrated into the existing Flockfly platform. Challenges The first challenge was choosing the right tool granularity. One giant “update spreadsheet” tool would have recreated the same whole-file problem I was trying to solve. Very small cell-by-cell tools, however, would require excessive calls and make common tasks tedious. A1 ranges became the useful middle ground: precise enough to limit changes, but expressive enough for meaningful operations. Another challenge was preserving spreadsheet semantics. A cell is more than its displayed value. It may contain a formula, style, merge relationship, row height, or column width. Reading and writing those properties independently was necessary to support targeted edits without damaging unrelated parts of the workbook. Permissions were also important. An agent should not become a path around application authorization. Flockdoc derives its WebMCP capabilities from the same editing context used by the human interface, so view-only access does not expose mutation tools. What I learned I learned that designing tools for agents is just like building multi-user applications. Real-time collaboration required separating durable operations from full snapshots. Replacing entire workbook snapshots during live edits caused refresh flicker, revision conflicts, and the risk of overwriting newer work. Moving to operation-based synchronization and explicit recovery checkpoints made collaboration much more predictable. I found that synchronous collaboration with agents creates a magical experience that feels similar to having a human collaborator working alongside you. The same enhancements that make human collaboration delightful do the same for agent-to-human collaboration. title: ScopeShift: Evidence Lease — Native WebMCP
pitch: AI proposes, you approve, WebMCP executes — exactly once. Refunds bound to human-approved evidence, verifiable end-to-end on Google Cloud.
about_excerpt: AI proposes, you approve, WebMCP executes — exactly once. Refunds bound to human-approved evidence, verifiable end-to-end on Google Cloud. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Reasoning and authority are separate: Gemini + ADK propose, a human approves, the gateway validates, native WebMCP executes. The evidence: an order-issued invoice states the duplicate $18 charge and exact refundable balance. Document AI parses and binds it. Executed via the shop's own native WebMCP tool - exactly once. One $18 refund committed; balance $14 to $32, captured $36. Durable truth in Firestore: exactly one refund document - 1800 cents, duplicate_charge, demo_credit - matching lease and order. The crash test, disclosed on screen: the purchase intentionally records two $18 captures to reproduce a real duplicate charge. The audit trail: six Cloud Run log events for one order - purchase, invoice, Document AI evidence, lease, execution, denied replay. Paired and verified: the server checks the shop's 4 native WebMCP tools before anything runs. The merchant declares the surface. Replay attack on camera: the used approval is submitted again. Server rejects it - lease_replayed. Refund count stays at 1. Approval mints an Evidence Lease: 120 seconds, one execution, bound to this order and invoice. Countdown live: 1:58 remaining. Explicit WebMCP pairing: a one-time code pairs exactly one shop tab. The Chrome extension is only a relay - no cookies, no other tabs. Inspiration An AI agent that can act needs a clear boundary between a proposed action and permission to carry it out. We built ScopeShift around one question: what exactly did the user approve, and is that approval still valid when the action executes? Approval can become unsafe if it is reused or if the supporting evidence changes. We wanted it to behave like a single-use ticket: specific to one action, time-limited, and checked when presented. ScopeShift: Evidence Lease connects native WebMCP execution with evidence-bound human approval. What it does ScopeShift turns a duplicate-charge complaint into an approved, auditable refund. Important demo notice: We deliberately configured one USD 18 purchase to produce two USD 18 charges. This is an intentional error scenario, not an accidental checkout malfunction. All amounts are synthetic demo credits; no real payment processor is involved. The workflow separates four roles: Role Actor Responsibility Propose Gemini 3.5 Flash + Google ADK Analyze accepted evidence and propose a refund Approve Human Approve the exact action and amount Validate Policy gateway on Cloud Run Check evidence, approval, browser binding, expiry, and prior use Execute Paired shop tab through native WebMCP Invoke the shop's refund tool; the gateway commits the authorized result Approval creates a 120-second, single-use Evidence Lease bound to the approved action and evidence through SHA-256 digests. The gateway rechecks those conditions at execution time and permits only one committed refund per lease. The model cannot approve its own proposal or directly commit a refund. Two verified flows, one system. The video demonstrates the duplicate-charge flow; the /judge reader page documents a second verified flow — evidence change wi th automatic re-approval ($18 approved → $8 prior credit found → old approval invalidated → new $10 approval). Same lease rules, different evidence story. Why WebMCP matters The shop declares its own structured tools through native WebMCP . The ScopeShift Chrome extension discovers and relays those tools without DOM scraping, synthetic clicks, or cookie export. The AI workspace and shopping site run on separate origins. Explicit pairing connects one authenticated shop tab, and the server verifies its tool catalog before purchase. The recorded demo shows four verified native tools. WebMCP provides the execution interface. ScopeShift adds evidence-bound human approval and server-enforced replay protection. The recorded native flow was tested on Chrome 151 with WebMCP enabled and the ScopeShift extension. The intentional duplicate-charge scenario We chose a scenario with a clear expected result: USD 36 captured for one USD 18 item, leaving USD 18 to refund. The user confirms the purchase, and the shop intentionally records two charges. The shop issues a PDF invoice for that order after purchase. Document AI reads the uploaded invoice, and the gateway checks it against the order's issued document. Gemini proposes a USD 18 refund. A person approves that exact amount. The paired shop invokes its native refund tool. The server records one refund, raising the demo balance from USD 14 to USD 32. We deliberately attempt to reuse the approval. The server returns lease_replayed ; the refund count remains one. The Google Cloud Console segment reviews stored logs and Firestore records from that same order after execution. It is recorded verification, not a new live run during submission. How we built it Agent: A private Python service uses Gemini 3.5 Flash through Vertex AI and Google ADK, with structured output validation. Evidence: Document AI extracts invoice information; the gateway validates it and stores an order-bound evidence record. Policy: A Node.js/TypeScript gateway on Cloud Run owns approval, evidence checks, expiry, and execution authorization. Persistence: Firestore transactions update the refund, balance, and lease state atomically. The lease ID also identifies its refund record. Audit: Cloud Logging records key events, including purchase, invoice issuance, evidence acceptance, approval, execution, and replay denial. Challenges we ran into Making evidence belong to the action. The invoice had to be issued after purchase and matched to the current order. We added rejection paths for documents from other orders, modified files, and stale revisions. Getting Document AI to read the intended amounts. It initially separated invoice labels from their values. We revised the generated PDF layout to keep them together while preserving strict rejection of missing or conflicting evidence. Enforcing single use across the browser and server. A disabled button could not enforce the policy. We placed the decisive checks and refund update in the gateway's transaction path, then demonstrated rejection of a used approval. Accomplishments that we're proud of Connected human approval to native WebMCP execution across separate AI and shop interfaces. Recorded one USD 18 refund and visibly rejected reuse of its approval. Matched the demonstrated order and lease to Firestore records and Google Cloud logs. Made the intentional duplicate charge and synthetic-credit boundary explicit. What we learned Structured output is not execution authority. schema_valid confirms output structure; the gateway must independently validate the proposed action. Evidence changes require renewed approval. Digests identify changes, while explicit server checks invalidate outdated authorization. Tool access and action authorization are separate responsibilities. A callable browser tool still needs policy checks before changing merchant state. What's next for ScopeShift Separate development work covers revised and conflicting invoices; the submitted video focuses on one refund and replay rejection. Our next priorities are shared relay routing across gateway instances, broader validated invoice formats, stronger multi-merchant authentication, and extending the existing capability-grant model to additional action types. The current demo supports allowlisted demo sites and their own order-issued PDFs. Real payment integration remains outside its scope. Built With chrome cloud-run document-ai firestore gemini google-adk google-cloud webmcp Try it out github.com scopeshift-gateway-fhw3pwjsja-uc.a.run.app Submitted to All Things Agentic Hackathon Created by Solo project — I designed and built everything: the Evidence Lease concept and policy gateway (Cloud Run/TypeScript), the WebMCP relay Chrome extension, the Gemini + Google ADK agent (Python), the Document AI evidence pipeline, Firestore exactly-once ledger, Terraform infra, and the demo shop, video, and docs. title: Companion
pitch: Turn human observations into confirmed, traceable memory that AI agents can query through WebMCP—preserving evidence, distinguishing hypotheses, and leaving missing information unknown.
about_excerpt: Turn human observations into confirmed, traceable memory that AI agents can query through WebMCP—preserving evidence, distinguishing hypotheses, and leaving missing information unknown. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable at reasoning, but I became interested in a different problem: What happens to the human context they need to reason well? People constantly produce valuable context through observations, measurements, decisions, hypotheses, conversations, and experience. Much of it remains unstructured: spoken aloud, written in notes, or trapped inside applications that were designed for humans rather than agents. My initial idea was simple: let a person describe something naturally, preserve what they actually said, and make that context reusable by an AI agent later. But that immediately raised a harder question: If AI helps structure that memory, how do we prevent the AI's interpretation from silently becoming part of the human evidence? That question became the foundation of Companion. Companion is a human-to-agent memory layer : Human context → Confirmed memory → WebMCP → Agent reasoning The application owns the evidence. The agent owns the reasoning. What Companion does Companion starts with unrestricted natural-language human input. A person can describe an observation without learning a schema or filling out a complex structured form. Companion proposes a subject, but the person reviews and can correct both the original text and the subject before confirming it. Once confirmed, the original evidence is preserved first. AI then helps construct a semantic representation of that evidence, but model output does not automatically become factual memory. Semantic construction happens in two stages: Semantic discovery finds candidate relations. Epistemic classification determines how each candidate is supported by the confirmed source. Relations are classified as: SOURCE_EXPLICIT SOURCE_STRONGLY_IMPLIED AGENT_INFERRED Only source-grounded relations are eligible for factual memory after deterministic validation. AGENT_INFERRED relations are kept outside that factual boundary and are never silently exposed as human-confirmed facts. This means AI can help build the memory without being allowed to redefine the evidence. Why WebMCP The next problem was retrieval. My first instinct was to make Companion intelligent enough to decide which stored information an agent needed. Experiments changed that design. If the external agent already understands the user's question and will ultimately reason over the answer, adding another AI inside Companion to predict what that agent needs duplicates intelligence and creates another place where interpretation can go wrong. Instead, Companion exposes two read-only WebMCP capabilities: get_companion_vocabulary Returns a deterministic, reusable vocabulary of factual semantic relations available for a subject. query_companion_memory Retrieves exactly the factual relations identified by the vocabulary IDs selected by the external agent. This creates an incremental protocol: Agent inspects vocabulary → selects evidence → retrieves it → evaluates sufficiency → requests more if necessary → reasons Companion does not interpret the question, rank evidence, decide sufficiency, or generate the final answer. WebMCP is a particularly good fit because it gives the application a discoverable and invocable capability without coupling Companion to one specific agent runtime. The same architecture could be implemented with custom APIs and agent-specific integrations. WebMCP changes the integration boundary: Companion can expose its memory capability directly from the application so compatible agents can discover what evidence exists, request only the evidence they need, and reason over it without Companion being coupled to a specific agent runtime. What becomes possible is a collaboration in which a human can capture context naturally once, while multiple compatible agents can later discover and retrieve that confirmed memory through a shared application-owned interface. How I built it Companion was built as a sequence of small architectural experiments rather than by implementing the first design that seemed plausible. The core pipeline became: Human natural-language context ↓ Human review and confirmation ↓ Persist confirmed raw evidence ↓ Stage A: semantic discovery ↓ Candidate semantic graph ↓ Stage B: epistemic classification ↓ Deterministic validation ↓ Factual memory / inference boundary ↓ Reusable factual vocabulary ↓ WebMCP deterministic lookup ↓ External-agent reasoning The AI-assisted part is deliberately bounded. Everything that can be checked mechanically—IDs, references, schema compliance, candidate correspondence, source excerpts, routing, lookup—is validated deterministically. One design principle emerged from this: Pay for intelligence once, then reuse the structured result deterministically. The confirmed rawText remains the authoritative primary source. Semantic memory stays traceable to it, and semantic-processing failure cannot erase the original evidence. Persistent semantic IDs are also owned by Companion rather than by the model, preventing temporary model-generated identifiers from becoming accidental persistent authority. Challenges I faced Semantic correctness is not factual correctness One of the biggest lessons came from deliberately trying to break the semantic builder. A model can identify a relationship that is completely reasonable and still not be justified by the source. For example, observations may strongly suggest a diagnosis. That does not mean the human actually reported that diagnosis. This forced me to separate semantic discovery from epistemic classification . A useful semantic candidate is not automatically a fact. Preventing silent information loss Another problem appeared when increasing epistemic strictness. A strict prompt could reduce unsupported inference but also cause legitimate semantic relations to disappear. The solution was a no-deletion architecture: Stage A discovers candidates first, and Stage B must classify every candidate exactly once. That makes three different failures observable: discovery failure, classification failure, inferred semantic content that should not become factual memory. Deciding where retrieval intelligence belongs I also experimented with retrieval strategies. The important realization was that Companion does not need to understand the user's question if the external agent already does. The external agent can inspect Companion's reusable vocabulary, choose the IDs it needs, retain previous context, and request additional evidence incrementally. That removed an unnecessary intelligent selector from Companion and produced a cleaner responsibility boundary. Keeping the demo honest The public challenge demo uses synthetic evidence and browser-session-local memory. It intentionally does not claim production readiness, universal semantic correctness, or objective truth. Human confirmation means that the representation corresponds to what the human confirmed. It does not mean the human statement itself is objectively true. That distinction became important enough to be part of the architecture rather than just a disclaimer. What I learned The most important thing I learned was that memory for agents is not just a storage problem . It is an authority problem. A useful agent-memory system needs to know where human evidence ends and machine interpretation begins. I also learned that adding more AI is not always the answer. Companion uses AI where semantic interpretation is useful, but deterministic software owns validation, persistence rules, identity, routing, and retrieval. And WebMCP helped reveal a particularly clean separation of responsibilities: The human provides the evidence. Companion preserves and structures it. WebMCP exposes it. The external agent decides what it needs and reasons over it. Validation I treated the hackathon prototype as an experiment that should be falsifiable rather than as a polished product claim. The final automated suite contains 52 passing tests , covering the semantic authority boundary, deterministic validation, factual/inferred routing, WebMCP vocabulary projection, exact-ID lookup, and incremental retrieval behavior. The final production walkthrough also verified: natural-language capture and human confirmation; real semantic construction; WebMCP tool discovery and invocation; reusable factual vocabulary; exact lookup of agent-selected IDs; incremental retrieval across multiple calls; resolvable source references; explicit handling of unknown IDs; zero evidence for an empty ID request; exclusion of AGENT_INFERRED relations from factual WebMCP results. The public demo starts empty and all challenge examples are synthetic. What's next Companion v0.1 deliberately leaves several problems open. The semantic metamodel is small. title: Nest — Hunt flats with your agent
pitch: Nest is an agent-native flat hunt: you and ChatGPT share one live London board - map, shortlist, viewings, and offers - via WebMCP tools with your confirm on anything that commits.
about_excerpt:
Nest is an agent-native flat hunt: you and ChatGPT share one live London board - map, shortlist, viewings, and offers - via WebMCP tools with your confirm on anything that commits.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Flat hunting is a messy human workflow: filters, maps, shortlists, viewing slots, and offer letters all fight for attention. Agents already talk about housing well, but they usually fail when they have to click through a UI built for a mouse. WebMCP flips that: the site can expose the real actions (search, pin, compare, hold a viewing, draft and submit an offer) as structured tools on the same live page the person is looking at. 

 Nest is that idea made concrete — a London rental board where you and your agent share one session, one map, and one shortlist. 

 What it does 

 Nest is an agent-native flat hunt: 

 
 Browse seeded London listings on a live map 
 Pin and compare homes side by side 
 Propose and hold viewing slots (agent proposes; you confirm commits) 
 Draft and submit an offer letter from the shortlist 
 Inspect board state and registered WebMCP tools on an in-app Agent tools panel 
 

 You steer in plain English in ChatGPT; Nest’s site tools update the UI in real time. Anything consequential (holding a viewing, submitting an offer) is a non-read-only tool so the browser can require confirmation. 

 How we built it 

 
 Vite + React + TypeScript for a fast, deployable SPA 
 Zustand store shared by the human UI and every WebMCP execute handler (one source of truth) 
 Leaflet map with OSM tiles for the spatial board 
 WebMCP via document.modelContext.registerTool (with navigator.modelContext fallback), feature-detected, registered on the top-level page 
 Seeded demo listings (no paid APIs) so judges can try the full path offline-friendly 
 Built with Codex 
 

 Core tools include search_listings , get_listing , pin_listing / unpin_listing , compare_shortlist , propose_viewings , hold_viewing , cancel_viewing , draft_offer , submit_offer , get_board_state , and set_preferences . 

 Challenges 

 
 Same-state collaboration — agent tools and UI clicks must never drift. We solved this by routing both through one store. 
 Read vs commit — WebMCP’s value is trust. Marking search/compare read-only and viewings/offers as side-effecting was deliberate product design, not just annotations. 
 Demo realism without backends — landlords, holds, and offers are simulated with structured JSON so the agent can reason, while the product still feels complete. 
 Judges’ path — a clear happy path (search → pin → compare → hold viewings → draft → submit) plus a tools panel so WebMCP leverage is obvious in under three minutes. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP isn’t “MCP in the browser” as a slogan — it’s best when the agent and the human must see the same thing : a map marker lighting up, a shortlist changing, an offer panel filling. Housing is a perfect stress test because the workflow is multi-step, spatial, and full of confirm-worthy actions. 

 Try the demo path 

 
 Open Nest in ChatGPT’s in-app browser (or Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled) 
 Ask: “Find 2-beds under £2200 in Zone 2 that allow pets, pin the best three, compare them, hold two viewings, and draft an offer for my favorite.” 
 Watch the board update; confirm when the browser asks on commits

AI-powered incident response through WebMCP: investigate attacks, resist prompt injection, and execute containment only with explicit human approval.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 BreachGlass was inspired by a simple question: what should incident response look like when an AI agent can actually use the security console, not just summarize screenshots? 

 Security teams already deal with fragmented alerts, timelines, assets, evidence, and response actions. AI can help analysts investigate faster, but giving an agent unrestricted autonomy in a high-stakes workflow is dangerous, especially when the agent may read attacker-controlled evidence. 

 BreachGlass explores a safer model: the AI investigates, the human decides, and WebMCP connects both inside the same live interface. 

 What it does 

 BreachGlass is an agent-native cybersecurity incident response console powered by WebMCP. 

 The demo simulates a critical incident involving credential theft and lateral movement. Through WebMCP tools, an AI agent can: 

 
 load the active incident; 
 search critical security events; 
 inspect affected assets; 
 reconstruct attacker movement; 
 inspect forensic evidence; 
 detect untrusted prompt-injection-style content; 
 propose containment actions; 
 request execution of containment. 
 

 The key safety boundary is that containment cannot execute automatically. When the agent calls execute_containment before approval, BreachGlass returns HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED . Only after the human analyst approves the proposal in the UI can the agent execute the containment action and update the incident state to INCIDENT CONTAINED . 

 How we built it 

 BreachGlass is built as a React and TypeScript web application deployed on Cloudflare Pages. 

 The application exposes seven WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_incident 
 search_events 
 get_asset 
 trace_activity 
 inspect_evidence 
 propose_containment 
 execute_containment 
 

 The tools are intentionally separated by risk. Investigation tools are read-only. Evidence inspection marks hostile content as untrusted. Containment proposal is safe and read-only. Containment execution is state-changing and requires explicit human approval. 

 This lets the agent work with structured capabilities instead of scraping the UI, while keeping dangerous actions under human control. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing a workflow where the AI agent is genuinely useful without becoming unsafe. 

 I wanted BreachGlass to show more than a chatbot summarizing an alert. The agent needed to investigate a realistic incident, encounter hostile evidence, ignore malicious instructions, propose containment, and then be blocked until a human explicitly approved the action. 

 Another challenge was making the demo understandable quickly. The product had to show the incident state, the attack path, the untrusted evidence, the agent activity, and the human approval flow in one coherent experience. 

 Accomplishments 

 I am proud that BreachGlass demonstrates a complete human-agent incident response loop: 

 
 structured WebMCP investigation; 
 prompt-injection-aware evidence handling; 
 attack path reconstruction; 
 containment proposal; 
 human approval; 
 state-changing execution after approval. 
 

 The most important moment in the demo is not that the agent can execute an action. It is that the agent cannot execute it until the human approves it. 

 What we learned 

 Building BreachGlass reinforced how important tool design is for agent-native applications. 

 WebMCP makes it possible for a website to expose clear, structured actions to an AI agent. But the application still needs to define trust boundaries: which tools are read-only, which data is untrusted, and which actions require explicit human approval. 

 The lesson is that good agent experiences are not just about giving AI more tools. They are about giving AI the right tools with the right safety model. 

 What's next 

 Future improvements could include: 

 
 multiple incident scenarios; 
 persistent audit logs of WebMCP tool calls and approvals; 
 integrations with SIEM, EDR, identity, and ticketing systems; 
 role-based approval workflows; 
 richer evidence sandboxing; 
 replayable incident timelines for security training and tabletop exercises. 
 

 The long-term goal is to explore how AI agents can help security teams respond faster while keeping humans in control of high-impact decisions.

Like 2 Comment Story Updates 1 banner GIF demo What it does Draw_generatoe lets Codex control a live tldraw canvas through WebMCP. Users can ask it to create pages, draw scenes, add shapes and text, search and decribe youtube embed url in canvas ,Mermaid js ,finds non CC wikipedia commons image , arrange objects, and refine designs through natural-language instructions. For example, Codex can create a welcome screen, draw a car on a road, notice misaligned text, and correct the layout without replacing the user’s existing work. Inspiration The idea was inspired by OpenAI’s YouTube video, Math Problems with GPT-4o featuring Imran Khan from Khan Academy , published on May 13, 2024. Watching someone interact naturally with AI , made me wonder: what if we could do the same thing on a visual canvas? The original repository had been on my computer since 2025 . With the arrival of WebMCP, I returned to it and added tools that let Codex place, resize, move, and arrange canvas objects. The goal was simple: describe a scene in plain language and watch Codex draw it directly on the canvas. How we built it We built the interface with React, Vite, and tldraw. The application exposes structured WebMCP tools that Codex can use to inspect pages and create, move, resize, align, layer, and draw canvas objects. Codex inspects the current canvas, preserves populated pages, performs bounded mutations, fits the result into view, and visually checks the finished composition. We packaged the client application and deployed it publicly through ChatGPT Sites. Tool vocabulary Domain Tools Discovery list_tools describe_tools Canvas reading review count inspect_pages inspect_embeds Pages and camera create_page zoom_out Shape creation create pen createHtmlPreview create_mermaid_diagram Shape editing update label delete clear Layout and positioning move place align distribute stack arrange_grid Transform and layers rotate resize bringToFront sendToBack External inspiration getInspiration Open-license images search_commons_images add_commons_image This reflects all 29 tools currently listed in repo tool.txt https://github.com/mayank-devac/draw_generetoe Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was translating creative language into exact canvas coordinates, sizes, and layer ordering. Text and shapes can have different measured bounds, so something that looks centered mathematically may still appear misaligned. We also had to preserve existing pages, manage overlapping objects, verify WebMCP tool schemas, handle tldraw licensing for the deployed domain, and ensure that public client-side configuration did not expose real secrets. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created a working bridge between natural language and a live visual canvas. Codex can produce complete multi-object scenes, native shape-based layouts, hand-drawn decorations, mermaid js ... We are especially proud that it can inspect its own result, identify visual problems such as incorrect layering or alignment, and improve the canvas while leaving unrelated work untouched. What we learned We learned that reliable AI drawing requires more than generating shapes. The agent needs structured tools, clear object identities, page awareness, predictable coordinate systems, and visual verification after every meaningful change. We also learned that small corrective tools—move, align, resize, reorder, and inspect—are just as important as the initial creation tools. title: Alza
pitch: A floor plan is coordinates, not buttons. Alza publishes its geometry as 31 typed tools, so your agent draws the plan, checks its own work, buys from another origin, and raises it to walkable 3D.
about_excerpt: A floor plan is coordinates, not buttons. Alza publishes its geometry as 31 typed tools, so your agent draws the plan, checks its own work, buys from another origin, and raises it to walkable 3D. Like Comment Story Updates 3d-orbit-hero traced-over-the-drawing plan-2d tool-runner cross-origin-supplier supplier-product-placed constraint-engine agent-notes-on-ambiguity approval-gate approval-rejected-feed agent-authored-pieces catalogue-3d-previews 3d-top 3d-doors-open 3d-walk-eye-level Inspiration I had a floor plan as a photo and wanted to see it in 3D. That should be a solved problem, but every tool I found wanted me to redraw it by hand, wall by wall, in an editor built for a mouse. So I tried handing it to an AI agent instead. That was worse. An agent can read a screenshot and it can talk about a floor plan, but it cannot use one. There is no button that means "make this wall four point six metres" . There is no DOM worth scraping. A drawing is coordinates, joints and constraints, and none of that is reachable from the outside. WebMCP looked like the missing half. Not a way to describe the page to an agent — a way to hand it the actual geometry. What it does Alza is a floor-plan editor that publishes its own tools. You draw walls, rooms, doors, windows and furniture in a metric 2D canvas, then raise it to a 3D model you can walk through. An agent joins the same live page and works with the same tools you do. The demo is the honest test: I gave the agent a photo of a plan it had never seen. The drawing carries no scale, so it asked for one real dimension , set everything from that, and traced it — 12 walls, 14 openings, 10 rooms, 34 pieces of furniture . The drawing underneath is the source photo. The dark geometry on top is what the agent built from it. When the catalogue had no honest match for a symbol, it modelled the piece itself: an L-shaped sofa, a corner shower, a compact bath, a fitted L wardrobe, a washing machine Then it checked itself. The constraint engine reports in metres — this wardrobe crosses that wall, this basin blocks that door's swing — and the agent reads the complaint and fixes it. And where it could not be sure, it said so instead of guessing: it left a note that one symbol was ambiguous and explained how it had read it. How I built it Vite, React, TypeScript, Three.js. No backend at all — it is a static site, and plans never leave the browser. The 31 tools are typed and registered on document.modelContext at load: document.modelContext.registerTool(descriptor, { signal, exposedTo }) There is a 32nd that only exists when it is relevant: select a wall in the UI and extend_selected_wall appears; deselect and it is gone, unregistered by aborting the AbortSignal its descriptor was registered with. The constraint engine is oriented-rectangle SAT: furniture against walls, door swing paths, whether an opening fits the wall it sits on, whether a room has a door at all. The part I am most pleased with is the partner. Nordika is a genuinely separate website on its own origin, deployed to a different host. It registers its own tools with exposedTo , and the studio discovers them with getTools({ fromOrigins }) and calls them with executeTool() . One instruction crosses that boundary and a real product lands in the plan at its real size — with no server anywhere in the path. Challenges I ran into The plan I first traced turned out to be copyrighted. I had pulled it off Google without thinking, and by the time I noticed, it was committed to a public repo — and the whole demo model was traced from it, so the layout was derived too, not just the image. Deleting the file did nothing: git keeps history. I deleted the repo, generated my own plan, and re-traced everything from scratch. That cost a full rebuild of the model, the film and the screenshots. The video fought me for a long time. The 3D looked juddery no matter what I did, and it took a while to find out why: the tool I was recording with caps at 25 fps and renders in software. Continuous camera motion at 25 fps with no motion blur reads as stepping, and no amount of conforming fixes it. I switched to real GPU screen capture at 60 fps and it went away. The worst bug was silent. The production build was shipping without its cross-origin headers, so the partner iframe was never allowed to publish its tools — the flagship feature, quietly dead on the live URL. The cause: Vite loads .env into import.meta.env but not into process.env , and the plugin that writes the headers was reading process.env . It failed by emitting a header that looked plausible. And building the demo found real bugs in my own app: the walk camera passed straight through walls and furniture, looking around orbited instead of turning your head, and the 2D auto-fit anchored the plan to a corner instead of centring it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The agent recovered from its own mistake without help. Running in Codex, it invented a wall id, the tool answered Wall "wall_10" not found , and its next call used the real one — then get_issues came back "0 issues — the plan is clean" . I did not script that. It is what happens when tool errors are sentences instead of failure codes. The constraint engine caught something about the drawing itself. It rejected the catalogue's standard 1.70 m bath — "Bathtub crosses wall" — because that alcove is 1.68 m wall to wall, 1.58 m clear. The drawing sizes its own bath shorter, at 1.53 m, so that is what got modelled instead. A geometry checker noticing that a drawing is tight is exactly the point. And the second origin is real . A different site on a different host, not a folder pretending to be one. What I learned That "the agent can see the page" and "the agent can use the page" are completely different problems, and only the second one matters. That an error message is an interface . Half of what makes the agent look competent is that when it gets something wrong, the tool tells it what is wrong in words it can act on. That degrading matters more than I expected. Cross-origin discovery is not in every runtime yet — ChatGPT and Codex register the page's own tools fine but fall back to postMessage for the partner. Because the same protocol runs over both, the feature gets quieter instead of disappearing. And that a build can fail silently and look fine . I now check the artefact, not the exit code. What's next for Alza Multi-floor plans, and stairs between them Export to IFC, so the model can leave for real CAD Cost and materials as tools, so an agent can answer "what does this room cost to finish" from the same geometry A shared session, so a person and an agent can work the same plan at the same time and see each other move Why this generalizes None of this is really about architecture. The pattern underneath is that a page already holds a rigorous model — geometry, a cart, a spreadsheet, a timeline, an audio track — and right now the only way an agent can reach it is by pretending to be a mouse. WebMCP lets the page hand over the model itself, with its validation still attached, so the agent works on meaning instead of pixels. I picked the hardest case I could think of to make that argument. A canvas has no DOM to scrape, and 5 cm of error is a wall through a sofa — which is exactly why the app can prove whether the agent got it right. If the pattern holds here, it holds for the easier ones. What building this taught me about the spec I ran into four of the explainer's open questions as actual problems, not as reading material. Here is what I did about each, in case any of it is useful to the people writing the standard. User prompting and elicitation ( #165 , #50 ). I needed this on day one. A tool that wipes someone's floor plan cannot just run because a model decided to call it. My answer lives entirely in the page: a tool marked destructive does not execute when it is called — it parks as a request bar in the UI, and the promise stays pending until a person presses Approve or Reject. Reject hands the agent an actionable failure ("the human declined; ask them what to do instead") rather than an error, so it recovers instead of retrying. The registration AbortSignal releases the request if the agent gives up first. It works, but every site has to build its own, and the confirmation UI is only as trustworthy as the page drawing it — which is the argument for the browser mediating it instead. One thing I hit there and want to flag: destructiveHint is in MCP's ToolAnnotations but not in WebMCP's, which right now defines only readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint . I keep it on my own descriptors and enforce it page-side, so nothing depends on the browser passing it through. But if the browser is ever going to mediate confirmation itself, it needs some way to know which tools are destructive — so aligning the two sets looks worth doing. Multimodal input and output ( #41 , #86 , #81 ). This is the gap I felt hardest. Tracing a plan means the agent has to s
video_title: Alza — WebMCP Challenge: a floor-plan studio your agent can actually use
video_transcript_excerpt: This house was drawn, measured, furnished, and checked by an AI agent. It never touched a mouse. Agents can't drag a wall. A floor plan is coordinates, joints, and constraints. There is no button that means make this wall 4.6 m. And there is no DOM to scrape. Every trick an agent has has nothing to grab onto. So, Alza stops pretending the page is clickable and hands the geometry over directly. 31 typed tools published to the page that the agent calls the way you would use the editor. Nothing gets installed. Alza publishes its tools to the page, so any agent looking at the tab already sees them. You give it a photo of the plan and one sentence it asks for one real dimension and sets the scale from that. Give it a plan to reproduce and it draws. Walls, then the doors and windows that sit on them, then rooms, then the furniture. The same actions your mouse fires against one shared model. With every call logged on the page as it happens, and it checks its own work. A wardrobe placed through a wall, the constraint engine says so in meters, and the agent reads the complaint and fixes it. You never see the mistake. The furniture shop is a different website. Different company, different origin, publishing its own tools and sharing them with this page. One instruction crosses that boundary with no server in between and a real product lands in the plan at its real size, where the checker can tell you whether it fits before you buy it. And when the agent reaches for something destructive, it doesn't get it. It gets a request. The call waits on the page until a person decides, and if the answer is no, the agent is told so in words it can act on. Then the plan rises. Walls with real openings, doors on hinges that actually swing, and the whole house turning in front of you. Then step inside and walk it, room by room, at eye level before anyone has built a thing. Alza. 31 tools, one shared model, and a plan your agent can actually build. Open source. And live now.

Remix: Cook with an AI agent on one live board. Add ingredients, let the agent compose recipes, invent its own, and re-theme the UI in real time. One human, one agent, one board.

 What inspired me. Cooking apps are single-player: they talk at you with recipes you'll never use. Chat agents fixed the conversation but not the problem — an agent that only answers can't do anything. The WebMCP moment is that the page itself becomes the tool surface, so I built the app I wanted: a teammate that cooks with you on one live board. You type what's in your fridge — "tomatoes, soy sauce, basil" — and the agent doesn't reply in a bubble, it acts: recomposes the board, drops in a card it invented, re-sorts, re-themes. Every action mutates the real DOM in front of both of you. That shared, visible state is the whole idea — visible execution is what keeps trust and control with the human. 

 How I built it. One zero-dependency index.html + a node serve.mjs dev server, deployed on GitHub Pages. On load the page registers 7 tools through the native WebMCP API (document.modelContext.registerTool) with JSON-schema inputSchema, readOnlyHint annotations and async execute callbacks that return clean JSON. Ingredient input normalises through an alias map and Unicode NFD stripping, so "poivron", "œufs", "sauce soja" and "baguette" all land on canonical ids. A stdio MCP server (mcp-server.mjs) re-exposes the same 7-tool surface, so any MCP host can drive the live UI too. I verified with a headless visual check and a full MCP JSON-RPC end-to-end test before pushing.

I rewrote it to feature-detect, register natively, and degrade honestly into a labelled demo mode. Matching messy human input took real engineering: quantifiers ("2 eggs", "half an onion") get stripped, plurals folded, and the match never depends on typos I could normalise away. And agents break things: add_recipe crashed on partial args (needs.map of undefined), so every tool now validates its inputs and returns {ok:false, error} instead of throwing, while get_board/get_pantry give the agent truthful grounding before it acts.

And the best pattern for human-AI trust isn't explaining what you did — it's letting the human watch you do it.

Your AI personal stylist that understands your style, searches the web, compares products, and builds your outfit using WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Have you ever spent 30 minutes shopping online just to find one good outfit? 

 I do. 

 Sometimes I even ask ChatGPT, "Does this shirt look good on me?" After using AI so much, it probably knows more about my style than my girlfriend does. 

 Sad, but true. 😄 

 That made me think: 

 If AI already understands me, why am I still doing all the searching myself? 

 That's how StyleMate started. 

 We wanted to build a shopping experience where you don't have to think like a search engine. You can simply tell the agent what you're looking for, and it can understand your preferences, find the right products, and help you build your outfit. 

 What it does 

 StyleMate is an AI-powered personal stylist built for fashion shopping. 

 Instead of searching through hundreds of products and manually applying filters, you can simply give StyleMate a natural-language request. 

 For example: 

 
 "I'm 5'7", I need a formal outfit for office — a shirt, trousers and shoes. My shirt size is 40, trouser waist is 32, shoe size is 9, and my budget is around ₹10,000." 
 

 StyleMate can understand the request along with the user's existing style profile. 

 It can then: 

 
 Understand the user's style preferences 
 Find personalized recommendations 
 Search the product catalog 
 Compare products 
 Check size and inventory availability 
 Build a complete outfit 
 Add selected products to the cart 
 

 The interesting part is that the AI doesn't just recommend products. 

 It can actually interact with the website through WebMCP. 

 How we built it 

 Our main idea was: 

 One brain, two front doors. 

 A user can interact with StyleMate through the normal website UI, while an AI agent can interact with the same application through WebMCP. 

 Both use the same underlying product and business logic. 

 For the agent experience, we exposed purpose-built WebMCP tools: 

 
 getUserStyleProfile — read the user's style preferences 
 getRecommendations — find suitable products 
 searchProducts — search the product catalog 
 compareProducts — compare product options 
 checkInventory — verify availability 
 addToCart — add selected products to the cart 
 

 We also use browser page controls to update the visible website, show products, display confirmation dialogs, navigate to the cart, and keep the user involved in the process. 

 The flow is simple: 

 User intent → AI reasoning → WebMCP tools → Website interaction → Human confirmation → Cart 

 We built the application using modern web technologies including Next.js, React, TypeScript, and WebMCP. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was not simply connecting an AI agent to a website. 

 We wanted the agent to interact with the actual application in a reliable and structured way. 

 We had to think carefully about: 

 
 Designing useful WebMCP tools instead of exposing generic actions 
 Keeping the agent and human UI connected to the same business logic 
 Making product search and recommendations work with natural-language requests 
 Handling size and inventory checks 
 Keeping important actions under human control 
 Making the website visually respond to agent actions 
 

 We also had to think about the difference between what an agent can do and what an agent should be allowed to do . 

 For example, searching and comparing products are safe actions, while adding something to a cart or placing an order requires more user involvement. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The biggest accomplishment is that StyleMate is not just an AI chatbot placed on top of an ecommerce website. 

 The website itself is agent-operable. 

 An agent can discover StyleMate's capabilities through WebMCP and use those capabilities to perform real shopping tasks. 

 We can start with a simple sentence like: 

 
 "Find me a formal office outfit under ₹10,000." 
 

 And turn that into a complete interaction: 

 Understand my style → Search products → Compare options → Check availability → Show me the choices → Get confirmation → Add to cart 

 We are also proud of keeping the architecture simple. 

 One brain, two front doors. 

 The human experience and the agent experience are powered by the same underlying application logic. 

 What we learned 

 We started this project thinking about AI recommendations. 

 We ended up thinking much more about agent-friendly websites . 

 Traditional ecommerce is built around the question: 

 "What product are you searching for?" 

 But people usually think in terms of intent: 

 "I have an office event tomorrow. What should I wear?" 

 That's where we see the potential of WebMCP. 

 Instead of an AI simply telling you what to click, the website can expose structured capabilities that an agent can actually use. 

 We also learned that giving an agent more control doesn't mean removing the human. 

 The best experience is: 

 AI does the searching and decision support.
Human makes the important decisions. 

 What's next for StyleMate 

 Today, StyleMate focuses on fashion discovery and shopping. 

 But the idea can go much further. 

 We want StyleMate to understand how a person's style changes over time and become a long-term personal stylist rather than a one-time shopping assistant. 

 Future possibilities include: 

 
 Smarter personal style profiles 
 Outfit planning for specific events 
 Wardrobe-aware recommendations 
 More brands and product categories 
 Better fit and size intelligence 
 Wishlist and purchase-history intelligence 
 Personalized seasonal collections 
 Agent-driven shopping across multiple stores 
 

 The bigger vision is simple: 

 Don't search. Be understood.

title: True GEO Engine
pitch: WebMCP enables True GEO Engine to discover where your website is invisible to AI, identify gaps, and guide improvements. helping make your site more discoverable, understandable, and actionable.
about_excerpt:
WebMCP enables True GEO Engine to discover where your website is invisible to AI, identify gaps, and guide improvements. helping make your site more discoverable, understandable, and actionable.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 TRUE GEO ENGINE 

 Inspiration 

 Search stopped being the only front door. People now ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude what to buy, who to trust, and which vendor to shortlist — and a brand either appears in that answer or it doesn't. Marketing teams have twenty years of tooling for the blue-links era and almost nothing for this one. 

 The tools that do exist have a credibility problem. Most GEO dashboards burn API budget hammering four models with the same prompt, then present whatever came back as if it were a measurement. Run it twice and the numbers move. That isn't visibility analytics — it's a screenshot of a coin flip. 

 We wanted the opposite: an evidence workspace where the same input always produces the same output , every synthetic value is labeled as synthetic, and no .env file, API key, or paid inference is needed to see exactly how the reasoning works. If a claim can't be traced to a rule and a row, it shouldn't appear on the screen. 

 What it does 

 TRUE GEO ENGINE is a brand- and industry-agnostic GEO/AEO workspace with two independent workflows that never share evidence. 

 AI Visibility takes one public page URL as a deterministic seed and generates a synthetic raw-HTML versus post-hydration comparison — without fetching the target page. The post-hydration state supplies one ordered master list of h1 – h6 , p , li , figcaption , blockquote , and td blocks. Both columns render that identical list in identical order, and each block is marked Fully extractable or Not visible to AI by signature membership: 

 status ( b ) = { Fully extractable if  σ ( b ) ∈ Σ raw   Not visible to AI otherwise 

 where $\sigma(b)$ is the normalized signature of block $b$ and $\Sigma_{\text{raw}}$ is the signature set of the synthetic raw HTML. Metadata, Schema.org JSON-LD types, and FAQ schema live in a separate machine-readable-signals section so structural signals never inflate the content score. Four deterministic crawler perspectives vary the evidence feeding answer-engine scores. Private-network URLs are rejected. 

 Run a Prompt replays a selected prompt from a bundled fictional benchmark — no LLM call, no API key, no page URL, no external request. The catalog holds eight scenarios across automotive, B2B technology, financial services, healthcare, travel, telecommunications, consumer products, and education. Each carries one high-intent prompt and measured brand, a benchmark answer, three competitors, four evidence sources, four answer-engine interpretations, and six sentiment topics. At runtime it expands to 

 8  prompts × 4  engines × 6  dimensions = 192  deterministic evidence rows 

 from which the pipeline computes visibility, coverage and citation rate, sentiment and recommendation quality, competitor leaders, ranked answer gaps, and next steps. 

 Both workflows populate the same five views — AI visibility, answer engine scores, content/answer gaps, next steps, and agent activity — while results stay isolated, so URL evidence is never relabeled as prompt evidence. 

 Eight WebMCP tools are registered imperatively in the browser, letting an agent drive the workspace directly: 

 
 
 Tool 
 Purpose 
 
 
 
 geo_ai_visibility_audit 
 Generate the synthetic URL-scoped page analysis 
 
 
 geo_analyze_prompt 
 Replay one exact prompt from the curated benchmark 
 
 
 geo_visibility_overview 
 Read the active score and evidence components 
 
 
 geo_list_tools 
 Export the browser WebMCP catalog 
 
 
 geo_content_gaps 
 Explain one ranked gap from active evidence 
 
 
 geo_generate_next_steps 
 Open page- or prompt-specific next steps 
 
 
 geo_download_package 
 Download the active evidence package 
 
 
 geo_export_action_plan 
 Export the active action plan 
 
 

 Each workflow exports a 16-file ZIP — disclosure, consolidated llms.txt , FAQs, JSON-LD and schema, preview HTML, the block audit or benchmark answers, scores, gaps, action plan, and WebMCP manifests. 

 How we built it 

 Next.js and TypeScript, with Drizzle for schema and a Vite-driven test setup. The whole app runs from npm run dev with no .env , no key, and no network dependency for either challenge workflow. 

 Determinism layer: 

 
 lib/synthetic-page-scan.ts — URL-derived raw and hydrated fixtures plus the four simulated crawler perspectives 
 lib/page-audit.ts — the ordered block classifier and structural-signal extractor 
 lib/visibility-scanner.ts — URL-scoped prompt and score analysis fed by those fixtures 
 

 Benchmark layer: 

 
 components/true-geo/demo-prompts.json — the curated benchmark, single source of truth 
 components/true-geo/demo-prompts.ts — deterministic expansion into the 192 evidence rows 
 

 Interface layer: 

 
 components/true-geo/TrueGeoApp.tsx — isolated workflow state and all tab wiring 
 components/true-geo/PageVisibilityAudit.tsx — the aligned Human vs AI block view 
 components/true-geo/PromptBar.tsx — mode pills, prompt selector, URL input 
 components/true-geo/page-audit.ts — the audit data model and client normalization 
 

 WebMCP layer: components/true-geo/webmcp.ts registers directly against the browser contract, and tool-manifest.ts keeps a portable catalog of the same eight tools so the manifest can travel with an export: 
 document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: entry.name,
 title: entry.title,
 description: entry.description,
 inputSchema: entry.inputSchema,
 execute: async (input) => JSON.stringify(await execute(entry.name, input)),
});
 
 API surface: POST /api/page-audit { url } , plus deterministic prompt and visibility endpoints. services/page-renderer/ holds an optional local Playwright reference for future live auditing — deliberately not wired into the public routes. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Keeping two workflows from bleeding into each other. Both feed the same five views, which makes cross-contamination easy and disastrous — a page-derived gap shown under a prompt run is a fabricated claim. We had to make workflow isolation a property of the state model itself rather than something the UI remembers to respect. 

 Making a schema that can't be misused. geo_analyze_prompt was an obvious injection point: give it a free-text field and an agent will pass an arbitrary prompt the benchmark has no data for, and the pipeline will happily score it. We constrained the field to the eight bundled catalog values and removed any URL or model parameter, so the tool cannot be talked into analyzing something that doesn't exist. 

 Honest columns are harder than pretty ones. The first Human vs AI view built each column from its own source, which meant the two lists drifted out of alignment and the comparison stopped meaning anything. Deriving both columns from one ordered master list and marking extractability per block was more constrained but is the only version where a row-by-row read is truthful. 

 Labeling everything without burying the product. Every synthetic value and every downloaded file needed a disclosure, and it would have been easy to end up with a workspace that reads like a legal notice. Getting "verify before publishing" to sit visibly on results and exports without drowning the analysis took more iteration than the scoring math. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Reproducible by construction — the same URL or prompt always yields the same evidence, so two people looking at one run see one set of numbers 
 Zero-key, zero-quota, zero-network for both challenge workflows; a reviewer clones, runs npm run dev , and sees the full product 
 192 evidence rows from a transparent expansion , not from an opaque model call 
 Eight WebMCP tools registered imperatively, plus a portable manifest that ships inside the exports 
 A schema that refuses out-of-catalog input rather than scoring it anyway 
 SSRF-conscious from the start — private-network URLs are rejected at the boundary 
 Synthetic labeled as synthetic , everywhere, including inside every one of the 32 exported files 
 

 What we learned 

 Determinism is a feature users can feel. We expected reviewers to treat the simulated benchmark as a limitation. In practice, being able to re-run a prompt and get the identical answer made the tool feel more trustworthy than a live-model version would have. 

 A tool schema is an access-control surface. Once an agent can call your functions, an unconstrained string field is an open door. Enumerating valid values isn't a UX nicety — it's what stops

title: RELAY — Proof Before Power
pitch: Human-governed WebMCP authority for incident response.
about_excerpt:
Human-governed WebMCP authority for incident response.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for RELAY — Proof Before Power 

 RELAY — Proof Before Power 

 Human-governed WebMCP authority for incident response. 

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are increasingly capable of investigating incidents and proposing production actions. 

 But sensitive execution creates a governance problem: an ordinary approval workflow can leave the underlying agent capability continuously available, with only a permission check standing between investigation and production change. 

 RELAY explores a different model: 

 What if the human decision changed what the agent was actually capable of doing on the web? 

 What it does 

 RELAY gives an agent nine persistent WebMCP capabilities for incident investigation, evidence gathering, deployment comparison, hypothesis building, recovery preparation, and verification. 

 The sensitive production execution capability does not exist. 

 The agent can investigate the incident and stage one bounded recovery proposal, but it still cannot execute production recovery. 

 Only the visible human action: 

 AUTHORIZE THIS ACTION 

 changes the live WebMCP capability surface. 

 At that moment: 

 09 → 10 

 One exact temporary capability is registered: 

 execute_authorized_recovery 

 The agent can use it once to carry out the approved recovery. 

 In the demo: 

 
 deployment #4821 becomes #4819 
 error rate falls from 31% to 0.8% 
 recovery is verified 
 execution count becomes 1 
 

 Immediately after execution, the temporary capability is removed: 

 10 → 09 

 A replay cannot execute another recovery. 

 Why WebMCP 

 RELAY is not simply an API call hidden behind an approval button. 

 The important state is the actual browser-visible WebMCP capability surface. 

 Before authorization, the production execution tool genuinely does not exist. 

 After the human decision, one exact capability appears. 

 After its single use, it disappears. 

 WebMCP makes that authority native to the interaction between the web application and the agent. 

 How it improves the user experience 

 The human does not need to manually perform the entire incident response. 

 The agent can investigate, assemble evidence, compare deployments, form a hypothesis, and prepare a bounded recovery proposal. 

 At the same time, the agent does not receive standing production authority. 

 The consequential decision remains human. 

 The resulting flow is: 

 investigation → human judgment → bounded execution 

 rather than forcing users to choose between full manual operation and persistent agent authority. 

 What humans and agents can do together 

 The agent handles the evidence-heavy investigative work. 

 The human decides whether production authority should come into existence. 

 After authorization, the agent completes the exact approved recovery without requiring the human to manually execute the production action. 

 Then the authority disappears. 

 RELAY expresses human governance as a change in agent capability, not merely as an approval flag. 

 How we built it 

 RELAY uses real document.modelContext WebMCP registration. 

 Nine persistent tools support investigation and recovery preparation. 

 The state-changing recovery execution capability is intentionally absent. 

 A human-only UI authorization dynamically registers execute_authorized_recovery for the exact approved recovery. 

 After its single execution, that capability is removed. 

 Final live QA verified the registry lifecycle directly: 

 09 → 10 → 09 

 The execution capability was absent initially, appeared only after human authorization, executed once, and was genuinely removed afterward. 

 What's next 

 RELAY is a focused demonstration of ephemeral, human-governed agent authority. 

 The same capability pattern could be explored for other consequential web actions where investigation can be delegated broadly but execution should be created narrowly, explicitly, and temporarily.

title: alpha-investing
pitch: - Bittensor is network for blockchain - Bittensor have subnets - Token be called alpha in bittensor - Token of each subnet can swap to Tao (coin of bittensor that listed)
about_excerpt: - Bittensor is network for blockchain - Bittensor have subnets - Token be called alpha in bittensor - Token of each subnet can swap to Tao (coin of bittensor that listed) Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Inspiration Bittensor Subnet 88 penalizes duplicate portfolios: any two allocation vectors within an L1-normalized distance of 0.01 get scored down. Before this project, the only way to fix that was trial and error by hand. We wanted to see if WebMCP could let an agent actually close that loop — propose, measure, adjust, re-measure — instead of the app just saying "no." What it does Alpha Investing lets a human and an AI agent build the same Bittensor Subnet 88 portfolio on the same screen, sharing one state. It exposes 12 WebMCP tools covering the full workflow — query subnets, generate a portfolio from two ranking criteria, edit allocations, and save it. The centerpiece is escape_dedupe : when save_portfolio rejects a duplicate, the agent can call it to perturb weights until the portfolio clears the safety threshold, then save — all visible in a live Agent Activity panel. How we built it React 19 + Vite, entirely client-side — no backend, no real funds, simulated subnet data. WebMCP tools register via document.modelContext.registerTool (with a navigator.modelContext fallback, since the spec is still moving), sharing the exact same state and validation path as the UI buttons, so an agent can't bypass any rule a human can't. Tool descriptions were iterated against a real agent (Gemini, through Chrome's WebMCP testing flag) until it reliably found the escape_dedupe recovery path on its own. Challenges we ran into No WebMCP-native browser was available for most of development, so we built a debug bridge that mirrors every registered tool onto window.__webmcpTools , letting us call the exact execute() path a real agent would — on the real production build — before we ever had a WebMCP-capable browser to test in. Once we did get a live agent running, we found that bundling multi-step instructions into one prompt confused it into picking the same ranking metric for both portfolio groups; one natural instruction per turn fixed it. Getting the agent to autonomously reach for escape_dedupe , rather than just reporting the rejection, took a few rounds of sharpening the tool descriptions. Accomplishments that we're proud of The generate → save → rejected → escape_dedupe → save loop is verified working end-to-end on the live production deployment, not a simulation. A real agent correctly reconstructed multi-part portfolio criteria from natural language and self-recovered from a dedupe rejection without being told how. The WebMCP layer is fully additive — the app behaves identically for anyone on a browser without WebMCP support. What we learned Tool descriptions are a real interface, not documentation — wording (units, when to call a recovery tool, when to switch tabs) measurably changes what an autonomous agent does. Building a bridge to test real tool code independent of browser support was more valuable than trying to hand-simulate agent behavior. What's next for alpha-investing An Undo action wired into the Agent Activity panel, a compare_portfolios read tool, and highlighting the rows an agent just changed so the human/agent shared-state story is legible in real time, not just in the log.
