title: Seigyo
pitch: Seigyo lets browser agents investigate production incidents, correlate live evidence, propose safe recoveries, obtain exact human approval, execute actions, and verify recovery through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Seigyo lets browser agents investigate production incidents, correlate live evidence, propose safe recoveries, obtain exact human approval, execute actions, and verify recovery through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Production incident response is fragmented. Operators jump between monitoring dashboards, logs, deployment records, service maps, runbooks, and customer reports while an outage continues to affect users. AI agents can help investigate this information, but recovery introduces a serious safety problem. An agent should not make a production change simply because it found a likely cause. A human must understand and approve the exact intervention. Seigyo explores a better collaboration model: the agent investigates and verifies, while the human keeps control of consequential actions. Seigyo is the Japaese word for control. What it does Seigyo is a human-governed incident investigation and recovery console powered by WebMCP. A browser agent can use structured tools exposed directly by the application to: List and inspect incidents Query service metrics Search operational logs Review deployments Map service dependencies Correlate evidence and identify likely causes Prepare a specific recovery proposal Execute an approved intervention Verify recovery against the customer path Reverse an intervention when necessary Every tool call is shown in an animated Agent Console using clear activity labels such as “Searching logs” and “Verifying recovery.” Before a recovery action can run, Seigyo presents the human with the exact action, target, evidence, expected effect, risk, and expiry. Approval grants permission only. The agent must still call the execution tool and then verify the result. MyShop is a connected storefront used to demonstrate the complete customer impact loop. A faulty checkout release creates a real incident in Seigyo. After the agent investigates and the human approves the recovery, the storefront becomes healthy and the customer can complete the same purchase. The storefront is only one example. The same interaction model can support infrastructure operations, security response, data systems, internal platforms, and other environments where agents need structured access with human control. Why WebMCP WebMCP allows the visible application and its agent interface to exist together. Instead of making the agent interpret screenshots or rely on hidden automation, Seigyo exposes explicit tools with typed inputs and structured results. The operator can continue using the normal interface while the agent works through the same live environment. This makes the interaction clearer for both sides: The agent receives reliable operational data. The human can see what the agent is doing. Approval happens inside the relevant application. Recovery remains bound to the exact incident and action. The agent can verify whether the customer-facing problem was actually fixed. This kind of live, browser-native collaboration would be difficult to deliver through a traditional dashboard alone. How we built it The Seigyo and MyShop interfaces are built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. The operations API runs on Cloudflare Workers. Persistent environment state is stored in a SQLite-backed Cloudflare Durable Object, which provides a serialized boundary for incidents, services, deployments, metrics, logs, approvals, executions, carts, and orders. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a defined input schema and an asynchronous execution callback connected to the operations API. Shared TypeScript contracts and Zod schemas keep the browser tools, interfaces, and backend aligned. WebSockets distribute operational changes so Seigyo and an already-open storefront remain synchronized. Recovery approvals are short-lived and bound to the operator session, proposal, action, and current causal state. Execution is idempotent, stale approvals are rejected, and completed interventions produce verifiable recovery records. The environment models connected services and causal behavior. Correct interventions restore the affected customer path, while unrelated actions do not magically resolve the incident. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was designing human approval without turning it into a decorative confirmation button. Approval had to authorize one precise action while keeping execution and verification under the agent’s control. We also had to keep multiple browser surfaces synchronized, preserve the customer’s cart during an outage, prevent stale or replayed approvals, and make repeated demonstrations deterministic without deleting operational history. Another challenge was presenting service dependencies clearly across different screen sizes. The topology now calculates every connection from the measured card positions instead of relying on fixed SVG coordinates. Accomplishments We built an end-to-end incident story that starts healthy, introduces a checkout regression through a new release, exposes the resulting customer failure, supports evidence-based agent investigation, requires exact human approval, executes a reversible recovery, verifies multiple healthy samples, and ends with a successful customer purchase. The normal interfaces remain usable without WebMCP, while WebMCP adds a structured collaboration layer for agents. What we learned The strongest use of WebMCP is not simply giving an agent more buttons. It is giving the agent a precise operational contract while keeping important human decisions visible and enforceable. We also learned that recovery should be measured from the customer path, not merely from whether a command returned successfully. What's next Next, Seigyo could connect to real monitoring, deployment, ticketing, and change-management systems. The same approval and verification model could also support security response, database operations, infrastructure maintenance, and other high-impact workflows. title: Barge In
pitch: A human and an AI drawing on the same canvas — and the page can say no.
about_excerpt: A human and an AI drawing on the same canvas — and the page can say no. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most WebMCP demos hand an agent tools that read the page. I wanted to hand it tools that touch something a person is touching at the same time, and see what breaks. Everything broke immediately, and in an interesting way. In the first experiment a human drew seven strokes across the agent's work-in-progress. The agent never noticed. Not a bug — WebMCP is pull-only. A page cannot speak to its agent. It has no notify , no event, no way up the pipe. It can only answer when it is called. So the question became: with only that one channel, how much control can a page take back? What it does The page gives an agent nine drawing tools. Ask it for a lion; it draws one. Then pick up the mouse and draw two wheels underneath it while it works. 19:18:40 You Drew a line (9 points) ← you barge in mid-batch … You × 7 more 19:18:48 AI ⛔ Blocked canvas_batch — canvas changed by human 19:18:48 AI Inspected the updated canvas 19:19:02 AI Updated the plan — A cute smiling male lion car, using the completed red user-drawn wheels and connecting them to the mane-body with a simple axle. 19:19:12 AI Drew 39 shapes in one batch Its half-finished mane stops where it stopped, because the rest of that batch was dropped . It cannot draw again until it has looked, and then said what your wheels changed about the plan — and what it is giving up because of them. In this run it said, unprompted: "Both red wheels now have hubs, inner rims, and tread marks. I'll keep those wheel details untouched and add only the axle connection." Then it drew the axle. Not a lion that happens to still have wheels beside it — a lion joined to your wheels by a bar it decided to add. About sixty seconds, start to finish, with nothing scripted anywhere. Every one of those decisions came out of the agent reading tool output. The drawing is deliberately crude. An image model would draw a better lion. The log is the deliverable. How I built it First, a word on what this is not . WebMCP already has a human-in-the-loop hook — requestUserInteraction , which lets a tool pause and ask the person to confirm. That is agent-initiated : the agent decides to ask, the person waits in front of a dialog, and says yes or no to something already drafted. It is consent. This is the opposite shape. It is human-initiated : the person acts whenever they like, without asking, and the agent finds out afterwards that it has been overruled. It is pre-emption. Both belong in a page people and agents share, and the spec currently offers only the first. Someone who is making something does not want to approve the agent's plan — they want to reach in and change it, and have the agent catch up. Then four rules, each one arrived at by watching the previous version fail. 1 — Refuse, don't stop. A page cannot interrupt an agent. But an agent calls a tool every few seconds, so refusing the next call feels, to the person watching, like an instant stop. Every writing tool calls guard() first. 2 — If you cannot push, answer when you are pulled. Everything the page needs to say rides back on the tool the agent already calls. canvas_describe always appends what the human did since the last check. It is the only channel WebMCP offers, so the page uses it as one. 3 — Seeing is not accepting. The first version asked , in prose, for the agent to re-plan around the interruption. It obliged — narrated the change beautifully, then carried on drawing its original picture. So looking stopped being enough: canvas_describe now hands over to a second gate, and only canvas_replan(observed, new_plan, abandoning) opens it. All three fields are required. abandoning is the load-bearing one — a plan you have given nothing up for is the old plan wearing a new sentence. 4 — The human's marks are never painted over. Told to incorporate the wheels, the agent laid its mane straight over them. Nothing was deleted and the counts were honest, but half the wheels vanished from the picture, and the picture is what people read. Paint order is now fixed: whatever the agent draws goes underneath. Challenges I ran into Requests land; prohibitions do not. "Check the canvas before you draw" was ignored, however it was worded. Refusing the call was not. Every rule here is enforced by a code path, not by asking nicely. Batching fixed the speed and broke the premise. A realistic lion took six minutes — the agent called canvas_stroke with three points every four seconds. Adding canvas_batch cut it to one call . The next tester's report was one sentence: "It drew everything at once, so I had no time to barge in." Painting the batch slowly to look interruptible would have been a lie — the picture was already decided. So a batch is now accepted and laid down one shape at a time over a few seconds, and if the human draws during that, the rest is dropped and never happens. Batching gained an honest price: bigger is faster, and bigger loses more. The agent answers in the conversation's language. Asked in Japanese, it wrote its new plan in Japanese, onto an English canvas. Fixed by asking for English in three places — the tool description, each parameter's description, and the return value read immediately before the call. One place was not enough. Accomplishments I'm proud of The measured finding that surprised me most has nothing to do with drawing: A tool's description changes how an agent batches its work. With a neutral description, the agent drew a spiral as 2 points per call, ~40 calls, over a minute. After adding "Pass every point in one call. Each call costs a few seconds, so the number of calls is the wait the user sees" — 121 points in a single call, in 4 seconds. Same tool, same model, 15× fewer round trips, from one paragraph of prose. What I learned That a page under WebMCP is not a passive surface. It is the only party in the room that knows what the person just did, and the return value of a tool is a real communication channel — one the agent reads carefully and acts on. Almost all the design work turned out to be writing. What's next The mechanism is now a standalone file, barge-in.js , that knows nothing about drawing. It knows only who touched the page last, and it is four lines to add to a page: const bi = BargeIn.create({ describeTool: 'doc_read', replanTool: 'doc_replan' }); editor.addEventListener('input', () => { bi.note('you', 'edited a paragraph'); // look() reports this bi.humanActed(); // this refuses the agent }); function doc_insert(p) { bi.guard(); /* … */ } // guard every write function doc_read() { return Object.assign({ text: editor.value }, bi.look()); } The first application already runs, as a second page in the same repo: examples/doc.html , a document a person and an agent write at the same time — six tools, the same barge-in.js behind them, about 250 lines of page on top. Rule 4 changes shape there, and that is the interesting part. On the canvas it means the agent's paint goes underneath. In a document it means a paragraph you have typed in is yours : ⛔ That paragraph belongs to the user — they typed in it. It can never be rewritten or deleted. Write around it: use doc_insert to add a paragraph before or after, and leave theirs exactly as it is. The agent has to compose around you — and on the first live attempt it went further than the rule required: "You replaced paragraph 2 during the edit, so it now belongs to you and must remain unchanged. I'll adapt the surrounding paragraphs to present your sentence as the central instruction and keep the document concise." It did not just leave the sentence alone. It restructured the document around it : the one paragraph it was forbidden to touch became the thing the other two were rewritten to support. That is the difference between a lock and a collaboration, and it came out of the same barge-in.js , with none of the canvas's code. Next in line is a form: an agent fills fifteen fields, you correct the third while it works, and rule 4 becomes a field the human has touched is never written again . A canvas is simply the smallest place where you can see this conflict happen. The rest — a spreadsheet, a slide deck, a whiteboard, a CAD model — is the same four rules with different nouns. Two pages to try Live (canvas): https://mcp.kitemir.jp/canvas/ Live (shared document): https://mcp.kitemir.jp/canvas/examples/doc.html Repo (MIT): https://github.com/zz08matsujp-max/barge-in Video: https://youtu.be/B3qbrK8W5Kw Requires the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser with Settings > Browser > Permissions > Enable site tools on, and GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra. The badge at the top right says whether WebMCP is live; if it is not, click it and the page prints a diagnostic table instead of failing silently. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP
video_title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: Archipelago
pitch: Map your Notion workspace as a shared visual interface for humans and AI agents, powered by WebMCP and running entirely in the browser.
about_excerpt: Map your Notion workspace as a shared visual interface for humans and AI agents, powered by WebMCP and running entirely in the browser. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Ask your AI to map your Notion. That single sentence is all it takes: Archipelago draws the chart on the right. Each database is an island sized by its rows; used relations become routes. The lighthouse marks the hub, a black flag an isolated base. The four WebMCP tools: draw a map, read it as structured data, highlight a computed set, annotate islands. Human and agent share one screen. One call to archipelago_draw_map: database names, row counts and relation metadata in, a live chart out. Rendered locally in the browser. Why I built it I'm a certified Notion consultant. A lot of my work is helping companies turn collections of databases, documents and workflows into actual operational systems. The problem is that systems are hard to explain. Most people are not technical, and looking at a workspace page by page makes it difficult to understand the whole thing. Is everything connected? Where does the structure actually live? Which databases are sitting alone? So I wanted a very simple visual language. In Archipelago, databases become islands, relations become routes, and linked data becomes convoys on those routes. You can look at the map for a few seconds and start asking better questions. That was the original idea: make a complex workspace easier to see and discuss. What it does Drop a Notion .zip export into Archipelago and it builds the map directly in your browser. Nothing is uploaded and Archipelago never connects to your Notion account. The result is deliberately playful rather than overly analytical. No score, no grade. The map gives you the structure and a one-line reading of it; what it means stays your call. It also makes a useful teaching tool when discussing a workspace with people who would never want to look at a database schema. Then came WebMCP The WebMCP part felt obvious to me quite quickly. If a human can use the map to understand a system, an AI agent should be able to use the same map rather than living in a separate chat window. So during the Challenge I added four WebMCP tools that let an agent: build a map from structured workspace data; read the map currently on screen; highlight databases; add its interpretation directly to the map. A user can now ask something like: "Show me everything connected to Clients." and the answer appears on the map they are already looking at. The actual challenge I'm not a developer by background, so part of the challenge was simply understanding a very new standard well enough to implement it properly. But the harder problem is still the one I'm working on: How do you make an agent visiting a website immediately understand that it can act there? I don't want the user to have to explain: "This site supports WebMCP. Go read the documentation, find the tools, then use them." The ideal experience is that the agent arrives, understands the capabilities exposed by the page, chooses the right tool and acts. Because WebMCP is still experimental, getting that discovery and tool-routing behavior to feel reliable across agents and browsers has been the most interesting part of the project. I have tried to follow the emerging best practices closely: explicit tool names, precise descriptions, structured schemas, state-aware error responses , and additional agent-oriented documentation. There is still a lot to learn. How I built it Archipelago is intentionally small: vanilla JavaScript, static files, no application backend and no build step. I built it with extensive AI assistance: ChatGPT as a strategic and tactical sparring partner, and Claude Code as the primary implementation agent. That workflow is also part of what made this project interesting to me. I don't come from a traditional software engineering background, but I could still spend most of my time on the parts I care about: the concept, the interaction model, the visual language and what the tool should actually do. What's next Notion is the first use case because it is the environment I know best, and because it already has a large community of people building increasingly complex systems with it. But I think the underlying idea can go further than mapping. Once a human and an agent can share the same visual representation of a system, the next step is to design and evolve that system together . The map could become a working surface for proposing a new structure, comparing it with the current one, highlighting dependencies, testing changes and progressively co-constructing an operational system. Archipelago starts with visibility. What interests me next is what happens when that shared visual interface becomes a place where humans and agents can actually build together. title: Lemma
pitch: Live LaTeX workspace, co-authored with your agent.
about_excerpt: Live LaTeX workspace, co-authored with your agent. Like Comment Story Updates Demo render error Agent inserted equation Error fixed by agent Dark theme Agent margin comment Tool inspector webmcp tools Inspiration I write a lot of math in LaTeX, and the AI workflow for it has been stuck in copy-paste mode: paste the source into a chat, get an edited copy back, paste it into an editor, hit a compile error, paste the error back, wait, repeat. The model never sees the document, only a stale snapshot from three messages ago, and I'm the courier running between them. Models are also shaky at LaTeX in a way people don't expect. The TeXpert benchmark puts even frontier models near 50% on compile tasks, and most of those misses are plain syntax slips, the kind a live renderer catches instantly. I mistype \alpha as \alpa more often than I'd like to admit. So does GPT-5.6. The fix the model needs is already on the page, and until WebMCP nothing could hand it over. I read the spec and started sketching a block-based pad that same evening, one where the agent and I share a single live document. What it does Lemma is a live LaTeX workspace your agent can edit with you. You type in a CodeMirror source pane, KaTeX renders every block as you type, and the agent (in ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome 149+, or Brave) works on the same live document through 15 imperative WebMCP tools plus one declarative form. It can list documents, read the block structure with render status and equation numbers, search, and make surgical edits: update one block by ID, insert labeled equations, leave margin comments, and undo its own changes. The seeded demo document is an integration by parts derivation whose last step hides a typo, \alpa where \alpha should be: $$ I = \int_0^1 x e^x\,dx = e - (e - 1) = 1 $$ Say "fix the render errors" and you watch get_render_errors return the typo with the block ID, the position, and a suggested fix, then update_block apply it, and the equation snaps clean with the edit attributed to the agent and one click to undo. Then ask it to add the product rule ( (fg)' = f'g + fg' ) with a label and a referencing paragraph. The new equation is numbered (2) and the reference in the new paragraph resolves live. No copy-paste, no server round trip, everything stays in the tab. How I built it Next.js 16 static export, React 19, TypeScript strict mode, Tailwind 4 with a custom token set, CodeMirror 6, KaTeX, Zustand, IndexedDB. The document model is a list of blocks (preamble, text, equations, theorems, tables), each with a stable ID. Agents edit by ID, never by quote matching, and a fuzzy reconciliation pass keeps IDs anchored when I hand-edit the source underneath them. A document-wide render context does real equation numbering, theorem numbering per kind, and \ref / \eqref resolution, and the tool payloads expose labels and numbers so the agent can cite equations correctly. The tool layer follows the spec and the security guidance closely: readOnlyHint on the five read tools, untrustedContentHint on everything that returns user-authored LaTeX (a math comment can carry a prompt injection), tight input caps, and abort-aware execute. Errors are returned as values with a hint, never thrown, because the spec reduces a thrown reason to a generic UnknownError the agent can't act on. That one decision is what makes the self-correction loop actually close. It's tested the boring way: 175 unit tests, plus two end-to-end suites that drive the real document.modelContext.registerTool and executeTool APIs (89 calls in one, 1043 calls in a soak test with concurrency, fuzzing, and hostile inputs, zero thrown exceptions). A built-in Tool Inspector wraps the same registered tools in UI, so anyone without a WebMCP-capable browser can still exercise every tool and see the exact JSON schemas. Challenges I ran into The ChatGPT browser implements a subset of WebMCP and skips declarative form tools. My sidebar search was declarative only, so to ChatGPT's browser it simply didn't exist. I added an imperative search_documents tool and now nothing depends on the form. The nastiest bug was silent. A bracket-corrupted netlify.toml dropped my custom headers on the deployed build with no warning, which meant no origin-keyed agent cluster, which meant registerTool threw a SecurityError in production while working perfectly locally. Headers are now checked on every deploy. There was also the day Codex told me my tools were "available in Lemma, but not connected to this task's tool interface." I went down the rabbit hole on that one. The spec is clear: tools live in the tab, and only agents that drive a WebMCP-capable browser can reach them. A sandboxed CLI has no bridge. Running the agent in the desktop app's built-in browser fixed it, and that investigation turned into the agent-compatibility matrix in the README. KaTeX is not LaTeX, and the gaps needed real engine work: \label needs space-padding so error positions stay honest, tables render through a custom HTML path with booktabs rules, and errors map back to source positions so the editor, the preview, and the agent all agree on where the problem is. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The self-correction loop is real and closed: write, render, read the structured error, fix, re-render, attribute, undo. The 1043-call soak test runs against the live registered tools with zero exceptions, and the app works in ChatGPT's actual in-app browser, which was the point of the whole exercise. It also holds up as a product rather than a demo: five document templates, live numbering and cross references, a mobile layout with a math key bar, a real print surface, compilable .tex export, and light and dark themes that got the same care as the editor. What I learned Designing tools for an agent is a lot like designing UI for humans. The error payload is the interface: if it says "position 22, suggestion \alpha", the model fixes it in one shot; if it says "compile failed", you get another round trip. Honest annotations matter more than I expected, both for how the agent behaves and for anyone auditing the integration. And tab-bound, ephemeral tools turned out to be a feature for this use case rather than a limitation: a scratch pad that lives and dies with the tab is exactly what a working draft should be. What's next for Lemma The next priority is honest LaTeX coverage: expanding what renders correctly without pretending to support what doesn't. More agent support comes right after. Right now the compatibility matrix is ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome 149+, and Brave. That's it. I want Lemma working in every browser and desktop agent that ships WebMCP, and I'll keep the compatibility matrix in the README honest as that list grows. On the LaTeX side, the gaps that matter most to users get filled first; the rest stay labeled unsupported rather than silently broken. The spec is still moving, and every new browser that ships WebMCP makes the whole thing more useful without a single line of change on my end. video_title: Lemma: a live LaTeX workspace co-authored with an agent.
video_transcript_excerpt: This is Lemma, a live LaTeX workspace co-authored with an agent. On the left is the LaTeX source. On the right, the document renders instantly as I work. But Lemma is more than a split editor. It uses WebMCP to let an agent work with a live document inside this browser tab. The agent does not need me to copy LaTeX into chat, paste an error message back, and then manually apply a suggested fix. Instead, it can use site tools to read the document's current structure, inspect render errors, and make precise updates to individual blocks. This document begins with one deliberate error. The command alpha has been mistyped as alpa, so the preview shows a render failure. I'll ask the agent to inspect the current document, identify the render error, and fix only the affected block. The agent reads the live document state, receives a structured render error with the exact block and a suggested correction, and updates that block directly. The preview re-renders immediately. The error is gone. The equation is correct, and the edit is visibly attributed to the agent. That is the core experience behind Lemma. Write, render, inspect the error, repair it, and re-render, all in one shared workspace. Now, I'll ask the agent to add a numbered equation for the product rule, label it, and add a short paragraph that references it. Rather than overriding the document, the agent inserts a new block in the right place. Lemma assigns equations and paragraphs stable block identities, so the agent can make focused changes while preserving the author's existing work. The equation receives a live number, its label is registered, and the reference resolves in the new paragraph. This precision matters for technical writing. A document is not just a string of text. It has structure, equations, references, comments, and context. Lemma exposes that live structure to the agent through WebMCP. Finally, I'll ask the agent to leave a comment on the theorem without changing the mathematics. The result is a margin comment anchored to the relevant block and clearly marked as agent-authored. The author stays in control. Every change is visible, targeted, and undoable. Lemma turns AI-assisted LaTeX from a copy and paste workflow into genuine collaboration. The agent sees the same live document state as the author, acts through browser-native tools, and helps keep mathematical writing correct, structured, and moving forward.

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most.  ApplyFlow: a job-search workspace for people + agents 

 I built ApplyFlow for The WebMCP Challenge because I kept hitting the same wall: applying to jobs is half product, half chore, and no tool today lets an AI assistant genuinely help without fighting the UI. Chat agents can write a cover letter in a chat box, but they can't see your board, work your pipeline, or edit the same document you're editing. Raw MCP servers operate on data, not on the page you're looking at. WebMCP is the missing bridge — agents finally run inside the app you use. 

 The idea. ApplyFlow is one workspace where a person and an AI agent work the same live page in the same session. The human browses roles, filters, and writes like always. The agent calls the exact same app: it searches and scores jobs against a résumé, drafts tailored cover letters, advances applications through a pipeline, and pins notes. The critical rule: every state-changing action the agent takes is staged as a pending action and must be approved by the human in a shared activity feed. The agent does the tedious work; the human keeps ownership. That's the collaboration model WebMCP is designed for, and it shows up in every one of my tool choices. 

 How I built it. Next.js 16 + React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind, no backend — the whole product is a static SPA whose state lives in localStorage, so it deploys anywhere and works fully offline. WebMCP was brand new, so the WebMCP layer was built from the Chrome/W3C specs and iterated on: 

 Imperative tools — 9 registered via document.modelContext.registerTool: list_jobs, get_job_details, score_cv_match, get_application_overview (read-only, readOnlyHint: true); create_application, update_application_status, draft_cover_letter, tailor_cv_highlights, add_note (write tools that stage a pending action the human approves or dismisses).
Declarative API — the application form uses toolname, tooldescription, and toolparamdescription attributes so the agent can pre-fill it, and deliberately omits toolautosubmit so only the human submits.
Security hints the WebMCP spec cares about: readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint on the tools that deserve them.
Shared documents — the cover letter and CV-highlights playground live in one editor both parties mutate, so a draft from the agent is immediately visible to the person.
Challenges. WebMCP is simultaneously public and moving fast. The spec changed between the docs I first read and the API surface, which taught me to build a thin adapter and keep tool behavior decoupled from registration. Speech-to-text and event APIs like toolactivated aren't in the standard WindowEventMap, so I had to extend types carefully. My React+TS setup needed module augmentation to expose the declarative attributes (toolname, toolparamdescription, …) as typed JSX props. And there was the usual 10-day crunch: decide the demo, cut scope, ship a build that passes, then make the human-in-the-loop experience the star rather than an afterthought. 

 What I learned. The biggest lesson is that the human-agent boundary is a product decision, not an API detail. Every Write tool in ApplyFlow returns "staged for approval" — the agent never mutates state unilaterally — and that one design constraint is what makes the experience feel safe and fun instead of scary. I also learned that a great WebMCP app doesn't need to be more than a static page; the agent is a full environment away. The judge's ChatGPT browser is the demo machine. 

 I hope ApplyFlow shows what "agent-native" means in practice: software a person can use alone, an agent can use alone, and — for the first time — both can use together.

title: Heatline
pitch: A tenant and a legal-aid advocate each get an agent on one NYC building's own enforcement record.
about_excerpt: A tenant and a legal-aid advocate each get an agent on one NYC building's own enforcement record. Like Comment Story Updates 52 degrees at 7am, eleven mornings in a row That was the reading in a fourth-floor apartment on Barnes Avenue in the Bronx this winter. The landlord stopped answering in January. What the tenant did not know, and what I did not know until I pulled the data, is that the city already had a file on the building: 102 open class C violations. Class C is HPD's word for "immediately hazardous." The oldest has been open 601 days. All of that sits on NYC Open Data. No key, no login, one SODA query. It has never been in the same room as the tenant. What Heatline does with it Two people open one case page from two different links. The tenant gets 12 WebMCP tools; the legal-aid advocate helping them gets 9. Same origin, same deployment, different agents. I want to be precise about the difference because it is the whole product: Only the tenant's window has log_condition , file_packet , answer_evidence_request , share_case and the 311 form. Only the advocate's window has assemble_hp_action_packet and request_evidence . Open DevTools, Application, WebMCP in both windows and the lists are not the same. The role is a capability key in the URL. The server re-derives it on every write, so when the advocate's agent forges a file_packet call (I tried) it gets a 403 that reads: "Only the tenant can file packet. You are the advocate: this stays with the tenant's session." The hidden tool is a convenience. The server is the boundary. A tenant does not know what a BBL is The first version of building_violation_history required a 10-digit borough-block-lot number. The advocate's agent called it with {} and got "bbl is required." That is a tool written for a database, not for a person freezing in an apartment. It now reads the BBL off the open case and only takes one if you want a different building. Fixed the same hour, in the commit log. The same instinct runs through the rest. The tenant types "no heat again, 52 degrees at 7am." match_condition_to_code returns section 27-2029 with the rule in plain English: 68F from 6am to 10pm when it is under 55F outside, heat season October 1 to May 31. log_condition then stops inside a confirmation card until the tenant presses Confirm. The agent proposes; the person decides. Every number on the page carries the SODA URL that produced it. Paste the URL and you get the same 102. Four NYC Open Data feeds become one per-building index, the page registers a different tool set per link, and the server re-checks the role before any write lands. The loop the two agents run The advocate's agent asks for a photo of the thermostat at 7am tomorrow. That request lands in the tenant's window over a live stream, no reload. The tenant's agent answers. The advocate's agent then calls assemble_hp_action_packet , which writes five sections from the case plus the city record: parties (owner name and portfolio size from the HPD registration), conditions with code sections, the building record with a block comparison, a timeline, relief sought. It saves a draft. In the tenant's window, file_packet 's description now says "one draft packet waiting"; the agent calls it, a person presses Confirm, the packet is filed. The 311 complaint is a real <form toolname="draft_311_complaint"> with toolparamdescription on each field and deliberately no toolautosubmit . The agent fills it. Only a human can press Send. You cannot do this with a chatbot wrapper or by scraping the page. Nothing else knows which window is asking. The tenant's window and the advocate's window on the same case. The gate in the middle is the server, not the tool list. The parts that are not glamorous document.modelContext.registerTool , never navigator.modelContext . Native first, @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill as fallback, and a badge on the page says which one is live. Fourteen tools. untrustedContentHint on list_conditions and build_timeline , because those return text another person typed; that text is wrapped in <untrusted-user-text> on the tool path, the REST path and the SSE stream. Confirm gates are built inside each mutating tool's execute , since WebMCP has no destructive-action annotation. Seventeen eval fixtures. The negative ones assert the denied tool is absent from that session's toolsForRole , so "just file it for them" from the advocate expects zero calls. 125 tests. Read tools fetch through /api/building/* so the 1.3 MB index stays server-side; importing it into the client broke the production build on day one, and that fix is in the history too. The index covers 40 buildings in zip 10467, the Bronx zip with the most open class C heat violations, 6,077 rows. The build script and every query URL are in the repo. Everything here was written on 4 September 2026 with Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind 4, Upstash Redis, Vitest and NYC Open Data. The build script, every SODA query URL and the eval fixtures are in the repo. title: Shopfront Copilot
pitch: Shop together with your AI agent, but only you can hit "buy."
about_excerpt: Shop together with your AI agent, but only you can hit "buy." Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The WebMCP spec's own authors flagged the sharpest risk in agentic commerce in their own draft. Section 6.3.2.3 walks through an ambiguously named tool, finalizeCart , that an agent could call and silently complete a real purchase. An agent shopping "on your behalf" today has two bad options: screen-scrape the UI (brittle, no ground truth), or call a private backend API directly (bypasses whatever safety rails the storefront's own UI enforces). WebMCP offered a third path: let the agent call the exact tool the UI itself uses, on the exact same page state a human is looking at. We wanted to build a storefront that took the spec's own warning seriously enough to actually engineer around it, not just write a paragraph about "responsible AI" in a README. What it does Shopfront Copilot is a storefront where a shopper and their AI agent browse, compare, and buy together. The agent can: Search & filter the catalog by price, category, and other bounded fields Compare 2-4 products side by side in a real on-page comparison table Check return policy for a product Add / remove cart items , reversible either direction Watch a product for price drops All of it runs through the same WebMCP tools registered on document.modelContext that the storefront's own UI calls. A shopper also controls an Autonomy Dial (read-only vs. browse-and-cart) and an optional spending cap , both enforced with machine-readable refusal codes the agent can act on. The checkout gate: the headline feature Action Exposed to the agent? Can it complete a purchase? checkout (WebMCP tool) Yes No. Always returns { status: "confirmation_required", cart_summary } . Never mutates the cart. Confirm-purchase click Not a registered tool at all. Yes, this is the only thing that finalizes an order, and it's gated behind WebAuthn on a plain onClick handler an agent can't reach. There is no tool an agent can call, no matter how it's worded, that completes a purchase. How we built it Stack: Next.js (App Router), TypeScript, React, Tailwind State: client-side React context persisted to localStorage , no backend database Tools: defined once in lib/webmcp/tools/ , registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() , so a human's click and an agent's tool call run through the identical code path into the identical shared cart The safety layer is factored out into its own framework-agnostic package, webmcp-guardrails : Autonomy tiers & spending caps that gate mutating calls Structural-absence check that proves confirm_purchase was never registered, rather than just asserting it in prose Flight recorder that logs every tool call as structured, timestamped data Intent-snapshot diffing that freezes what an agent saw when it called checkout and flags anything that changed by the time a human confirms To prove the pattern holds against a real model, not just scripted scenarios, we added a live agent mode backed by Groq , driving the exact same tool registry and guardrails a simulated harness uses. Checkout confirmation is server-verified through WebAuthn with zero database, and everything degrades gracefully in browsers without document.modelContext support, which today is most of them. Challenges we ran into Making the checkout gate airtight meant resisting the temptation to "just add a permission check" to a confirm_purchase tool, since a runtime check is something an agent, or a future refactor, could route around. We made the property structural instead of declarative : the function that finalizes an order simply is never wired into the tool registry. We also hit five places where the WebMCP spec doesn't yet define an answer: No standard classification for irreversible actions No agent identity to key a per-agent rate limit or trust tier on No way for a shopper's consent decision to persist and reach the agent before it fails once No push channel for telling an idle agent a watched price actually dropped No standard primitive for an agent to pause and ask a human a question We wrote up each gap and our workaround as an RFC rather than silently papering over them. Keeping the demo honest against a real model was its own challenge: a live Groq-backed agent will happily try creative phrasings to get a tool to do more than its contract allows, which made for a good adversarial test of whether our guardrails actually held. Accomplishments that we're proud of confirm_purchase cannot be reached by an agent under any circumstance, and we can prove it structurally , not just document it webmcp-guardrails is genuinely reusable: pure TypeScript, no dependency on React or this app's domain Live agent mode means the checkout gate is tested against a real model actively trying to complete a purchase, not just scripted scenarios What we learned The safest thing you can do with a dangerous capability isn't a well-worded permission check, it's not exposing the capability's implementation to the caller at all . We also came away convinced that several of the gaps we hit (agent identity, a standard human-question primitive) sit upstream of a lot of other trust problems in agentic web tooling, and are worth pushing at the spec level rather than solving per-site forever. What's next for Shopfront Copilot Publish webmcp-guardrails to npm so other WebMCP sites can adopt the structural-absence pattern without rebuilding it Prototype an irreversibleHint annotation as a concrete proposal back to the WebMCP spec Prototype a standard ask_human -shaped primitive for the same reason Built With next react typescript webmcp Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Yanfunmi Jeje Like Share this project: Updates Yanfunmi Jeje started this project — Sep 03, 2026 04:47 AM EDT

title: MCPixels
pitch: A collaborative pixel-art canvas where people and AI agents draw, edit, and export together live in the browser using page-native WebMCP tools, with no backend required.
about_excerpt: A collaborative pixel-art canvas where people and AI agents draw, edit, and export together live in the browser using page-native WebMCP tools, with no backend required. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every AI drawing tool I'd used treated the model the same way: describe a thing, receive a finished image, regenerate. None of them let me keep working on what came back, and none of them let the model keep working on what I made. AI gives you the speed and the general idea, but the details are the user's job, and the user should be able to change what the AI made without starting over. The interesting position isn't "agent makes art". It's two hands on the same document, where either can pick up where the other stopped. WebMCP is what makes that possible in a browser, or at least much easier and cheaper. The page can hand an agent the same verbs the person has, so there's no separate API surface, no plugin, and no copy of the document living somewhere else. What it does MCPixels is a 1024×1024 pixel-art canvas that a person and an agent edit at the same time, in the same tab. For the person it's an ordinary pixel editor: pencil, eraser, shapes, flood fill, selections, mirroring, PNG import and export, undo. In a WebMCP browser the page also registers six site tools , covering everything (mostly, TBD) a person can do: draw_pixel_art : the only tool that carries pixel data read_canvas : reads any region back in exactly the format a draw goes out in selection : duplicate, move, erase, flip, rotate, copy/cut/paste edit : undo, redo, clear view : frames a region for the person export_pixel_art : saves a PNG to their download folder The two of you share one canvas and one undo stack, so the agent's edits sit on the same timeline as yours and either of you can step back through the other's work. Agent actions appear in a notice feed. How we built it A static React and TypeScript app on Cloudflare Pages. No server, no database. The tools are registered by the page itself with document.modelContext.registerTool , and their handlers call straight into the editor's own reducer, so an agent action and a mouse action take the identical path through the code. The design constraint that shaped everything is that a tool surface lives in the model's context on every turn, competing with the art for room. So: Pictures, not coordinates. Sprites travel as rows of single-character palette keys, like "..kkkk.." , rather than [{x, y, color}, …] . It's dramatically cheaper, and the model can see the shape it's writing. . leaves a cell alone and - erases, so stamping never scrubs the art underneath. A closed loop. read_canvas returns the same {origin, palette, rows} shape draw_pixel_art accepts, so read → edit the rows → draw back needs no reformatting in between. Geometry goes through an ops string. rect , ellipse , poly , path , bucket , recolor , and ordered-dither fills, so large flat areas cost almost nothing. Rearranging sends no pixels at all. selection moves art the canvas already holds. The site also advertises itself to agents through static discovery documents: an RFC 9727 API catalog, an MCP server card, an agent-skills index and a SKILL.md , llms.txt , plus Link headers and DNS records pointing at them. Challenges we ran into The hard problems were all about budget and about two actors sharing one document. Getting the encoding right took the longest. The obvious wire format for pixels is a list of coordinates, and it is completely unaffordable. A single sprite eats a meaningful fraction of a context window. Rows of palette characters fixed the cost, but then the read path had to return that exact shape or the agent would spend its remaining budget reformatting. Reads also needed a hard ceiling. A read has to cost about the same whether the canvas is empty or covered, so read_canvas caps the region it will return exactly and falls back to a coarser overview beyond that, with an exact flag saying which you got. Then the shared-document problems. One undo stack for two actors means an agent call has to be exactly one history step, or none, if it changed nothing. Edits that land off-screen are invisible, so the view eases across and the area flashes; but that must never fight the person, so it's skipped mid-gesture or while a panel is open, and can be switched off entirely. And view deliberately only ever zooms out . An agent should be able to show you something, never shove your workspace around. Accomplishments that we're proud of That the agent is a participant rather than a pixel pipe. It reads what you drew, rearranges what it drew, undoes your mistakes and its own, and hands you a PNG at the end, all through the same six verbs, with no backend anywhere. The encoding, in particular. Sending art as pictures instead of coordinates is roughly an order of magnitude cheaper, which is the whole reason a full-featured tool surface fits alongside real work. A ten-frame walk-cycle spritesheet gets built from one draw call plus a handful of selection ops. The other nine frames never travel over the wire at all. What we learned Token budget is a design constraint, not an optimisation you do later. Every choice here came from the fact that descriptions and schemas are re-sent every single turn: the row format, the ops string, the read ceiling, keeping the surface to six tools instead of twenty. The second lesson was that shared-state UX is most of the work. Making an agent able to draw is easy. Making its edits legible, undoable, and non-disruptive to someone already holding the mouse is where the actual product is. What's next for MCPixels Accounts and saved sessions , so a canvas survives the tab closing and you and the agent can pick the same piece back up days later. Layers , so a person and an agent can work without painting over each other. Animation as a first-class object rather than frames laid out on a grid, with onion skinning and an export that knows what a frame is. Image import for agents , the one editor capability the tool surface doesn't yet cover. Tighter reads. Run-length rows already exist on the write path; the read path could use them to return much larger regions inside the same budget. Multiplayer , which the architecture already half-implies. The canvas doesn't care whether the second set of hands is a model or another person. title: Dispatch
pitch: A shared decision memo for an ad account. Agents file findings through the page's own WebMCP tools — every claim must cite a number, and the number is verified before the finding lands.
about_excerpt: A shared decision memo for an ad account. Agents file findings through the page's own WebMCP tools — every claim must cite a number, and the number is verified before the finding lands. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every week, somebody writes the memo for each ad account. It is asymmetric work: a media buyer can tell in seconds whether a reading is plausible, but pulling the numbers that justify it across five campaigns and thirteen ad sets is an afternoon. An agent is the reverse — it reads every line instantly, but it has nowhere to put what it finds, and no way to be held to the numbers it quotes. Today that gap is bridged by copy-paste. The agent writes a summary in a chat window, the buyer retypes the useful parts into a document, and the link back to the specific metric is lost on the way. That matters more than it sounds: "CPM is climbing in Creative Testing" is worth nothing if nobody can check it, and a memo full of unverifiable claims is worse than no memo, because people act on it. What it does Dispatch is a room built around one shared decision memo for one ad account. Open it, send the link to a colleague, and both of you — plus any agent driving either browser — work the same memo live. Agents call file_finding , and the finding appears in the memo as a claim with a citation you can click through to the numbers behind it. The claim is verified before it lands. file_finding re-reads the cited metric from the account and refuses the finding if the value is wrong. An agent that cannot point at the number does not get to make the claim. A human accepts or dismisses each finding. Dismissed findings stay visible, struck through, with the reason — so next week's memo can be read against this week's argument. Press Send the analyst team and three agents join: an Analyst files findings with citations, a Skeptic rules on each one, and a Strategist files what happens Monday. In a real run the Skeptic dismissed a rip-current claim as "single-period snapshot; cannot verify a rising CPM trend" , and accepted a scale recommendation on evidence of 8.40x ROAS and $10.27 CPA. Two agents disagreeing in front of the person who has to act — that argument had no natural home on the web before. How we built it A useWebMcpTool hook wraps document.modelContext.registerTool : one tool per component lifetime, registration tied to an AbortController so unmounting unregisters, and execute held in a ref so tools read current state without re-registering on every render. Ten tools are registered from src/components/memo-tools.tsx — get_account_summary , get_breakdown , check_metric , file_finding , set_finding_status , read_memo , dispatch_analyst_team , set_focus , join_room , list_participants . The UI and the tools call the same endpoints, so a number an agent cites is the number on the buyer's screen, not a second implementation that can drift. Shared room state lives in Upstash Redis. Because judges cannot connect a Meta ad account, the room runs on a seeded deterministic account — 5 campaigns, 13 ad sets, 28 days — shaped so each situation in the taxonomy actually occurs. Every visitor sees identical numbers, which is what makes a citation checkable. Challenges we ran into Concurrency was the real one. Modelling the room as a single JSON document with compare-and-set lost 4 of 10 concurrent writes in testing. Splitting the state into separate Redis structures — RPUSH for findings — held 20 parallel writes from three agents. Safety was the other. There is no free-form query tool, so a steered agent has no vocabulary beyond the fixed shapes; campaign names written by people outside the buyer's organisation are fenced in guillemets so the model reads them as data, never instruction; every tool validates its own input; and nothing writes to an ad account. Accomplishments that we're proud of Fabrication is refused, not caught later. A finding citing a CPM of $4.10 when the real figure is $20.88 is rejected with the true number, at the moment it is filed. What we learned Putting the tools in the page changes what an agent is for. A conventional MCP server can fetch these metrics; it cannot put a finding in front of you, take your verdict, and let a second agent argue with it. What's next for Dispatch A live Meta Marketing API connection behind the same tool surface, so the citation check runs against a real account; and memo history, so this week's argument is read against last week's. Turn a founder’s natural-language business story into an authoritative exit-readiness assessment. ChatGPT uses WebMCP to operate Exit Desk’s real M&A scoring engine—not simulate it.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most AI agents still interact with websites the way humans do: reading pages, interpreting interfaces, and clicking through forms. 

 Exit Desk already existed as a real buyer-lens exit-readiness product for business owners. Its free assessment asks eight questions and evaluates a company across revenue quality, founder dependence, financial health, competitive position, and timing alignment. 

 The WebMCP Challenge gave us a simple question: 

 What if ChatGPT did not have to operate Exit Desk by guessing how its interface works? What if Exit Desk could expose its actual capability directly to the agent? 

 That became Exit Desk × WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 A business owner can describe their company to ChatGPT in ordinary language: 

 
 “We do about $5M in revenue. Customers repeat but aren't contracted. I still own key client relationships. Our largest customer is about 15% of revenue. The team handles daily operations, margins are stable, our moat is reputation, and I'm exploring a sale.” 
 

 Instead of clicking through Exit Desk's eight-question interface, ChatGPT discovers a WebMCP tool exposed by the site: 

 run_exit_readiness_assessment 

 ChatGPT translates the owner's natural-language description into the structured inputs required by Exit Desk and invokes the tool. 

 Exit Desk then runs its existing deterministic assessment engine and returns the same score, dimension scores, weakest dimension, findings, and next-step information that the human-facing application produces. 

 The human and the agent therefore work from the same authoritative result. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 The important architectural distinction is that ChatGPT does not recreate Exit Desk's M&A logic. 

 ChatGPT handles conversation, intent, and translation. 

 Exit Desk remains the authoritative application performing the assessment. 

 Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer the interface and manipulate eight separate questions. With WebMCP, the website declares what it can do and the structured inputs it requires. 

 The interaction becomes: 

 Natural language → ChatGPT → WebMCP tool → Exit Desk assessment → structured result 

 This turns Exit Desk from a website an AI can read or click through into a capability an AI can reliably operate. 

 How we built it 

 The production Exit Desk assessment runs at mikeye.com/exit/score . 

 For the challenge, we added a WebMCP integration using the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. 

 The tool defines a structured input schema for the eight assessment dimensions and maps those inputs into Exit Desk's existing assessment application. It invokes the same scoring and results logic used by the human interface, then returns structured output to the agent. 

 The WebMCP source lives in the public GitHub repository and is deployed through Vercel. The production Webflow page loads that repository-backed implementation. 

 We tested the integration using ChatGPT's in-app browser. ChatGPT successfully discovered run_exit_readiness_assessment , invoked it, and received Exit Desk's resulting score and dimension analysis. 

 What we built during the challenge 

 Exit Desk itself predates the WebMCP Challenge. 

 The WebMCP capability does not. 

 During the challenge period we: 

 
 Designed the agent-facing assessment interface. 
 Implemented run_exit_readiness_assessment . 
 Defined the structured input schema and mappings. 
 Connected WebMCP to Exit Desk's existing scoring engine and human-facing results. 
 Deployed the integration to the production Exit Desk website. 
 Tested the complete flow using ChatGPT's in-app browser. 
 Added public implementation documentation and challenge-period source history. 
 

 The GitHub commit history documents these additions separately from the pre-existing application. 

 What we learned 

 The most interesting lesson was that WebMCP is not primarily about making agents better at clicking websites. 

 It can remove the need to click them. 

 A website can retain ownership of its domain logic while allowing an AI agent to provide a much more natural interface to that capability. 

 For Exit Desk, that means the AI does not become the M&A assessment engine. It becomes the conversational layer through which a founder can access that engine. 

 What's next 

 The same architecture can extend beyond the initial assessment. 

 Future Exit Desk tools could help owners prepare diligence materials, identify buyer-readiness gaps, evaluate founder dependence, compare buyer types, and prepare for acquisition conversations. 

 The broader idea is simple: 

 The web is moving from machine-readable to machine-operable.
