title: OpenOperator
pitch: Your operations workspace, built for people and AI agents.
about_excerpt: Your operations workspace, built for people and AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates OpenOperator One website, two interfaces: visual for people, structured for agents. Inspiration AI agents can already operate websites, but most sites make them work through interfaces designed only for people. The agent has to inspect text, infer the purpose of controls, guess selectors, move through several screens, and recover whenever the layout changes. That is especially fragile in business operations. A single customer request can cross CRM, fulfillment, policy, billing, and support. The agent may understand the goal perfectly and still struggle to perform a reliable sequence of clicks. WebMCP suggests a better model: the website can state its capabilities directly. Instead of asking an agent to reverse-engineer the UI, the site provides named, typed tools that invoke its real application logic. OpenOperator explores that idea through one concrete promise: The same live application should be naturally usable by a person and precisely operable by their agent. What it does OpenOperator is a multi-user small-business operating system with four connected modules: CRM for customers, lifetime value, balances, and internal notes Orders and shipping for line items, fulfillment, tracking, and delay detection Support for customer cases and auditable resolutions Billing for credits, refunds, and explicit human approval Every signed-in user receives an isolated, durable workspace. There are no seeded customers, mock orders, or shared demo records. People and agents add real records through the visual interface or through WebMCP, and both see the same state immediately. The page registers 32 WebMCP tools. ChatGPT can create, search, read, connect, update, and delete owned records; calculate whether a shipment is delayed; evaluate the compensation policy; request a credit or refund; add or edit a CRM note; and resolve a ticket. OpenOperator deliberately withholds one capability from the agent: approving a financial action. Credits and refunds remain pending until the signed-in person approves or rejects them in the visual Billing interface. The core demo The main scenario begins with a natural request: “A customer says their package hasn’t arrived. Figure out what happened and take care of them.” ChatGPT can then: Search for the customer. Load a compact context containing recent orders, shipment state, tickets, notes, and financial history. Inspect the relevant order and tracking record. Determine that the shipment is late from its promised date. Read the compensation policy. Request an eligible customer credit of up to ₹2,000. Wait while the person reviews and approves the financial action. Add an internal CRM note. Resolve the support ticket with a saved summary and timestamp. The person can watch the same dashboard update after every tool call. There is no second agent database, hidden automation service, or eventual synchronization step. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Without WebMCP, this workflow asks an agent to repeatedly interpret a changing visual interface across several sections. With WebMCP, OpenOperator exposes the application’s semantic boundaries directly: get_customer_context returns the cross-domain context an agent actually needs. track_shipment returns structured dates, status, delay state, and delay duration. get_compensation_policy turns a business rule into an explicit read capability. request_customer_credit creates a validated pending action instead of bypassing human judgment. Mutating tools and UI forms invoke the same server dispatcher, so behavior cannot drift between interfaces. Read-only and destructive annotations help the client understand each tool’s intent. WebMCP is not an accessory in OpenOperator. It defines the product architecture: domain actions are designed once, authorized once, and then offered through the interface best suited to the current participant. What people and agents can do together The person does not need to manually collect order IDs, copy tracking details between tabs, interpret a policy, and enter the same resolution in multiple systems. The agent can gather context and prepare the work using structured calls. The agent does not receive unlimited authority. The person remains in control of consequential financial decisions, can inspect the source-attributed activity history, and can delete any owned resource through the UI. This produces a collaborative loop that is difficult to achieve with conventional browser automation: Person states intent ↓ Agent gathers structured private context ↓ Agent performs safe record work ↓ Person reviews consequential decision ↓ Agent completes the operational follow-through How we built it OpenOperator is hosted as a ChatGPT Site using the Sites-provided TypeScript/Vinext application structure. The implementation combines: Sign in with ChatGPT for authenticated identity document.modelContext.registerTool() for page-owned WebMCP tools A shared same-origin action API used by both the UI and WebMCP Cloudflare D1 for durable relational storage Drizzle schema definitions and a generated SQL migration Server-side ownership, relationship, policy, and input validation The UI requests /api/data to load the signed-in user’s workspace. Human forms and WebMCP tools send named actions to /api/actions . Both routes require the platform-provided authenticated user. The server dispatcher executes only a fixed action allowlist and binds the stable user ID to every database operation. Human UI ──────────────┐ ├─ authenticated action API ─ validation/policy ─ owner-scoped D1 WebMCP page tools ─────┘ └─ activity trail WebMCP implementation The client registers 32 tools when document.modelContext.registerTool becomes available. Each definition contains: A stable action-oriented name A description optimized for agent discovery A narrow JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false Required fields and descriptions for every argument readOnlyHint for searches and reads destructiveHint for deletion tools An execute function that calls the authenticated shared action endpoint The tools cover: CRM create_customer , update_customer , search_customers , get_customer , get_customer_context , add_customer_note , update_customer_note , delete_customer_note , delete_customer Orders and shipping create_order , search_orders , get_order , update_order , update_order_item , delete_order_item , delete_order , upsert_shipment , track_shipment , delete_shipment , get_compensation_policy Support create_support_ticket , update_support_ticket , search_support_tickets , get_support_ticket , resolve_support_ticket , delete_support_ticket Billing and activity request_customer_credit , request_order_refund , update_financial_action , get_approval_status , delete_financial_action , delete_activity The agent can request a credit or refund but cannot approve one. Approval is a separate human-only application action and is intentionally absent from the WebMCP registry. Order status is explicit and validated across both interfaces: Processing , Confirmed , On hold , Shipped , Delivered , and Cancelled . Shipment status is modeled separately with Label created , In transit , Out for delivery , Delivered , Delivery exception , and Cancelled ; fulfillment updates synchronize the parent order lifecycle. The WebMCP schemas expose both lists as enums, so agents can discover valid values before calling a tool. Live data and multi-user isolation Nine tables persist users, customers, orders, line items, shipments, tickets, notes, financial actions, and activities. Every business row has an owner_id . Ownership is not accepted from tool arguments or the browser. The server derives it from the authenticated Sites request and applies it to every insert, search, lookup, update, and deletion. This matters for agent safety: even if an agent supplies a valid record ID belonging to another account, the owner-scoped query returns no record. Relationship checks also prevent linking one customer to another customer’s order. Trust, safety, and human authority OpenOperator treats a structured tool as a doorway into application policy, not a shortcut around it. Credits require a shipment delayed by at least 48 hours. Refunds cannot exceed the stored order total. Duplicate pending or completed delay credits are rejected. Financial requests begin as Pending . Only the signed-in person can approve or reject a request in Billing. Every write records whether it came from a person or “ChatGPT via WebMCP.” Delete tools are owner-scoped and marked destructive. Cascading deletion maintains linked-data consistency. Prepared statements and a fixed dispatcher prevent arbitrary SQL or code execution. title: Machine Passport
pitch: Evidence-backed machine readiness for humans and AI agents. WebMCP lets agents compare machines, explain blockers, and stage the next safe step—while humans keep execution authority.
about_excerpt: Evidence-backed machine readiness for humans and AI agents. WebMCP lets agents compare machines, explain blockers, and stage the next safe step—while humans keep execution authority. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP compares the same machine evidence the human sees: Beacon is safer for the unattended AI workload, while Atlas remains NOT_READY. The agent stages a bounded next step; the human approves it for review, while execution remains NOT_EXECUTED and the machine stays untouched Inspiration I started Machine Passport from a very practical problem I keep running into: having several machines does not mean you actually know which one is ready for a specific job. A machine can have the best CPU, the most RAM, or the strongest GPU and still be the wrong machine for an unattended workload because qualification is incomplete, recovery is unproven, deployment is fragile, or an important security fact is simply unknown. That led to the question behind the whole project: What if an AI agent could help choose the safest machine for the job from evidence — without giving the agent authority to change the machine? That is Machine Passport. The central idea is simple: The fastest machine is not always the safest machine for the job. What it does Machine Passport turns machine evidence into a versioned passport and then evaluates readiness for a specific role across four dimensions: FIT DEPLOYMENT QUALIFICATION SECURITY The result is deterministic rather than an LLM opinion. One rule became especially important while building it: UNKNOWN stays UNKNOWN. If evidence is missing or a collector could not obtain it, Machine Passport does not silently turn that absence into a pass or a fail. In the public demo, Atlas has the strongest hardware, but for an unattended AI workload it is NOT_READY . Beacon is a more modest machine, yet it is READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS and has no hard blockers. That difference is the product. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, Machine Passport is already useful as a human dashboard. With WebMCP, the page becomes something an agent can work with directly. Instead of trying to infer machine state from rendered UI or DOM structure, the page exposes five typed tools over the same state the human sees: list_machines get_machine_passport assess_role_readiness compare_machines stage_change_proposal The first four are genuinely read-only. The fifth can stage a bounded proposal in application state. That means I can ask: Which machine is safest for an overnight AI workload, what blocks the runner-up, and what is the smallest safe next step? The agent can inspect the evidence, compare the machines, explain the result, and stage the proposed next step. The proposal then appears in the same page for human review. That shared state is the part I find most interesting about WebMCP: the human and the agent are not operating two separate versions of reality. Human authority is part of the design I deliberately did not give the WebMCP tools SSH, PowerShell, device access, or machine mutation. Machine Passport is the pre-action decision layer . The agent can inspect and stage. The human decides. Even after the human clicks Approve for Review , the proposal still says: execution_state = NOT_EXECUTED That is not unfinished functionality. It is the authority boundary of this version. Agents inspect and stage. Humans decide. Machines stay untouched. How I built it The public challenge version is intentionally small and inspectable. It is a static web application with: a normalized MachinePassport schema, strict JSON validation, explicit evidence provenance, deterministic readiness rules, conservative UNKNOWN semantics, five WebMCP tools, shared proposal state, and a human review interface. The public app uses three clearly synthetic machines: Atlas, Beacon, and Relay . The same frozen import and readiness core was also privately validated against one sanitized real machine passport . I kept that claim deliberately narrow. This is not a fleet-management product and I am not claiming production deployment. The current version has 157 deterministic tests , including malformed imports, UNKNOWN preservation, readiness aggregation, proposal transitions, blocker semantics, retry-safe staging, and machine-mutation invariants. Challenges I faced One of the most useful lessons came from testing the real agent journey instead of only testing the code. During a live ChatGPT run, an identical tool retry initially created a duplicate proposal. That exposed something unit tests had not made obvious enough: an agent-facing action needs to tolerate repeated calls. I changed staging so that an identical active request returns the existing proposal instead of creating another one. Another issue was blocker semantics. A limitation on an otherwise healthy readiness dimension was being presented too strongly. I changed the policy so a finding becomes a blocker only when its evidence intersects a dimension that is actually NOT_READY or UNKNOWN . Those fixes reinforced the same lesson: the contract exposed to an agent has to be stricter than the UI alone suggests. What I learned Building Machine Passport changed how I think about agentic interfaces. The interesting question is not only: What can the agent do? It is also: What should the agent be able to know, what should it be allowed to stage, and where should its authority stop? WebMCP made that separation tangible. It also showed me that machine readiness is different from telemetry. Telemetry tells you what a machine has or what it is doing. Machine Passport tries to answer a different question: Given the evidence we actually have, is this machine ready for this role — and if not, what is the smallest safe next step? What's next The natural next step is to let specialist collectors and diagnostics feed Machine Passport evidence while keeping collection separate from adjudication. That could make the passport useful across local workstations, GPU nodes, lab machines, and unattended AI systems without changing the core idea: evidence first, deterministic readiness second, bounded agent action third, human authority last. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. pitch: A secure, agent-ready learning experience where people and AI use WebMCP to find training, build learning paths, track progress, and take permitted actions together.
about_excerpt:
A secure, agent-ready learning experience where people and AI use WebMCP to find training, build learning paths, track progress, and take permitted actions together.

 Inspiration 

 LearnLogos has a large collection of instructional videos, captions, and sentence-level timestamps. Learners often Blackjack remember what John taught but cannot remember the course, video, or terminology
 needed to find it. We wanted agents to retrieve LearnLogos teaching directly instead of generating a generic answer or guessing how to navigate the website. 

 ## What it does 

 The LearnLogos WebMCP Learning Assistant turns a natural-language question into the most relevant approved teaching excerpt. 

 A supported browser agent can discover and invoke learnlogos.search_training.v1 . The result includes: 

 
 The relevant lesson title and summary 
 Exact source timestamps 
 An SBL-style citation 
 An explanation of why it matched 
 Controlled video playback with captions 
 

 The visible demonstration provides eight alternative questions across two topics. Different ways of asking about program scaling find “Set Exact Program Scaling,” while reading-plan questions find “Jump to Your
 Next Reading.” 

 This demonstrates how people and agents can find the same authoritative instruction without knowing its essentially compression reti Bots exact title or location. 

 ## How we built it 

 The application uses TypeScript, Next.js, React, and Zod. The page registers a structured tool through document.modelContext.registerTool , while both the human interface and browser agent use the same
 validated search service. 

 The contest deployment is separate from the production LearnLogos website. It uses: 

 
 A hard server-side content allowlist 
 Two exact, rights-approved demonstration excerpts 
 Synthetic session state with no customer information 
 Dedicated Upstash Redis rate limiting 
 Short-lived, session-bound media grants 
 Exact media and caption digest verification 
 Same-origin restrictions and a strict content security policy 
 Automated tests covering tool registration, retrieval, authorization, media access, and browser behavior 
 

 ## Challenges 

 The largest challenge was combining a useful demonstration with strict security and intellectual-property boundaries. We needed to show real question-to-video retrieval without exposing production Nz content,
 customer data, full transcripts, or unrestricted media URLs. 

 Natural-language ranking also required care. Common words such as “the” initially created ties between unrelated lessons. We corrected this by excluding conversational filler words from ranking and added
 regression tests for every demonstration question. 

 ## What we learned 

 WebMCP works best as an interface over reusable application services—not as a separate business-logic layer. Structured tools give agents reliable inputs, validated outputs, and clear authorization boundaries
 while preserving an accessible experience for people. 

 We also learned that retrieval quality depends on preserving provenance. A useful answer should remain traceable to the exact lesson, source recording, timestamp range, and access decision. 

 ## What's next 

 The contest entry is a secure vertical slice of a larger LearnLogos vision. Future work includes searching customer-owned training first, coherent transcript segmentation, hybrid semantic retrieval,
 personalized learning paths, progress-aware recommendations, and secure previews of additional approved lessons. 

 LearnLogos is an independent training provider. It is not owned, operated, sponsored, or endorsed by Logos.

 Inspiration 

 Inspiration 

 My brother was killed, leaving his children orphaned. That loss became part of the foundation of my mission. I am building Gadaa Eco Builder to create a more secure future for them and for other vulnerable children in Ethiopia. 

 The Oromo Gadaa system is inscribed by UNESCO on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. It is a living indigenous governance system associated with justice, conflict resolution, social cohesion, protection of women's rights, and knowledge transmission across generations. 

 At the same time, communities in Oromia face land degradation, environmental pressure and climate-related risks. I saw an opportunity to connect cultural knowledge with practical environmental action. 

 I have already cleared approximately 1.5 km of roadside by hand and planted more than 1,500 native trees in the Amerti-Nashe valley. This physical work is the foundation behind the digital idea. 

 Gadaa Eco Builder connects these two challenges: using gamification to make Gadaa knowledge accessible to younger generations while creating pathways toward real-world restoration. 

 How I Built This 

 I built Gadaa Eco Builder as a Telegram-based game where players learn about Gadaa, respond to environmental challenges, plant virtual trees and progress through Gadaa stages. 

 For this hackathon, I used WebMCP to build an AI-powered assistant that: 

 
 retrieves information from the Gadaa Eco Builder waiting-list website; 
 helps users explore their Gadaa stage based on age; 
 answers questions about Gadaa and tree planting; and 
 connects users with information about restoration activities in the Amerti-Nashe valley. 
 

 The project has also gained international visibility. My work on Gadaa Eco Builder has been published through UNDRR's PreventionWeb community platform, where the project is presented as an example connecting indigenous knowledge, disaster-risk reduction and ecosystem restoration. 

 What I Learned 

 I learned how WebMCP can allow an AI agent to interact with web-based information rather than simply provide generic answers. For Gadaa Eco Builder, this creates a way to make indigenous knowledge more accessible through an interactive digital experience. 

 I also learned that technology is most meaningful when it remains connected to the physical reality it is trying to improve. The game is therefore not an end in itself; it is a tool for connecting cultural learning, participation and restoration.

 The project connects three things that are often treated separately:

My goal is to make participation in restoration understandable and accessible to young people and diaspora communities while keeping physical restoration at the centre.

connects users with information about restoration activities in the Amerti-Nashe valley.

Instead of simply answering questions, it should help users explore the Gadaa system, understand their connection to different Gadaa stages, learn about environmental stewardship, and discover how their digital participation connects with restoration work.

 What it does 

 Waveframe is a browser-based audio studio for product videos. Import a video, create narration and background music, arrange the timeline, adjust the mix, and export the finished result—all locally in the browser. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Audio editing is iterative: people make creative decisions while agents can handle repetitive production tasks. WebMCP lets an agent inspect the active project, transcribe audio, generate voiceover and music, edit timeline clips, adjust the mix, and export—without relying on fragile screen automation. 

 People stay in control of the visual timeline and creative direction, while the agent can quickly carry out structured actions. Both use the same project and see the same changes immediately, making it much easier to turn a raw product video into a polished deliverable. 

 How we built it 

 Waveframe uses React, TypeScript, IndexedDB, Web Audio, and browser-native media export. Speech transcription, text-to-speech, and music generation run in Web Workers to keep the app responsive and media stays local to the browser. 

 WebMCP is implemented with document.modelContext.registerTool . The app exposes 13 typed tools, and both the UI and the agent use one shared command bus. This keeps agent actions consistent, validated, and visible in the studio.

title: WIDGENTIC
pitch: Widgets for agents. Your agent drafts into the designer you are looking at over WebMCP, you save, and ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot render it inline over MCP.
about_excerpt: Widgets for agents. Your agent drafts into the designer you are looking at over WebMCP, you save, and ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot render it inline over MCP. Like Comment Story Updates The loop Agent creates widgets using WebMCP tools Keys & Connect Agent uses the widgets Widgentic, widgets for agents - https://widgentic.dev/ Co-author with a browser agent - https://docs.widgentic.dev/develop/co-author-with-an-agent Widgets for agents, designed with one Inspiration widgentic started from a simple observation: agents are good at fetching data and bad at showing it. Every MCP tool result was a wall of JSON or a paragraph of prose. So we built widgets for agents : a payload contract { kind, data, hints?, meta? } , a built-in catalog (card, table and tree), a template DSL that is data rather than code, and an MCP server that renders any of it inline in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, VS Code Copilot Chat and ChatGPT. Then we noticed the two authors never met. An agent could read the authoring guide and draft a perfect widget definition, but it had no way to put it anywhere. A person had to copy the JSON, paste it into the designer, fix it, and save. We had made that separation a rule on purpose: there is no agent write path . API keys travel into prompt-injectable hosts, so they only read. People save. WebMCP lets us keep the rule and close the gap. A page registers tools; the agent in the person's own browser calls them, under the person's session, while the person watches. The designer the person is looking at becomes the agent's tool. The agent drafts, the person saves (or tells the agent to), and every agent with a key renders the result. What we built The product, before the challenge Three open-source npm packages under @widgentic : core (contract, adapters, mapper, catalog, theming, template DSL, actions, in-place reactive rendering), designer (embeddable widget, theme, schema and action designers, also as custom elements), mcp (the tool-output convention, server assembly, per-principal store, secrets). Zero runtime dependencies; MIT. Docs at docs.widgentic.dev , source at github.com/widgentic/widgentic . An MCP server with eight tools ( list_widgets , list_schemas , list_actions , list_themes , list_theme_tokens , get_authoring_guide , render_widget , execute_action ) whose widgets mount inline through MCP Apps and update in place as data changes. The host matrix records what each host does. widgentic.dev : sign in, design widgets, themes, shared data schemas, actions and secrets, mint read-only API keys, and see every save on the next tool call. Actions are declared as data: prompt proposes a message, http runs server-side behind an SSRF guard with secrets injected by name and never shown again. A self-host example : one container image, the authoring app plus the MCP endpoint over a single SQLite file. For the challenge @widgentic/webmcp (beta, published with provenance): the mounted designers as fourteen WebMCP tools. Read the draft, check a definition without touching it, load a definition, set example data, set the preview theme, load or merge a theme entry, load a schema or an action, read the authoring guide, list the theme tokens. One call after mounting; a reported no-op in a browser without a model context. Read tools carry readOnlyHint . No tool saves anything. After the first live round the tools gained the full authoring guide and a dry-run check, so an agent drafting through them follows the same rules as one reading the MCP guide. Co-author with a browser agent documents it. The loop on real hosts. demo.widgentic.dev is the unmodified self-host image running as a single Azure Container App, with /mcp forwarded so one origin serves both surfaces. widgentic.dev adopted the same package the same day. A Chrome origin-trial token on both origins, so a plain Chrome or Edge exposes the tools without a flag. ChatGPT Desktop's browser lists all fourteen under "Available site tools", and ChatGPT renders the saved widgets on web, mobile and desktop. How we built it Spec-first, with OpenSpec: every capability has requirements and scenarios, every scenario has a test that asserts rendered content rather than CSS class names, and each change is archived with its design decisions. The repository enforces its own rules in the test gate: dependency direction between packages, browser-safety of the browser packages, a snapshot of every public export so surface changes are reviewed diffs. Releases are Changesets with npm provenance. Our own hosts live in a private repository that consumes the published packages the way anyone else would. We built it with an AI coding agent as a pair, which is fitting for a project about agents and people co-authoring. The commits carry that attribution. Three decisions shaped the whole project, and the WebMCP layer inherited them: Templates are data, not code. No expressions; data selects and the author supplies every literal. That is what makes a template safe to store from an untrusted author and safe for an agent to draft. Refuse at the door, never lose a save. Invalid entries are rejected on write with a structured code and re-validated on read. The WebMCP tools relay the designer's own errors so the agent can fix its draft. The person saves. Keys read; sessions write. For WebMCP that meant getters resolved on every call (hosts remount designers on tab switches), results that are structured and never thrown, and no save tool at all. A host agent that can operate the page may still click Save when the person asks it to; our tools never do, and the draft is on screen first. What we learned MCP is becoming a UI protocol, not only a tool protocol. When we started, inline rendering was an experiment in one host. Within months the MCP Apps standard was shared by claude.ai, Claude Desktop, VS Code Copilot Chat and ChatGPT, and the vendor-specific way kept working only as an alias. Building on the open shape and treating each host's extensions as optional was the right bet. Same protocol, different manners. Hosts agree on the wire and disagree on everything around it: what they advertise, when they confirm, how they cache, how they treat a proposed message. A host matrix of verified behaviour became a product artifact in its own right, and "never guess a host, probe it" became a rule. Templates as data are what make agents welcome. No expressions means an untrusted author cannot execute anything, a validator can say exactly what is wrong, and an agent can draft a definition from the same rules a person edits by. Every guide and tool description is derived from the validators' own constants, so what the agent is told is what the code enforces. Trust has to be architectural. Agents read, people write. Keys that travel into prompt-injectable places must not be able to author; secrets are referenced by name and injected at execution. The boundary held under WebMCP without a new rule: the agent's tools act on the person's live session and never save; a host agent that can operate the page may click Save when the person asks, with the draft visible first. The browser is becoming an agent host, and the page is the interface. WebMCP turns the UI a person already uses into the agent's tool surface, so both see the same preview and the same diagnostics, and the copy-paste gap disappears. The standard is still moving — surfaces, argument shapes and permission models differ between browsers — so the layer has to feature-detect, stay thin, and put the collaboration boundary into the words the agent reads. Spec-first is what makes pair-building with an AI fast and safe. Requirements and scenarios written before code gave the agent a contract, gave us a review surface, and left a record of every decision. The challenge work landed in about two days because the shape of the system was already written down. Challenges Cold starts. Scale-from-zero on Container Apps measured 33 seconds end to end, long enough for MCP hosts to give up. One always-on replica and a readiness probe fixed it. Live data never migrates itself. A persisted-shape change once crash-looped a deploy against existing documents. Every shape change now ships with a normalization seam and an old-shape regression test before it deploys. Guarding server-side actions. Node's BlockList checks IPv4 addresses against mapped-IPv6 rules, so a naive rule blocked every IPv4; embedded addresses are re-checked instead. Redirects are refused, bodies are capped, and the frame never touches the network. First publish of a new package. Trusted publishing binds to an existing package, so @widgentic/webmcp needed a one-time bootstrap token, minted and deleted the same night. The designer's public surface. Its handle drops sample data on load, so the example-data tool writes the persisted dataExample instead, which turned out to be the better target. Diagnostics reach a host only through a subscription, so the package subscribes once per handle and marks the first read as de

title: DOM-Surgeon
pitch: Your a11y CI is green and your checkout is still broken. DOM-Surgeon audits the live page where the bug actually is — then proves the fix in your DOM before you write it.
about_excerpt: Your a11y CI is green and your checkout is still broken. DOM-Surgeon audits the live page where the bug actually is — then proves the fix in your DOM before you write it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Your accessibility CI is green. Your checkout is still broken. Not because the rules are wrong — because of where they ran . Lighthouse and axe-in-CI load a cold, unauthenticated page and score the first paint. The defects that reach real users live somewhere else entirely: in step 3 of a logged-in flow, inside a modal that only exists after two clicks, in a computed colour that only resolves after the CSS cascade, in an accessible name that JavaScript removed during hydration. You cannot audit that from outside the tab. There is no server that can see it, no scraper that can compute it, and no static analyser that runs the JavaScript which caused it. DOM-Surgeon audits the page where the bug actually is — inside your running session, in the state you are currently looking at. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Everything being measured exists only in the live document: getComputedStyle after the cascade, the ARIA name after hydration, the real tab sequence, exceptions thrown in this session. WebMCP is what lets an agent execute inside that document instead of guessing at it from a screenshot or a DOM dump. So the developer keeps their session — logged in, three clicks deep, mid-flow — and the agent inspects it in place. No fixture, no re-login, no reproduction script, no "works on my machine". What people and agents can do together that was impossible before You can prove a fix before you write it. Every scanner tells you #pay measures 2.38:1 and stops. Ask DOM-Surgeon's agent to fix it and apply_fix walks the colour until it clears 4.5:1 in your live DOM , re-audits to confirm the finding cleared, and hands back the equivalent source change. You watch the defect go green in the browser, then take the diff to the codebase — instead of editing CSS, rebuilding, reloading, and re-checking on a hunch. make_page_usable does it for every repairable finding in one pass. Verified against the demo: 6 findings → 0 , then revert_fixes restores the original defective state exactly, so a before/after is one prompt apart. suggest_code_patch emits the source-level change list for the whole set. That loop — human asks in plain language, agent measures runtime state the human cannot see, repairs it in the shared surface, and returns a committable diff — is the collaboration WebMCP makes possible. It is not a report. It is a fix you can watch working. How it creates a better developer experience Accessibility triage today means opening DevTools, hunting an element, reading a rule ID, and translating it into a source edit yourself. Here you ask: "Why can't a keyboard user finish this?" → the agent chains get_focus_order , reproduce_interaction and get_console_log , and reports that a positive tabindex pulls the card field to tab position 1 and the submit handler throws. "What's wrong with this modal?" → scoped audit of the state on screen, not the homepage. "Fix it and show me the patch." → live repair plus the diff. Findings carry the measured ratio, the WCAG criterion, a unique CSS selector and the concrete fix — and highlight overlays bloom over the offending elements so you and the agent are pointing at the same button. Closing the loop for coding agents A terminal agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) has a shell and a filesystem, not a document — so it can never call a WebMCP tool. That was the harder half of the problem, and it is why the audit engine is UI-free and also ships as a CLI: npx dom-surgeon audit http://localhost:5173 --json --fail-on critical Playwright loads your page, injects the engine, audits the real hydrated DOM, and exits non-zero. The agent writes UI, gets told which selectors fail and why, edits the source, and re-runs until it exits 0. This is the post-generation quality gate for generated UI — the thing that stops an agent shipping three unlabelled inputs and a 2.38:1 button. --baseline reports only new findings, so you can adopt it on a large existing app without a wall of pre-existing failures, and multi-route sweeps catch the "we only ever checked the homepage" gap. Same command works as a pre-commit hook or a CI step. One engine, three surfaces: WebMCP tools for interactive triage in the browser, a CLI for the coding agent and CI, a bookmarklet for any page you can open. How we implemented WebMCP 15 tools on document.modelContext.registerTool , each execute returning a plain string capped to the documented 1.5K output budget, with readOnlyHint on inspectors and untrustedContentHint on everything that reads live page text — a tool whose whole job is reading the DOM is a prompt-injection surface, and the spec's security guidance says to mark it as one. Inspect: audit_page , get_a11y_tree , find_contrast_failures , find_missing_labels , get_focus_order , describe_element , get_console_log , reproduce_interaction , highlight_elements . Repair: apply_fix , make_page_usable , revert_fixes , suggest_code_patch . Adapt: describe_barriers , set_reading_preferences . All native browser API underneath — getComputedStyle for post-cascade colour, ARIA reflection plus label-association walking for accessible names, real tabbability resolution (correctly excluding tabindex="-1" , disabled and hidden inputs), the WCAG relative-luminance formula including the large-text 3:1 threshold, and a console.error / onerror patch installed at load. Zero backend, no runtime dependencies, one static bundle. Every capability is also reachable by button, so the app is useful with no agent attached. Where this goes next The same repair engine points at a second audience: the person a broken page is failing, who cannot fix the site and cannot wait for its next sprint. describe_barriers and set_reading_preferences exist for exactly that, and work today on any page the engine can be injected into. We are not overclaiming it — reaching that user at scale needs a browser extension so the engine loads without them installing a bookmarklet first, and that is the honest next milestone rather than something we are shipping here. Honest limitations Automated rules catch a real but partial slice of accessibility. Reading order, whether alt text is meaningful , and whether a flow makes sense still need a person — make_page_usable deliberately refuses to touch those and reports them for a human instead of silently papering over them. We also pointed it at ourselves, and it found 11 defects in its own interface — including the primary "Make this page usable" button sitting at 3.77:1, which is an embarrassing thing for an accessibility tool to ship. All 11 are fixed; the self-audit now scores 0 while the demo's 6 seeded barriers remain intact, and npm run verify reproduces both numbers. And a note on engineering method: verifying the repair cycle by running it rather than trusting a clean TypeScript build surfaced a real bug we would otherwise have shipped. cssPath was emitting #id without checking uniqueness, so a duplicated id — precisely the defect one of our own rules reports — produced a selector that resolved to the wrong element. Repairs were being applied to the wrong twin and revert could never find them again. Fixed, and the round-trip is now verified to restore identical state. Built With aria css node.js playwright typescript vercel vite wcag webmcp Try it out dom-surgeon.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Private user Like Share this project: Updates Devpost About Careers Contact Help

title: minesweeper
pitch: Minesweeper meets WebMCP: AI can learn the rules, analyze the board, play, and explain every move—turning a classic game into an interactive logic tutor for children.
about_excerpt:
Minesweeper meets WebMCP: AI can learn the rules, analyze the board, play, and explain every move—turning a classic game into an interactive logic tutor for children.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Game Over 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Initial Page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Game Over 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Initial Page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Game Over 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most websites are designed only for humans. People read instructions, click buttons, and learn how an interface works, while an AI usually has to rely on screenshots or simulated mouse movements. 

 I wanted to explore a different idea: what if a website could explain its capabilities directly to an AI and give it structured tools for interacting with the experience? 

 Minesweeper was a natural choice. The rules are approachable, but playing well requires observation, deduction, risk assessment, and patience. These qualities also make it a useful educational game for children who are developing logical and mathematical thinking. 

 The project began as a demonstration of WebMCP, but it also became an experiment in creating websites where AI can act as a guide, collaborator, and tutor. 

 What it does 

 Minesweeper — WebMCP Edition is a browser-based Minesweeper game that can be played by both humans and AI agents. 

 Human players can interact with the board using a mouse or keyboard. They can select beginner, intermediate, expert, or custom difficulty levels, reveal cells, place flags, chord numbered cells, and track their progress and best completion times. 

 The page also exposes nine client-side WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_game_rules teaches the agent the rules and coordinate system. 
 get_play_strategy explains deductions, safe chording, and risk management. 
 analyze_board recommends a deduction-backed move or a clearly identified low-risk guess. 
 start_new_game creates a preset or custom game. 
 reveal_cell reveals a hidden cell. 
 toggle_flag adds or removes a flag. 
 chord_cell reveals eligible cells around a number. 
 get_board_state returns the complete public board state. 
 get_game_status returns a compact game summary. 
 

 The AI does not receive the locations of hidden mines. It must reason from the same public information available to a human player. 

 A built-in AI assistant can analyze the board, suggest moves, perform actions, and explain its reasoning step by step using Chrome’s Prompt API. An action log records whether each move came from a human or an agent, making the interaction transparent and easy to follow. 

 How we built it 

 The project was built with React 19 , TypeScript 6 , and Vite 8 . It is deployed as a static application through GitHub Pages. 

 The game logic and interface share the same application state. This means that actions performed through WebMCP immediately update the visible board, counters, progress indicators, timer, and action log. 

 Each WebMCP tool has: 

 
 A clear and specific name 
 A description explaining when it should be used 
 A structured JSON input schema 
 Runtime validation for coordinates and game rules 
 A result containing the updated public game state 
 

 Read-only tools allow agents to learn the rules, inspect the board, and request an analysis without modifying the game. Action tools call the same underlying logic used by the visual interface. 

 The analyze_board tool first looks for moves supported by Minesweeper deductions. When no guaranteed move is available, it returns a low-risk probabilistic option and clearly labels it as a guess. It never reads hidden mine locations or changes the board itself. 

 The built-in assistant uses Chrome’s Prompt API to provide natural-language help directly inside the game. Personal-best times are stored locally in the browser, while every action is recorded with human or agent attribution. 

 The project also uses Vitest to test important game behavior and is publicly available in the GitHub repository . 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was translating a visual game board into structured information that an LLM could understand reliably. 

 The coordinate system, board dimensions, game status, and every possible cell state had to be represented clearly. The agent needs to distinguish between hidden, flagged, empty, numbered, and revealed-mine cells without having access to secret information. 

 Tool descriptions were another important challenge. It was not enough to explain what a tool does—the descriptions also needed to help the model understand when to use it and what risks were involved. This was especially important for chording, which can reveal several cells at once but can also cause a loss when flags are incorrect. 

 Keeping the human interface and agent tools synchronized also required careful design. A move can affect the board, remaining-mine counter, progress percentage, timer, game status, personal-best time, and action log. 

 Finally, WebMCP and browser-native AI APIs are still emerging technologies. The project needed feature detection and graceful behavior when WebMCP or the Prompt API was unavailable. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am proud that the project supports three ways of interacting with the same game: 

 
 Mouse controls 
 Keyboard controls 
 AI interaction through WebMCP 
 

 The AI does not depend on screenshots, image recognition, or fragile coordinate-based clicking. It discovers structured tools exposed by the page and uses them to understand and control the game. 

 I am also proud that the agent plays fairly. It can access the public state of the board, but it cannot inspect hidden mine positions. Its recommendations must come from logical deductions or explicitly identified probabilistic guesses. 

 The action log makes AI activity visible by recording whether each move was made by a person or an agent. This turns the AI’s behavior into something users can observe, understand, and learn from. 

 Most importantly, the project demonstrates an educational use for WebMCP. The AI is not only automating a game—it can explain strategies, demonstrate logical reasoning, and collaborate with a learner inside the application. 

 What we learned 

 I learned that building a website for AI requires thinking about user experience in a new way. 

 For human users, an interface communicates through layout, color, labels, and visual feedback. For an AI agent, the website also needs structured tools with precise descriptions, schemas, validation, and useful results. 

 I also learned that tool design directly affects agent behavior. Small, focused tools make actions easier to understand and reduce ambiguity. Separating rules, strategy, analysis, state inspection, and game actions helps the model create a clearer plan. 

 Another important lesson was that read-only and state-changing operations should be clearly separated. An AI should be able to inspect and reason about an application without accidentally modifying it. 

 Finally, the project showed that WebMCP can make a webpage more than a visual destination. A website can describe what it knows and what it can do, allowing AI to participate meaningfully in the experience. 

 What's next for Minesweeper — WebMCP Edition

title: Outcome Network
pitch: WebMCP turns business websites into capabilities agents can safely compose. Outcome Network coordinates providers, checks constraints, requires human approval, and uses reversible holds.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns business websites into capabilities agents can safely compose. Outcome Network coordinates providers, checks constraints, requires human approval, and uses reversible holds. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most web agents still interact with websites indirectly: read the page, inspect controls, then infer what action to take. WebMCP provides a cleaner model. A site can expose structured capabilities while still owning its UI, state, permissions, and business rules. Outcome Network explores what that looks like for a real multi-provider business workflow. What it does The demo coordinates opening a 15-person Toronto office with two constraints: CAD 12,000 maximum budget Everything ready by Friday Three providers supply furniture, networking, and facilities services. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can search offerings, check inventory and availability, and create temporary resource holds after the user approves the plan. Those holds are reversible. ChatGPT can release them and restore provider availability without changing the approved plan. Every action is recorded in a visible audit trail with the capability, provider, result, and whether it came from WebMCP or the human workspace. How we built it The app uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vercel, and the native document.modelContext WebMCP API. The production workflow exposes six tools, including: search_products check_inventory check_service_availability reserve_outcome_resources release_outcome_reservations WebMCP calls use the same domain logic and state as the UI rather than separate mock handlers. The production path uses same-origin WebMCP for reliability. I also built an experimental cross-origin implementation using allow="tools" , explicit exposedTo origins, and getTools({ fromOrigins }) . Challenges we ran into The main challenge was working with an emerging browser API. WebMCP support behaved differently across local Chrome, public HTTPS, and ChatGPT's in-app browser. Rather than hiding those differences behind a polyfill, I added runtime diagnostics and kept the reliable production path separate from the experimental cross-origin path. The other challenge was authority and failure handling. Approval is tied to the current plan, so changing the plan invalidates stale approval. Multi-provider reservation failures also trigger compensating releases so partial holds are not left behind. Accomplishments that we're proud of The WebMCP integration is part of the application rather than a demo wrapper. In the deployed app, ChatGPT can: invoke real provider capabilities mutate the same state shown in the UI create six temporary holds across three providers release those holds and restore availability leave a visible WebMCP audit trail The project also supports deterministic supplier failure, replanning, and rollback after partial reservation failure. What we learned Tool discovery is only the beginning. Once agents can change application state, the harder questions are around authority, stale approvals, partial failure, reversibility, and auditability. That led to explicit approval boundaries, typed schemas, shared state, reversible operations, and compensating rollback. What's next for Outcome Network The next step is connecting the same model to real independent WebMCP-enabled businesses across different origins. The goal is not to build another marketplace. Businesses should be able to keep their own applications and rules, expose the capabilities they choose, and let agents coordinate those capabilities into useful outcomes. title: StillHere
pitch: Human-approved continuity for work that can't stop.
about_excerpt: Human-approved continuity for work that can't stop. Like Comment Story Updates Problem Businesses rarely lose every file at once. More often, they lose the context, agreement, and authority required to continue safely. A website may still be online while its phone number, minimum order, export availability, or certification wording is stale. Giving an agent better access to that page improves actuation, but it does not establish which claims are still fit to publish or use. StillHere's thesis is: an agent-ready version of stale information is still stale information. Solution StillHere is a human-agent business continuity layer built around five visible stages: Recover → Reconcile → Approve → Publish → Transact . The challenge demo follows a fictional Ugandan coffee supplier. A bounded assessment separates website condition from business condition. Four recovered records then disagree about a trade phone, Instant Coffee minimum order, Japan availability, and an unsupported legacy certification claim. The Continuity Ledger keeps those sources separate instead of collapsing them into an unqualified profile. Why WebMCP This workflow needs structured, contextual browser-agent collaboration rather than scraping or hidden click automation. WebMCP gives the current page a small, typed capability surface. On the Ledger route, an agent can inspect bounded conflict counts and stage source-backed proposals. On the Passport route, it can read the exact published version, search current offerings without losing destination qualifications, and prepare the same visible inquiry form the human sees. The browser agent never receives an accept or publish tool. Source text cannot alter tool definitions. The human uses visible controls to accept, edit, reject, exclude, or keep a claim unresolved. Only accepted facts enter the Draft Passport, and only the human can publish a new version. What people and agents can do together The agent does the high-friction organizational work: it identifies fields needing review, cites recovered sources, stages bounded proposals, searches accepted offerings, and prepares a buyer draft. The human supplies authority: deciding the current phone, editing an MOQ from 2,500 to 3,000, preserving Japan as Available by inquiry , excluding an unsupported certification claim, publishing Passport v2, editing the buyer draft, and approving the exact final state. That combination was difficult before because an agent could operate an old webpage without knowing whether its contents were current, rejected, unresolved, or authorized. StillHere inserts a visible currentness and approval layer before agent-facing action. WebMCP implementation StillHere exposes six direct, route-scoped tools with literal document.modelContext.registerTool(...) calls. /recover registers inspect_business_truth and stage_claim_resolutions . The published Passport registers get_business_passport , search_current_offerings , and prepare_business_inquiry . submit_approved_inquiry is registered dynamically only when the visible valid draft, idempotency key, Passport version, and explicit human approval have the same fingerprint. Each registration is tied to an AbortController and disappears on route or authority changes. JSON Schema helps selection, while strict runtime parsers independently reject extra keys, invented values, unknown or mismatched sources, invalid qualifications, and stale approval. Editing one approved field removes the submit capability; even a retained executor cannot keep authority. Execution, resilience, and safety The public Next.js application is deployed on Vercel, needs no login, and uses a deterministic fictional scenario. IndexedDB retains Ledger, Passport versions, drafts, and receipts on the device. A service worker makes a best-effort cache of the Ledger and Passport after an online visit; cached documents and previously fetched assets may allow degraded-network use, but precaching can be partial. Simplified view persistently removes selected decoration and motion. It does not reduce network requests, and transfer values are cumulative visit-specific browser observations rather than measured savings. Recovered text is evidence, never an instruction or tool definition. Unsupported certification remains out. No agent can auto-publish. Preparation never implies submission. The receipt is fictional and process-local: no email, order, payment, webhook, or external message is sent. StillHere demonstrates a careful human-agent authority pattern, not identity verification, KYC, a signed credential, or a production delivery system. Challenges I ran into The hardest engineering problem was making authority temporary and visible. A normal tool server can stay available after the page state that justified it has changed. StillHere instead ties every registration to the active route and current browser-local state. The final submit capability must disappear when the draft, approval fingerprint, idempotency key, or Passport version changes. That required narrow schemas, independent runtime validation, pure domain rules, and careful cleanup with AbortController. Another challenge was resilience without overstating it. IndexedDB and a service worker can help after a successful online visit, but they do not make the application universally offline or reduce transfer by themselves. The UI and documentation therefore describe best-effort cached access and keep visit-specific transfer readings separate from claimed savings. Accomplishments that I am proud of Six direct, route-scoped WebMCP tools operating on the same state visible to the human. Human-only acceptance, editing, exclusion, and Passport publication. A dynamically registered consequential action that exists only for the exact approved draft. A complete no-login public demonstration with fictional data, local persistence, responsive layouts, and 86 deterministic tests across 14 files. Clear product boundaries: no autonomous publishing, no invented certification, no real message or transaction, and no claim that this demo is an identity or KYC system. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it does more than replace clicks. Its strongest role here is creating a shared contract between what a person sees and what an agent may do. JSON Schema improves tool selection, but it is not an authorization boundary; callbacks still need strict parsing, source checks, liveness checks, and revocation when visible state changes. I also learned that provenance and uncertainty have to remain first-class product objects rather than being compressed into a confident summary. What's next A production version would add authenticated organizations, encrypted shared storage, multi-user review roles, stronger provenance and source-signing options, hosted audit history, and opt-in delivery integrations. Those additions would preserve the same rule demonstrated here: currentness and human authority come before agent actuation. How to test No account is required. All business, buyer, and receipt data are fictional. Use ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled. Open https://stillhere-azure.vercel.app and select Try Demo . Run the prefilled assessment and select Review recovered evidence . On the Ledger, ask: “Inspect this business's recovered evidence and tell me what needs review.” Expect inspect_business_truth . Ask: “Propose source-backed resolutions for these conflicts, but do not accept or publish anything.” Expect stage_claim_resolutions and four visible proposals. As the human: accept phone, edit MOQ 2,500→3,000, accept Available by inquiry , and accept certification exclusion. Select Publish Business Passport . Ask: “Read the published Business Passport and find current private-label offerings for Japan.” Expect Passport read/search; Instant Coffee remains AVAILABLE_BY_INQUIRY . Ask: “Prepare an inquiry for 5,000 units of Instant Coffee for Japan, requesting samples, private-label packaging and Japanese labelling support.” The visible draft changes; nothing submits. Enter fictional buyer values, edit quantity to 6,000, and approve. Confirm submit_approved_inquiry appears. Edit any field to see it disappear; then review and reapprove. Submit through the agent. The SH-... result is a fictional demo receipt only. Reset is in the footer and requires Reset demo → Confirm reset . title: Askew
pitch: Point at what looks wrong. Say four words. Get a measured answer, and a safe fix.
about_excerpt: Point at what looks wrong. Say four words. Get a measured answer, and a safe fix. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Measured findings: spacing, radius, and contrast, with evidence Apply confirmation: the human's click is the only write boundary Real write, real HMR reconnect: settled measurements confirm the fix Hover pinned without the pointer: a state a screenshot can't show Inspiration Every frontend session with a coding agent hits the same wall. The agent writes a page, I open it, and something is off — but I can only say "this looks cheap." So I screenshot it, paste it into a chat, and the agent guesses. It cannot see that the padding is 13px while thirty-one other surfaces use 20px . It cannot measure a 3.1:1 contrast ratio from a JPEG. It has never seen the hover state, because a screenshot cannot hold one. The browser knows all of this. It just had no way to say it. What it does Askew is a development-only Vite plugin that turns a running React app into a shared debugging surface for a browser AI agent. Click one element in your live app. Tell the agent something vague — "this looks cheap." The agent reads the real runtime truth through WebMCP: the computed cascade, the design scale the page is actually rendering, the measured contrast ratio, and how many visible instances share that source. It stages three Tailwind alternatives. Hovering A/B/C morphs the real component in place. Nothing has been written. You click Apply. One static class string changes in source, Vite HMR reconnects the selection, and the change is undoable. Two sentences and two clicks. No screenshots, no rebuilds. How WebMCP makes it possible Every Askew tool had to pass one test: it must return state that exists only in this browser tab, right now, and is unavailable from any repo, API, screenshot, or MCP server. Four things Askew reads that nothing else can hand an agent: Live DOM selection — what the human pointed at, one second ago Computed cascade — the resolved outcome of every competing declaration, not the source declarations Runtime design scale — spacing, radius, and colour frequencies derived from the rendered page, because tailwind.config is aspirational and the DOM is the truth Held interaction state — :hover and native focus, pinned and measured without a pointer An agent with perfect repo access is useless here. That is the whole argument. The design decision I am most pleased with: file writes are not an agent capability. The four tools inspect, diagnose, and stage. askew_stage_variants returns sourceWritten: false . Only the human's Apply click in Askew's own UI crosses the write boundary. Tool descriptions are the only channel for steering an agent whose system prompt you never see, so they are written as instructions — diagnose before proposing, never invent a finding when Askew reports uncertainty, warn when multiple visible instances share a source. How I built it npm workspaces, strict TypeScript. The plugin is apply: "serve" , so it does not exist in production — production-build.test.ts runs a real vite build and asserts that no instrumentation, endpoint, or capability header survives. Element-to-source identity comes from code-inspector-plugin with its editor server disabled. React 19 removed _debugSource , which quietly broke every click-to-component tool built on fiber inspection, so compile-time attributes were the only reliable route. The write path is contained by construction: the client never sends a filesystem path, only a sourceId resolved against an in-memory index of already-transformed modules, then realpath -canonicalised, root-contained, extension-gated, schema-closed, and applied as a one-for-one token replacement that must still match the full expected class string or fail 409 and write nothing. Challenges Page JavaScript cannot force :hover . That is a DevTools capability. Askew parses direct hover: utilities and applies the equivalent declarations inline, then measures. It resolves literal colour values only — anything else returns an explicit UNSUPPORTED_STATE rather than a confident no-op, because a wrong measurement is worse than a declined one. A false positive is worse than a missing finding. A dominant design value requires at least three samples and no tie. Contrast requires a resolvable opaque background or it reports ambiguity. A healthy element is reported as consistent, not silently skipped. A public write endpoint. The capability token is served to every visitor, so it is not authentication. I accepted that early and made containment carry the security model instead: an unprivileged secret-free process, two allowlisted files, an explicit token allowlist, rate limiting, and automatic baseline restore. What I learned Scope discipline is the whole game. The spec named thirteen things I would not build — multi-select, general CSS attribution, breakpoints, group-hover , AST mutation — and holding that line is why one path works end to end instead of six paths working halfway. What's next Design-token file writing so fixes become the system rather than one-off patches, and broader source-shape support beyond static single-line className literals. AI usage disclosure Built with OpenAI Codex — this hackathon's sponsor — used throughout planning, PRD/spec iteration, implementation, test writing, deployment hardening, and live browser verification. Claude Code independently exercised the running golden path and identified selection/actionability gaps; those findings were reproduced and fixed. Gemini then performed a separate architecture and edge-case review, whose valid color parsing, token validation, selection, and HTTP-status findings were verified against the code and incorporated. I made the product, scope, security, and submission decisions and reviewed the resulting changes; the assistants accelerated implementation and acted as independent code reviewers. Notes for judges The hosted demo at https://askew.xpworx.com is a deliberately writable, disposable, single-user development environment. It restores itself on startup, after three idle minutes, and from the visible Reset Demo button. If two people explore at once, changes will conflict and fail stale rather than merge — press Reset Demo and try again. The video is the authoritative uninterrupted proof.
