video_title: Askew — WebMCP-native live UI debugging
video_transcript_excerpt: Ask you. Point at what looks wrong. Every time an AI-generated interface looks a little bit wrong, the usual fix is screenshot it, paste it into a chat, and hope the agent guesses right. It usually doesn't, because a screenshot can't carry what the browser already knows. This is Ask you, a WebMCP tool running inside a real dashboard. I select the AI confidence card, and Ask you reads its live source, its computed styles, and how many other elements are just like it. Clicking analyze, it measures three real problems. The padding is 13 pixels while the rest of the page uses 20. The corners don't match the surrounding cards. And the supporting text sits under the 4.5 to 1 contrast a screen reader test would require. These are measurements, not guesses. Now the agent stages three token-level fixes through WebMCP. Hovering a direction morphs the real card immediately. No clone, no reload, and nothing written to disk yet. I pin the direction I want and click apply. Only this human click crosses the right boundary. The exact source file updates. Hot module reload reconnects the same element, and the change is undoable with one click. Here's the moment a screenshot can't show at all. I ask Ask you to hold this button's hover state without touching it. It measures the exact style a real hover would trigger live with no pointer anywhere near it. And reset demo returns the whole page to its starting state for the next visitor. The current selection, the computed cascade, the live design scale, a held interaction state. None of that exists in a screenshot or a repository, only in this browser tab right now. That's why this had to be WebMCP.

title: AI ACT SHIELD WEBMCP
pitch: AI Act Shield App masks the personal data in your contract without sending to any LLM. WebMCP tools run in your browser page using deterministic checksums. No sensible datas will leave the page.
about_excerpt: AI Act Shield App masks the personal data in your contract without sending to any LLM. WebMCP tools run in your browser page using deterministic checksums. No sensible datas will leave the page. Like Comment Story Updates The agent was never told which tool to use, and reports only the types it received. Left: what the human sees. Right: what leaves the page. external mask_document_in_page {} — the agent called the tool with no arguments, because the app never gives it the document Inspiration Law firms and accountants across the EU are stuck in a small, expensive trap. Generative AI would genuinely help them review a contract — but the contract is full of client data they are not allowed to paste into a cloud model. Under the AI Act and the GDPR that is not a formality; it is their licence to practise. The usual answer is a cloud "anonymization API", which moves the leak one hop away and calls it a solution. I wanted the masking to happen where the document already is: on the lawyer's own machine, in the browser tab, with nothing to trust but code you can read. What it does AI Act Shield detects personal data — tax codes, national IDs, VAT numbers, IBANs, payment cards, names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, company names — and replaces each with a placeholder, so the masked draft can safely go to any AI. When the answer comes back, it puts the real values back where they belong. Detection is deterministic: regular expressions plus real checksums (ISO 13616 for IBANs, Luhn for payment cards, the Spanish DNI/NIE and CIF control characters, the official Italian VAT algorithm). Never an LLM. A model would answer differently on the same document from one run to the next, and sending a document to a model to ask what to hide from that model defeats the purpose. Coverage is Italian, Spanish and English/international. The WebMCP part The app is built on one constraint: the text never leaves the browser. That constraint turns out to be exactly what makes a WebMCP tool trustworthy, because registerTool().execute() runs client-side, in the visitor's own tab. The page registers four tools. The one that carries the argument is mask_document_in_page , and what matters is what it doesn't take: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "mask_document_in_page", description: "Masks the personal data in the document the user has already loaded into this page, without the caller ever receiving the document.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { customTerms: { /* ... */ } } }, execute: async (input) => maskPageDocument(input), }); No text parameter. The person loads the confidential document into the page; the agent calls the tool passing nothing ; the page reads its own content and returns a masked draft plus the types of what it found. The document never enters the agent's context, so it cannot leak one even if it tried. Asked in plain language to mask a contract — without being told which tool to use — ChatGPT's agentic browser produced this row in the page's own log: 1:48:34 PM external mask_document_in_page {} external means the call came from outside the page rather than from its own buttons. {} means there was nothing to pass. That empty object is the whole project. This is also the case for "people and agents using an app together": the UI and the tools share one page-local state, so the person watching the tab sees the masking happen live and can step in — switch a detected entity off, add a custom term — while the agent works. How I built it Vanilla JavaScript. No framework, no dependencies, no build step — you can clone it and open it. 37 tests on node:test , which is built in, so that promise holds for the test suite too. Served as static files from my own nginx, not a platform: the page is the same folder that nginx serves. The detection engine is a port of the one shipping in iaCiao , my platform for local — edge — AI: 32 iApps across health, security and mobility, all built so the model runs on your device and the data stays there. AI Act Shield is the clearest expression of that idea, which is why I brought it here. An app whose entire value is that the sensitive part never leaves your machine turns out to be the natural shape for a WebMCP tool, because that is exactly where execute() runs. Challenges The ecosystem moved under me during the ten days. ChatGPT Atlas was deprecated days before the deadline. The Model Context Tool Inspector extension reports nothing for my page, because it looks for navigator.modelContext while the specification (26 August 2026) exposes ModelContext on document and never mentions navigator. I left that audit check failing rather than shim an API that does not exist — and left the declarative toolname / tooldescription / toolaction checks failing too, since the spec marks that API "entirely a TODO". ChatGPT's Chrome extension looks like it works and doesn't. Asked to mask the document, it produced a fluent, accurate answer — by reading the DOM, without calling a single tool. That is precisely the difference this project is about, and it would have been very easy to film it as a success. Chrome's origin trial has a quirk. It returns inputSchema as a JSON string and rejects a plain-object argument to executeTool() with "Failed to parse input arguments". Nothing in the spec asks for a pre-serialised input, so the code calls the spec-shaped way first and falls back only when that build refuses. My own buttons sabotaged two takes. The "Agent console" had a button labelled CALL MASK_SENSITIVE_DATA() . Asked to "use the page's tools", the agent clicked it — twice. Not a dim agent: the button had named itself after the API, so it was the closest match to the instruction. Renaming it to "Preview the masking response", and adding a line in llms.txt telling agents to call the tool instead, fixed what a better prompt could not. Cloudflare hid three deploys. Assets are served with a four-hour browser cache, so the page kept running the previous build and no hard refresh changed it. I lost two hours because I was verifying with curl --resolve ...:127.0.0.1 , which goes to the origin and bypasses the edge — always showing me the correct file. What I learned The one that mattered: a tool that takes the sensitive data as a parameter cannot protect it. My first version was mask_sensitive_data(text) . It returns only placeholders, never an original value, and I wrote in my notes that "the agent never saw the tax code". That was false, and I did not notice until, halfway through recording, I asked myself whether pasting the contract into the prompt defeated the point of the app. It did — and so, more quietly, did passing it as a tool argument. Whoever calls that tool must already hold the document. There is a real difference between "the response contains no secrets" and "the caller never receives them" , and only the second is a guarantee. mask_document_in_page exists because of that question. The second lesson: instrument your claims. I added a panel that logs every execute() the page receives and marks whether it came from the page's own buttons or from outside. It exists because you cannot otherwise see WebMCP working — the page looks identical either way. That panel is what caught the Chrome extension reading the DOM, and both takes where the agent clicked a button instead of calling a tool. Without it I would have shipped a video of something that wasn't happening. And a third, smaller one: tests find the bugs you just wrote. Four surfaced in a single session, three of them minutes old — including a legal form matching inside an ordinary word, which rewrote the heading "CONSULTANCY AGREEMENT" as "[COMPANY_NAME_1]REEMENT". Honest limits Detection covers Italian, Spanish and English/international formats. A document in another language will still have its IBANs, cards, emails and international phone numbers found, but not its names, addresses or company forms. No PDF or OCR import in this build. Ambiguous candidates — a capitalised pair that may or may not be a person, an amount that usually belongs in the draft — are proposed switched off , and whatever stays readable after masking is listed rather than hidden. An incomplete mask the user trusts is the real failure mode. restore_sensitive_data only works in the tab that masked the document, because the vault is page memory. That is a privacy property, not a missing feature. The guarantee is that the app never hands the document to the caller . It is not that an agent driving a browser is unable to look at the screen. What's next PDF and OCR import, pattern packs beyond the EU, and a tool that lets an agent request a masked excerpt rather than the whole document. Written with Claude (Claude Code), pair-programming style: the specification research, the port of the engine, the Spanish and English coverage and the test suite came out of that collaboration. title: OpenDeal
pitch: Agent-native negotiation for the open web. AI agents discover, compare and negotiate structured offers via WebMCP while humans retain explicit authority over transactions.
about_excerpt: Agent-native negotiation for the open web. AI agents discover, compare and negotiate structured offers via WebMCP while humans retain explicit authority over transactions. Like Comment Story Updates OpenDeal OpenDeal is agent-native negotiation for the open web. It demonstrates how AI agents can discover suppliers, compare structured offers, negotiate price, verify delivery constraints, and recommend a transaction through WebMCP — while the human retains explicit authority over the irreversible financial action. The mission Buy 100 ANSI Z89.1 Type II safety helmets with four hard constraints: total budget ≤ $2,500 delivery by Friday no substitutions final purchase requires human approval Three supplier contexts expose WebMCP tools for inventory discovery, product specifications, quotes, counteroffers, and delivery checks. The deterministic negotiation produces: Alpha Industrial: $2,350, Friday — compliant Bravo Safety Supply: $2,325, Friday — compliant and selected Charlie Works: $2,290, Monday — cheaper, but rejected because it violates the delivery deadline The agent therefore optimizes for the buyer's actual constraints instead of simply choosing the lowest price. The core WebMCP idea: bounded authority OpenDeal does not treat human approval as a cosmetic modal. Authorization changes the browser's actual executable capability surface. Before approval, the suppliers' search, specification, quote, negotiation, and delivery tools are available — but bravo.create_purchase_order does not exist. When the human approves Bravo's exact $2,325 offer, OpenDeal dynamically registers the purchase capability. After the order executes, that capability is removed and replaced with bravo.get_order_status . A live Chrome/WebMCP run verified the lifecycle directly from document.modelContext : PRE-APPROVAL: 15 tools; purchase capability absent APPROVED: 16 tools; bravo.create_purchase_order present ORDERED: 16 tools; purchase capability absent; bravo.get_order_status present The workflow is: discover → evaluate → negotiate → recommend → human authorize → execute → observe Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without WebMCP, an agent would usually need supplier-specific APIs, DOM scraping, brittle browser automation, or a centralized marketplace integration. With WebMCP, each website intentionally exposes structured actions using explicit schemas. The website controls which capabilities exist, their scope, and their lifecycle. The agent gets reliable machine-usable actions without guessing how to click through a UI. That creates a better user experience: the agent handles repetitive discovery, comparison, negotiation, and constraint checking, while the person keeps control over the action that commits money. What people and agents can do together The human provides the objective and authority boundary. The agent performs the multi-supplier work that would otherwise require repetitive browsing, quote collection, comparison, and follow-up. The human only steps back in when the transaction crosses the approval boundary. The important distinction is that the system does not merely say the agent lacks purchasing authority — the purchase operation is genuinely unavailable until authorization occurs. Implementation OpenDeal is intentionally dependency-light so the WebMCP behavior remains visible and auditable. It uses: modern JavaScript ES modules HTML and CSS browser Web APIs document.modelContext.registerTool() getTools() and executeTool() structured tool input schemas deterministic supplier pricing and delivery policies AbortController -scoped tool lifecycles an explicit transaction state machine a visible execution ledger and WebMCP inspector automated domain and lifecycle tests Each supplier registers five base capabilities. The selected supplier's purchase tool is dynamically registered only after approval, then removed after use and replaced by an order-status capability. The implementation also includes explicit buyer-origin allowlisting support for deployments where supplier contexts live on distinct origins; the challenge deployment is kept same-origin on Netlify for simple, reproducible judging. Why it matters Procurement is only the demonstration domain. The same capability-boundary pattern can apply to travel, logistics, reservations, insurance, professional services, or any workflow where agents need meaningful autonomy without unlimited authority. OpenDeal explores a web where agents do not need to imitate human clicking. Websites become intentional participants in agent-mediated transactions, and humans retain explicit control over the boundaries that matter most. title: Consequence
pitch: An agent can fill out your visa application, but it can't sign your name. High-stakes paperwork with a permission boundary enforced in code, not just the UI.
about_excerpt: An agent can fill out your visa application, but it can't sign your name. High-stakes paperwork with a permission boundary enforced in code, not just the UI. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most WebMCP demos we looked at treat "the agent" as strictly upside: it fills things in faster, it clicks buttons for you. Nobody was building the other half of the story, the part where an agent's authority has to have a hard edge somewhere. High-stakes paperwork is the clearest place to make that argument: a visa or residency application has dozens of fields an agent can genuinely help with (dates, addresses, transcribing from a passport) and a handful it categorically should not be able to touch, because they're attestations. Signing your name is not a transcription task. So we built a fictional application (the invented "Skyward Residency Program," no real agency or form referenced anywhere) specifically to make that boundary concrete and testable, not just asserted in a README. What it does Consequence is a long, branching application where every field carries a permission class: agent_fillable , human_only , or evidence_required . An agent can fill addresses, employment history, and dates directly. If it calls answer_question on an attestation field, it doesn't fail quietly, it gets back a structured error naming the field and telling it to hand back to the human. For evidence_required fields like a bank-balance summary, the agent can only propose_answer , which lands as pending confirmation, never as answered, until the human accepts it. Every field also carries provenance (who set it, when, from where), and the whole mutation history is hash-chained and replayable, so a final review screen can show exactly who filled what. Conditional branches make the same point about tool existence . Answering that the applicant is self-employed reveals a Self-Employment Details section, and only then do fields like business_income_summary become part of what get_section and list_open_questions read from. The tool surface reconfigures itself based on answers already given. How we built it React + TypeScript + Vite on the client, Cloudflare Workers + a Durable Object as the authoritative backend, same architecture as our other entry, Cadence. webmcp-kit for tool definitions, shared across both apps. ~63 fields across 9 sections (7 base, 2 conditional), each declaring a PermissionClass in seed/schema.ts . One reducer ( src/shared/reducer.ts ) enforces the permission class on every mutation path, client UI, Durable Object, and every WebMCP tool call alike, so there's exactly one place the boundary is defined and no path that can skip it. check_consistency does real cross-field validation: an expired passport, overlapping employment dates, an unexplained income gap, checks that are genuinely tedious for a person and genuinely tractable for an agent, run against real answers in src/shared/derive.ts . submit_application is confirmation-gated and independently refuses while anything required is still open, on top of the per-field refusals. Challenges we ran into Making the refusal mean something. It would have been easy to add a client-side check that just hides the "sign" button for agents. That's not a real boundary, it's a UI suggestion. The actual fix was routing every write, human or agent, through the same reducer, so the refusal is enforced at the one place a mutation can happen, not duplicated (and driftable) across the UI and the tool layer. Seed data with nothing to catch. Early on, the seed application started blank, so check_consistency had zero contradictions to ever find, meaning the tool looked broken on every fresh demo even though the logic was correct. Fixed by seeding two fields that genuinely overlap (an employment start date before the prior job's end date), so the tool has real work to do the moment a judge opens the app. Shared-board demo entropy , the same problem we hit on Cadence: because a Durable Object's seed loads exactly once, repeated testing against one shared instance permanently consumed the demo state. Fixed with per-visitor isolated application instances plus a visible in-app reset button. Accomplishments we're proud of A refusal that's actually structural, not cosmetic: answer_question against a human_only field is rejected by the same reducer a human's own edit goes through, verifiable by reading src/shared/reducer.ts directly rather than taking our word for it. A tool surface that changes shape based on the application's own content, not just page navigation, extending the same dynamic-registration idea from Cadence into conditional business logic. A tamper-evident provenance trail (hash-chained mutation history) that answers "who actually filled this field" with cryptographic backing, not just a database column that could silently be edited later. What we learned The interesting design constraint wasn't "what can the agent do," it was "what can the agent be structurally prevented from doing, in a way that can't be bypassed by a differently-worded tool call." A permission check living only inside one tool's execute function is trivially circumvented by any other code path that touches the same state. Putting the enforcement in the shared reducer instead of the tool layer was the difference between a real guarantee and a suggestion. What's next A real evidence-extraction pipeline behind read_evidence (currently a clearly-labeled stub), a dedicated multi-party reviewer invite flow (the data layer already supports scoped reviewer tool grants), and extending the consistency checks beyond the current date/income rules. title: BuildCheck
pitch: Evidence before engineering: a shared product-validation workspace for founders and AI agents.
about_excerpt:
Evidence before engineering: a shared product-validation workspace for founders and AI agents.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Mock-first by default: optional public adapters, explicit consent, and transparent source availability. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Seven native, page-bound WebMCP tools connect an agent to the same human workspace. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Mock-first by default: optional public adapters, explicit consent, and transparent source availability. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Seven native, page-bound WebMCP tools connect an agent to the same human workspace. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Mock-first by default: optional public adapters, explicit consent, and transparent source availability. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI makes software faster to build, but it also makes it easier to build the wrong product faster. A founder can ask an agent to create an entire SaaS before testing whether the problem is painful, frequent, reachable, or worth paying for. BuildCheck adds an evidence-first checkpoint before implementation begins. 

 What it does 

 BuildCheck helps founders decide whether to build, validate, pivot, or stop before investing weeks of engineering time. It scores an idea across demand, pain, willingness to pay, distribution, competitive opportunity, build simplicity, and defensibility. It keeps confidence separate from the Build Score, preserves provenance, and returns one of four explicit outcomes: BUILD, VALIDATE FIRST, PIVOT, or KILL. 

 The human workspace provides guided validation, reports, comparisons, opportunities, methodology, settings, and an Agent activity log. The agent surface exposes seven native WebMCP tools: 

 
 validate_idea 
 roast_idea 
 get_project_analysis 
 generate_validation_mvp 
 estimate_build_cost 
 find_opportunities 
 evaluate_before_build 
 

 An agent can challenge an idea, inspect a saved analysis, estimate the full-build scope, and propose the smallest validation MVP. A write-capable validation call creates a project in the current browser workspace, so the founder can immediately continue in the dashboard. 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit 

 Product validation is not one isolated prompt. It is a sequence of decisions over structured project state: collect an idea, challenge assumptions, inspect evidence, compare the cost of a full build with a smaller test, and decide what happens next. WebMCP lets the agent operate the same product workflows that a human uses without a separate integration server or a duplicated scoring implementation. 

 BuildCheck is deliberately page-bound. The tools inherit the open workspace and current session, register only when the browser exposes the native WebMCP API, and are removed when the workspace unmounts. The human remains responsible for the final product decision; the agent provides structured evidence, warnings, and a smaller next action. 

 A better user experience 

 Without WebMCP, a founder copies an idea between a chat, spreadsheets, search tabs, and a planning tool. Context and provenance disappear along the way. With BuildCheck, the founder can ask in natural language while the agent calls typed product actions. The resulting project, score, evidence, MVP, cost range, and audit event remain visible in the same workspace. 

 The interface also makes uncertainty honest. Generated summaries do not count as market evidence. Public-source failures are visible. If there is not enough evidence, the agent returns INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE instead of manufacturing confidence. 

 How people and agents collaborate 

 People provide product judgment, consent to optional external research, and choose whether to invest. Agents handle the repetitive analytical chain: challenge the idea, retrieve the current analysis, calculate cost ranges, apply the pre-build guard, and propose a measurable validation MVP. Both use the same services and see the same locally persisted workspace state. 

 This makes a useful interaction possible: “Should I build this?” can become a traceable project decision rather than an ungrounded chat answer. 

 How we built it 

 BuildCheck uses Next.js 16, React 19, strict TypeScript, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and Vitest. The WebMCP bridge uses document.modelContext.registerTool with feature detection and an AbortController lifecycle. JSON Schemas are generated from Zod, every handler returns structured output, and annotations distinguish read-only tools from the write-capable validation tool. 

 The human UI, HTTP endpoint, and WebMCP handlers call the same domain services. The score, confidence model, verdicts, cost estimates, and ownership checks therefore have one implementation and one test suite. 

 We started mock-first behind AIProvider and DataSourceProvider contracts so the complete product and UX work deterministically without third-party credentials. We then added an opt-in public evidence aggregator with eight interchangeable adapters. External lookup is explicit per analysis, sends only a few derived keywords, preserves source URLs and provenance, tolerates partial outages, and falls back to clearly labeled demo evidence only when every source fails. Adapter availability depends on the source; RSS requires configured feeds. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest part was not registering seven functions; it was making agent actions obey the same product and safety rules as the interface. We had to keep generated narrative separate from evidence, separate confidence from score, prevent project enumeration, make external research consent explicit, and retain useful behavior when native WebMCP or public providers are unavailable. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Seven native WebMCP tools with strict schemas and structured results 
 Stateful human-agent continuity in the same browser workspace 
 Deterministic, explainable scoring with explicit insufficient-evidence behavior 
 Mock-first provider architecture plus eight opt-in public evidence adapters 
 English default UI with a complete optional French translation 
 PWA support, security headers, rate limits, ownership checks, and minimal safe logs 
 62 automated tests plus lint, strict typecheck, and production build validation 
 

 What we learned 

 The most valuable agent tool is often a guardrail, not a generator. A reliable pre-build tool must be able to say “not enough evidence,” expose why, and recommend a cheaper experiment. WebMCP is especially compelling when it connects natural-language intent to an existing, inspectable product workflow instead of hiding logic in a remote black box. 

 Current scope and what is next 

 This submission is a working demonstration, not a production multi-tenant SaaS. It uses a demo user, browser-local storage, and MockAIProvider. Demo evidence is labeled; optional public research is not a guarantee of market demand. 

 Next we would add real authentication and durable multi-tenant persistence, shared rate limiting, connector observability and caching, evidence deduplication, and controlled A/B evaluation of live sources against deterministic scenarios. Real AI providers remain optional because an LLM should summarize and challenge evidence, never invent proof or choose the final score. 

 Try the human-agent workflow 

 
 Open https://buildcheck-webmcp.vercel.app/agents in a browser with native WebMCP support, such as ChatGPT's in-app browser. No login is required. 
 Confirm that seven site tools are available. 
 Ask: “Should I build an AI CRM for freelancers? Use BuildCheck before writing code.” 
 Inspect the PIVOT result, clearly labeled demo evidence, full-build warning, and smaller proposed test. 
 Ask: “What is the cheapest way to validate it?” 
 Open the dashboard and Agent activity to verify continuity. The human interface also works without WebMCP support.

title: Motificons
pitch: 337,000+ open-source icons where the agent in your browser searches, restyles and curates - while you watch and art-direct.
about_excerpt: 337,000+ open-source icons where the agent in your browser searches, restyles and curates - while you watch and art-direct. Like Comment Story Updates One library, two doors for agents: the MCP server from your editor, and WebMCP tools on the site itself. How to try it today: Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag, or the ChatGPT desktop app's browser. Nothing to install. The icon page. The agent presses these same controls: size, color, stroke, transform. The preview changes in front of you. Search with the agent's rules shown: 893 results, real filters, and the same daily allowance a person gets. Inspiration I ship apps, and every app needs icons. When I ask an AI agent to add icons, it does a bad job. It makes up SVGs. It pastes old code. It mixes icons that don't look like each other. The funny part is that everything the agent needs already exists on icon websites. It just can't use them, because those sites are built for eyes and mouse clicks. Motificons is my icon site. I launched it in mid-August. I was in the middle of making it free and open source when I saw this challenge. WebMCP solves exactly the problem above, so it became the main feature of the release. What it does Motificons has 337,000+ open-source icons from 239 sets. You can search them, restyle them, and export them as SVG, React, Vue, Svelte, SwiftUI, Xcode asset catalogs or PNG. All free. With WebMCP, each page tells the agent in your browser what it can do there. There are 16 tools. On the search page the agent can search and filter. On an icon page it can change the size, color and stroke, read the code, and download it. On your collection it can add and remove icons and style the whole set. On the dashboard it can create collections. The important part: the agent uses the same page you are looking at. When it searches, you see the search box fill. When it restyles an icon, you see the preview change. When it adds an icon to your collection, you see it land in the grid. Nothing happens behind your back, and you can take over at any time. My favorite example is what it can do with one sentence on the dashboard: "Create a collection called New webapp, add user, settings, bell, lock, logout and moon from Tabler, and style everything to a 2px stroke in #748ffc." The agent does all of it while you watch. You only step in when you don't like a pick. There is even a tool made just for that handoff: the agent opens the icon picker, runs a search, and lets you choose. There is also a normal MCP server for coding agents in your editor, and a free Mac app that syncs the same collections. How we built it A small script on each page registers the tools with document.modelContext. Each tool presses the page's real controls instead of calling a private API. The tools are plain functions with unit tests - 456 of them pass. The agent gets exactly what a person gets: same login, same limits, same refusals. The daily search allowance applies to the agent too. If an icon cannot be recolored, the agent is told the same thing the page tells a person. Everything runs on Cloudflare: Workers, R2, D1 and KV. Challenges we ran into Chrome's WebMCP works a little differently than the spec text says, and you only find out by testing. getTools() returns a Promise. executeTool wants a JSON string. The input schema comes back as a string. Chrome does not check required fields, so every tool checks its own input. If part of a request is wrong, nothing is applied. Downloads in the ChatGPT browser kept dying. It turned out we were deleting the in-memory file right after the save click. Fast browsers won that race, slow ones lost it. We keep the file alive for a minute now. Style names are exact in our search engine ("Bold", not "bold"), and agents type lowercase. The tools now check the real names first, and when they cannot check yet, they run the search before applying the filter. Accomplishments that we're proud of The one-sentence flow. Watching a collection build itself on your own screen does not get old. The agent cannot do anything you cannot. No back doors, no hidden calls. This is a live product, not a demo. Open source, MIT. The tool descriptions changed how agents behave. During testing, an agent ended with "the search is left filtered to Tabler arrow icons". Nobody coded that. It read the descriptions and understood a person was watching. What we learned Writing tool descriptions is writing UI copy. The agent behaves the way you describe the room. Agents plan from responses. Every response should say what to do next. One product can serve both worlds: an MCP server for the editor, WebMCP for the browser. What's next for Motificons Zips built on the server, so downloads work in every browser. Tools on more pages. Google sign-in. More sets that restyle fully. Everything stays free and open source. title: Fix This
pitch: Repairs without the runaround.
about_excerpt: Repairs without the runaround. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Rental repairs turn into a runaround: the tenant repeats the problem, the property manager chases safety and access details, and contractor prices, availability, approvals, and confirmation live in separate conversations. Tenants should not need another portal just to get a leak fixed, and an agent should not be allowed to approve its own consequential work. What it does Fix This keeps the tenant in SMS and gives the property manager one shared repair case. A repair agent gathers safety and access facts, follows the building's stored contractor agreements in order, and prepares the next action through typed WebMCP tools. The property manager sees the evidence and explicitly approves one contractor call bound to the contractor, agreed price, and permitted time windows. In the recorded controlled-live run, one allowlisted tenant MMS woke the background agent. The agent triaged the repair and replied in the same thread. WebMCP prepared the stored-agreement path for the manager. After one explicit approval, the contractor heard a fixed AI disclosure and pressed 1 before any audio reached OpenAI. The contractor confirmed a time inside both authorized windows, Fix This booked the visit, and the tenant received the confirmation text. The public judge URL is a separate, resettable synthetic Pennsylvania build. It exposes the same shared-case and WebMCP boundaries without sending a real message or placing a real call. Why WebMCP The public build exposes twelve typed tools over the same workflow API and repair record used by the dashboard. The tools cover case discovery, triage, tenant messaging, preferred-contractor ordering, access evidence, contractor confirmation, and booking. The agent acts on structured state instead of guessing through DOM clicks. The most important tool is the one that does not exist: manager approval is deliberately absent from the WebMCP surface. The server rejects booking until the current proposal has matching manager approval, tenant access authorization, and contractor confirmation. What people and agents do together The tenant reports the repair in a channel they already use. The agent handles repeatable fact gathering and prepares the approved-contractor path. The property manager makes the consequential cost and contact decision. The contractor gives affirmative consent before the AI call and confirms the visit. Fix This then records the booking and notifies the tenant in the original thread. That replaces fragmented coordination with one causally ordered, auditable workflow without handing approval to the agent. How it was built Fix This uses React, Vite, TypeScript, Express, Node.js, an atomically written JSON store, Twilio, OpenAI Responses and Realtime APIs, Vitest, and Render. document.modelContext.registerTool() registers thin browser adapters over the same HTTP operations used by the dashboard. The controlled-live route validates provider signatures and exact allowlists, deduplicates wake events, serializes work per repair case, journals outbound effects for retry safety, and keeps the fixed disclosure plus keypad-consent gate outside the model. No raw call audio is retained. How Codex helped OpenAI Codex helped turn the product idea into decision tickets, challenge unsafe or vague assumptions, implement the shared workflow and controlled-live seams, write and run the tests, diagnose provider failures offline, review the deployment boundary, and assemble privacy-safe evidence. The final controlled-live commit passed 119 tests, the production build, and a production dependency audit with zero reported vulnerabilities. Jacob retained the product decisions and every consequential approval, provider mutation, live message, and call authorization. The recorded real-provider journey was one bounded, allowlisted controlled-live proof—not a pilot, production launch, or reliability claim. The controlled-live deployment is protected and single-operator; judges should use the public synthetic URL. WebMCP browser support is experimental. The public Render service may cold-start after idle. No measured savings, legal certification, general availability, or autonomous approval claim is made. about_excerpt:
A visual sugar and calorie tracker where people and AI agents use WebMCP to log drinks, adjust portions and see every change instantly.

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Sugar is everywhere, but grams on a nutrition label are difficult to visualize. People also drink different sizes, choose diet versions, share bottles, or only finish part of a serving. 

 We built SugarStack to make those everyday choices instantly understandable—and to explore how a human and an AI agent can work with the same health-tracking interface through WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 SugarStack is a visual sugar and calorie tracker that: 

 
 Tracks drinks and foods using flexible amounts and quantities 
 Distinguishes regular, diet and zero-sugar alternatives 
 Supports custom entries using values from the product label 
 Converts sugar into an easy-to-understand cube estimate 
 Displays sugar and calories together 
 Synchronizes the selected date, daily log, headline total and monthly calendar 
 Highlights low, medium and high-sugar days 
 Stores personal entries locally without requiring an account or API key 
 

 The values are presented as typical label estimates rather than medical advice, and users can enter exact information from their own product labels. 

 How we used WebMCP 

 WebMCP is a core part of the product rather than an extra chatbot feature. SugarStack exposes five focused tools: 

 
 sugarstack_get_day 
 sugarstack_search_catalog 
 sugarstack_add_items 
 sugarstack_update_entry 
 sugarstack_remove_entry 
 

 An agent can search the catalogue, add validated items, adjust portions, remove mistakes and summarize the selected day. 

 Most importantly, the agent operates on the same visible state as the person . When an agent changes an entry, the date, log, sugar total, calories and calendar update on screen. Users can immediately inspect, verify or correct every action. 

 For example, someone can ask: 

 
 Log a medium cola and two small lattes. Then change the cola to diet and show me the updated total. 
 

 The agent can complete that workflow using structured WebMCP tools while SugarStack provides a clear visual result. 

 How we built it 

 SugarStack was built with TypeScript, React, Vinext, Vite and Tailwind CSS. Its responsive interface uses reusable components and local browser storage for persistence. 

 The WebMCP layer registers structured tool definitions with narrow input schemas, catalogue identifiers, amount limits and quantity validation. Read-only and state-changing tools are intentionally separated so agents can inspect before acting. 

 The live experience includes preloaded demonstration history so judges can immediately explore the synchronized monthly view without creating weeks of sample data. 

 Challenges we faced 

 The hardest challenge was designing WebMCP tools that were useful without exposing a large, confusing interface. We reduced the contract to five actions that correspond directly to real user tasks. 

 Another challenge was keeping every part of the interface synchronized. Selecting another date or changing an entry needed to update the daily log, hero total, calories, cube estimate and calendar consistently. 

 We also had to balance simplicity with flexible data entry. SugarStack needed to remain approachable for someone who just wants to tap “Cola,” while still supporting different serving sizes, quantities, diet variants and exact label values. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that good agent integration is not about exposing the largest number of tools. It is about creating a small, predictable contract with visible outcomes. 

 WebMCP works especially well when the website remains the source of truth: the agent can act efficiently, while the person maintains context, control and trust. 

 What we are proud of 

 SugarStack combines a polished human interface with a practical agent workflow without requiring an external nutrition API, account or API key. 

 Every important capability can be understood and demonstrated in under two minutes. 

 What is next 

 Future versions could add optional barcode scanning, user-defined goals, additional nutrients, exportable reports and verified regional nutrition catalogues—while preserving the local-first, human-verifiable experience.

title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: AutoWebMCP: Teach an Agent to Fish
pitch: Turn human workflows into agent-ready WebMCP tools. AutoWebMCP learns what a user means, not just where they click, and publishes verified, typed semantic capabilities with guardrails.
about_excerpt: Turn human workflows into agent-ready WebMCP tools. AutoWebMCP learns what a user means, not just where they click, and publishes verified, typed semantic capabilities with guardrails. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a semantic interface for agents. But what about the enormous number of applications that were never built to expose one? Most browser automation approaches teach agents where to click or how to reproduce a sequence of UI actions. That makes the agent depend on interface mechanics rather than application meaning. We asked a different question: What if a user could teach an application a capability simply by demonstrating how they already perform the task? AutoWebMCP turns those demonstrations into agent-ready WebMCP tools. Teach → Semanticize → Validate → Publish → Agent The key idea is simple: the demonstration is evidence, not the automation. What it does A user performs a normal workflow while the AutoWebMCP Teach Mode extension observes the interaction. AutoWebMCP analyzes that evidence and proposes a typed semantic capability representing what the user intended, rather than exposing individual clicks as agent actions. For example, a human editing several controls in Salesforce can become: update_opportunity_details(opportunity_id, stage, close_date, main_sponsor) The user reviews and confirms the semantic contract. AutoWebMCP then establishes an execution binding, validates it against the live application, and publishes the capability as a WebMCP tool. The resulting pipeline is: Human demonstration → Semantic capability → Execution binding → WebMCP tool → Agent We tested this with two very different applications. SignalBase is a cooperative application. AutoWebMCP can bind a learned capability to an action supplied by the application itself. Salesforce Lightning is the harder case. It was not built for AutoWebMCP, so learned capabilities execute against the application's existing interface through the AutoWebMCP runtime. To an agent, both appear as semantic WebMCP tools with names, descriptions, typed schemas, identity requirements, and safety semantics. In our demo, one natural-language instruction composes three independently taught capabilities: Find a VP-level contact in SignalBase. Search Salesforce for the relevant Opportunity and obtain its exact record identity. Update that Opportunity. The sequence is not hardcoded. The model chooses among the live WebMCP tools using their published descriptions, schemas, and results. How we built it AutoWebMCP has three main parts. Teach Mode is a Chrome extension that captures evidence while a user performs a workflow. It observes the interaction without treating the resulting event sequence as a replay script. Training Studio turns that evidence into a semantic capability. A model proposes the business intent, capability name, description, and typed inputs. The user reviews and confirms that contract before publication. The demonstration alone is not enough to safely execute the capability. AutoWebMCP combines observed evidence with platform, application, and tenant intelligence to help ground concepts such as business meaning, valid value domains, entity identity, tenant-specific vocabulary, execution semantics, and verification behavior. Critically, the semantic contract remains separate from the execution binding . An agent operates on concepts such as stage , close_date , and opportunity_id , while the runtime resolves how those concepts map to the application when the capability executes. We do not persist CSS selectors, XPath expressions, or screen coordinates as the semantic contract. Finally, WebMCP is the publication surface . Confirmed capabilities are compiled into tools with descriptions, typed input schemas, required fields, value domains where known, and supported annotations. For the cross-application demonstration, we also built a small page-side agent harness over the actual WebMCP API. On every step it: reads the current tools from document.modelContext.getTools() gives those descriptions and schemas to the model validates the selected tool and arguments against the live tool set invokes the tool through document.modelContext.executeTool() feeds the structured result back to the model for its next decision There is no separately hardcoded SignalBase-to-Salesforce workflow. The model has to infer the composition from the semantic tools it is given. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem turned out not to be recording browser interactions. It was deciding when an inferred capability is trustworthy enough for an agent to use. A demonstration contains incomplete and sometimes ambiguous evidence. A field label may be tenant-specific. A choice may have a constrained value domain. Two records can have similar names. A successful request does not necessarily mean the intended state was persisted. That pushed AutoWebMCP toward a stronger principle: Search may be fuzzy. Mutation must be exact. Writes therefore require an exact target identity, and execution verifies both the target and the requested outcome. If the runtime cannot establish what happened, it reports uncertainty instead of manufacturing success or blindly repeating a potentially committed mutation. Testing against a live Salesforce org exposed failure modes we would not have found in a controlled demo. Navigation can destroy the browser context waiting for an execution result. Browser extension service workers can disappear between captured events. A mutation can succeed even when its caller never receives the result. Those failures shaped the runtime's guardrails, retry semantics, target-identity checks, and distinction between requested state and verified state. Cross-application composition created another challenge. WebMCP tools belong to documents, while our demo combines a capability taught from SignalBase with capabilities backed by Salesforce. We therefore made publication location explicit and created a control surface where selected capabilities can coexist while still being invoked through the WebMCP API. Accomplishments that we're proud of The biggest accomplishment is that the original idea survived contact with a real enterprise application. We demonstrated the full loop: demonstrate → semanticize → human confirm → bind → live validate → publish → discover → compose → execute → verify The same learning pipeline supports two very different execution strategies: a cooperative application-provided binding in SignalBase and a learned browser execution binding against Salesforce Lightning. We are particularly proud that the agent-facing abstraction is semantic rather than mechanical. The agent sees: update_opportunity_details(...) not: click_button(...) → fill_input(...) → choose_option(...) → click_save(...) We also demonstrated model-driven composition across independently taught capabilities. From one business instruction, the agent selected a SignalBase contact capability, a Salesforce Opportunity search capability, and a Salesforce update capability based on the published WebMCP metadata and prior tool results. The safety behavior became an accomplishment of its own. AutoWebMCP can refuse to mutate an entity it cannot identify, distinguish an attempted change from a verified outcome, stop when a write may already have persisted, and preserve ambiguity rather than silently choosing among multiple candidate records. Those are not theoretical safeguards. Several were added after the corresponding failure happened during live testing. What we learned Our biggest learning is that turning a demonstration into an agent capability is fundamentally different from recording a macro . The interaction trace tells us what happened. It does not, by itself, tell us what the action means. The difficult work lies in extracting a durable semantic contract from imperfect evidence, grounding that contract in the application's concepts and environment, and then resolving it safely when an agent invokes the capability later. We also learned that semantic understanding and execution should remain separate. A stable concept such as close_date should not become synonymous with whatever DOM element happened to represent Close Date during the demonstration. And we learned that verification is part of the capability, not an afterthought. For autonomous systems, "I attempted the action" and "I established that the intended state now exists" are materially different outcomes. This changed how we think about AutoWebMCP. What began as an experiment in automatically generating WebMCP tools increasingly looks like a semantic capability compiler . What's next for AutoWebMCP: Teach an Agent to Fish WebMCP is the first publication target, but the learned semantic capability does not inherently belong to WebMCP. The same architecture could eventually publish a confirmed capability through WebMCP, an external MCP server, an API, or another agent runtime while preserving the semantic
video_transcript_excerpt: What if you could teach existing web applications to become agent ready without programming every tool by hand? For this demo, AutoWebMCP has learned three capabilities across two applications. Signal base can find right contact, Salesforce can search and update opportunity. These are published as typed WebMCP tools, so I can give an agent one business level instruction. With these WebMCPs in place, I can in natural language ask my agent to perform a series of tasks. It first finds the VP in Signal base. It then realizes Salesforce update requires an exact opportunity identity, so it searches for the opportunity before attempting the update. Notice the guardrails. If Salesforce is not in the required state, the tool changes context but reports nothing was updated. A mutation only proceeds against the exact requested record. Finally, the system verifies both the resulting values and the target identity. The agent is working with semantic capabilities, not browser clicks. So, where do these tools come from? A user teaches AutoWebMCP simply by doing the work they already know. I start teach mode and perform the workflow normally. But AutoWebMCP is not recording just a macro. The interaction trace is evidence, not the automation. The interesting part happens next, where all these traces are sent to the studio. AutoWebMCP takes the evidence and tries to understand user's intent. Instead of exposing individual clicks, it proposes one business capability with a semantic description and typed inputs. Application and tenant intelligence help ground that capability in what the application means, what values are valid, and how it can safely execute. The semantic contract remains separate from the execution binding. The user reviews what AutoWebMCP understood, confirms it, and tests the binding against a live application. Only after the save is confirmed is the capability published as a WebMCP tool that an agent can discover and compose with other tools, as you saw in the first act. The user teaches by doing. AutoWebMCP semanticizes the intent. WebMCP makes the resulting capability available to agents. AutoWebMCP, teach an agent to fish.

pitch: A privacy-first virtual fitting room for sensitive-category retail.

 Project Story 

 Inspiration 

 Buying lingerie online creates a contradiction. 

 It is one of the categories where customers most want to understand how something might look on them, yet it is also one of the categories where uploading a personal photo can feel the most sensitive. 

 Most virtual try-on experiences solve one part of the problem: 

 “What might this look like on me?” 

 But after the rendering appears, the shopper still has to decide: 

 Which one do I actually want? 

 We built NUDE Private Fitting Room to explore what virtual try-on could become if privacy and decision-making were treated as part of the product from the beginning. 

 NUDE is a real direct-to-consumer apparel brand, so we did not build the project around a fictional catalog or mock products. We used real NUDE products, real product imagery, real construction details, and a real shopping journey. 

 The goal was simple: 

 Try privately. Compare clearly. Decide with confidence. 

 

 What it does 

 NUDE Private Fitting Room is a privacy-first virtual fitting and decision experience for intimate apparel. 

 A shopper can: 

 
 Browse a curated digital showroom of real NUDE products. 
 Open a product and review detailed construction information. 
 Upload a photo and generate a virtual fitting using Perfect Corp YouCam Virtual Try-On . 
 Save generated fittings locally in My Looks . 
 Compare two or three looks side by side. 
 Create a private comparison card and send it through their own messaging app. 
 Return to the fitting room and manually record Friend's Pick . 
 

 The full journey is: 

 Showroom → Product → Virtual Try-On → My Looks → Compare → Ask a Friend → Friend's Pick 

 Virtual try-on is therefore not the end of the experience. It becomes the visual input for a larger decision process. 

 

 How we built it 

 The application is built with: 

 
 Next.js 15 
 React 19 
 TypeScript 
 Tailwind CSS 
 Zustand 
 Framer Motion 
 IndexedDB 
 Canvas 
 Perfect Corp YouCam Virtual Try-On 
 Vercel 
 

 The virtual fitting flow integrates Perfect Corp's cloth-v4 API. 

 When a shopper starts a fitting, the application uploads the shopper photo and the selected garment reference through Perfect Corp's file flow, creates a cloth-v4 task, polls for completion, and returns the rendered result to the browser. 

 We built the integration with production safeguards including request-size limits, per-IP rate limiting, garment-category validation, API error handling, and fail-closed behavior. 

 If the Perfect Corp API is unavailable, the product does not pretend that an AI fitting was generated. Instead, it clearly presents a labeled side-by-side fallback. 

 We also prepared garment reference assets specifically for virtual try-on. Retail imagery is designed for merchandising, but a VTO system needs a clean garment reference, so supported products use dedicated garment crops rather than treating every storefront image as interchangeable. 

 

 Privacy by design 

 Privacy is especially important in intimate-apparel retail, so we did not want it to exist only as a disclaimer. 

 Before a shopper uploads a photo, the interface explains what happens to it. 

 The shopper photo is sent to Perfect Corp only when a fitting is generated. NUDE's server processes the request in memory and does not persist the uploaded photo. 

 The shopper's fitting-room state and generated looks are stored locally in the browser using IndexedDB. 

 Changing the source photo clears the previous fitting-room state. 

 The same principle shaped Ask a Friend . 

 We deliberately did not build a NUDE social network, friend account system, or voting backend. Instead, the comparison card is composed client-side and shared through the user's own messaging app. 

 The conversation stays where the shopper already talks to someone they trust. 

 Privacy is therefore reflected in the architecture, not only in the copy. 

 

 Building the decision layer 

 One of our biggest product decisions was not to stop at a successful virtual fitting. 

 A rendering may answer whether someone likes a single product, but shopping often involves comparison. 

 So we built My Looks and a two- or three-look comparison interface. 

 Each comparison can combine the visual fitting with real garment construction information such as cup structure, wire, padding, straps, closure, material, available colors, and sizing. 

 From there, Ask a Friend lets the shopper generate an A/B or A/B/C comparison card. 

 The friend does not need a NUDE account or another app. 

 The shopper can then return and record the recommendation as Friend's Pick . 

 This turned the project from a virtual try-on demo into a lightweight decision tool. 

 

 Challenges we faced 

 1. Retail images are not automatically VTO inputs 

 Product photography is optimized to sell a garment, not necessarily to act as a clean AI reference. 

 We had to separate the images we wanted customers to see from the garment references we wanted the VTO model to process. 

 That led us to prepare dedicated garment assets for supported colorways. 

 2. A failed AI result must still be honest 

 Virtual try-on can fail because of pose, source-image quality, garment references, file constraints, or API processing. 

 Instead of hiding those failures, we mapped API states into understandable product messages and built an explicitly labeled fallback. 

 A preview is useful. 

 A preview pretending to be a successful AI render is not. 

 3. Comparison usually creates more infrastructure 

 Once we added "Ask a Friend," the obvious architecture was to build accounts, voting links, friend profiles, and a backend. 

 We chose not to. 

 The comparison card is generated locally, sharing happens through the user's existing communication tools, and the final pick is recorded manually. 

 That made the feature both simpler and more consistent with the privacy thesis. 

 4. Keeping a hackathon project feeling like a real product 

 We wanted the technical integration to remain visible enough for judges to understand, without turning the experience into a developer console. 

 That meant balancing API evidence, privacy disclosures, loading states, product information, and branding while keeping the fitting room calm and usable. 

 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that virtual try-on quality is only part of the consumer problem . 

 After seeing a generated fitting, a shopper still has to remember what they liked, compare alternatives, understand product differences, and sometimes ask someone they trust. 

 The API creates the visual evidence. 

 The product still has to help the shopper make sense of it. 

 We also learned that privacy UX becomes much stronger when it describes a concrete data flow instead of making broad promises. 

 For a sensitive retail experience, the question: 

 “Where does my photo go?” 

 is not a legal footnote. 

 It is part of the user experience. 

 Finally, we learned that graceful failure matters in AI products. Allowing the system to say that something could not be rendered reliably creates more trust than quietly substituting a different result. 

 

 Accomplishments we're proud of 

 During the hackathon we built a complete end-to-end product flow around a real retail catalog: 

 Showroom → Product → Live Perfect Corp VTO → My Looks → Compare → Ask a Friend → Friend'

title: Pocket Change
pitch: Let your agent see everything and spend nothing — WebMCP tools that read your ledger and audit trail, with no route back to move money.
about_excerpt: Let your agent see everything and spend nothing — WebMCP tools that read your ledger and audit trail, with no route back to move money. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The premise: the agent is assumed compromised. Not "the agent might make a mistake" — assumed compromised, the same way you'd design a system if you knew an adversary was already inside it. Every design decision in Pocket Change follows from that one sentence: if you're going to hand an AI agent a wallet, the system has to hold up even when the agent itself is the threat, not just when it's well-behaved. What it does Pocket Change gives an AI agent bounded, revocable spending authority — enough to actually get things done, never enough to do real damage. A person authorises a mandate : a ceiling, a purpose, an expiry. The agent can act only within that mandate. Every payment request passes through a gateway enforcing nine deterministic checks — depth, budget floor, fan-out, per-node budget, cycle detection, conservation of spend, and a hard rail cap — none of which a model can argue its way around, including ours. Every decision (allowed, denied, or escalated to a human) is written to a hash-linked audit log, so the log can prove nothing was altered after the fact — not that it was never rewritten wholesale, but that no entry was quietly edited in place. Payments run through Razorpay in test mode — never real money — while the authority model itself is designed to be real. For this hackathon, the console also exposes six WebMCP tools , so an agent working through the browser can read everything about its own authority — spend status, counterparty history, the audit trail, the shape of an in-progress run, which safety layers are actually enforcing right now — without ever being handed a tool that can move money, mint a token, widen a mandate, or approve a held payment. It can look, and it can propose ( draft_requisition , which mints nothing), but the only path to actually spending still runs through a person clicking a button in the console. How we built it Gateway : a FastAPI service enforcing the nine checks server-side, so no client — including the browser console — can bypass them. Reads are public; writes require the demo token. Capability tokens : Biscuit tokens carry attenuated authority, so a delegated task can only ever have equal or narrower permissions than its parent, never wider. Decomposition/funnel model : complex requests get broken into a tree of smaller tasks, each with its own budget, depth limit, and fan-out cap — the console renders this tree live over SSE. Console frontend : a five-pane live view (via SSE) of an in-progress run, plus frontend/webmcp.js , which registers the six read/propose-only tools with the browser's WebMCP API ( navigator.modelContext.registerTool ), each one calling the same GET routes and /intake endpoint the console itself uses — no separate, more-privileged backend door for agents. Deployment : Cloud Run ( asia-south1 ), --min-instances=1 to avoid a cold-start during judging, --no-cpu-throttling . 424 Python tests and 20 Node tests, including a dedicated adversarial suite trying to get the gateway to approve something it shouldn't. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP spec itself is still moving. Documentation (including Chrome's own developer docs) describes the API as document.modelContext , but the actual shipped implementation in current Chrome exposes it as navigator.modelContext instead — with a separate navigator.modelContextTesting surface ( listTools() , executeTool() ) for verifying registration without a live agent. This meant tools were silently failing to register — no error, just an empty tool list — until we traced it back to a single feature-detection check on the wrong global. Deciding what not to build was harder than building what we did. It would have been easy to add a WebMCP tool for /delegate or /pay — more "impressive" on paper — but that would have meant putting a spendable capability inside a public page. The interesting engineering problem was making the read-only boundary airtight, not working around it. What we learned Emerging browser APIs ship inconsistently even across "the same" browser family — testing against the real, current implementation (not the docs) caught a bug that unit tests alone never would have, since Node has no navigator global to catch the mismatch. A safety boundary is most convincing when it's structural (no route exists) rather than behavioral (a tool declines to). No one has to trust that an agent chose not to spend; there's simply nothing on the other end of the wire that could. What's next for Pocket Change Extending WebMCP coverage as the spec stabilizes — particularly once cross-document tool discovery ( getCrossDocumentScriptToolResult , which we noticed on the navigator.modelContextTesting prototype but didn't use) has clearer semantics.
